dressing-koom, bed-chamber, and bah-room. The windows were long and wide like door; and opened upon a wide balcony. At the present moment, as the afternoon was sultry, all the win- dows were ajar, and the room was penetrated with the delicious summer breeze that was scarcely more than a zephyr, yet sufficient to relieve the air of deadness and oppressiveness.' v The furniture of the boudoir was upholstered in a pale blue satin, in a fine state of preservation. Flowers crowded the vases, looped up the lace window drapery, and filled the basket-frame which took the place of the winter grate. Their perfume was inexpressibly delightful. The Lady Barbara laid aside her bonnet and wrappings, and sat down in an armed chair by one of the windows.
OR, A WAR OF THE HOUSEHOLD.
By the Author of "The Double Life," "The Bailiff's Scheme," &c., &o.
• CHAPTER XXX. A CHANGE OF QUARTERS.

In one of the pleasantest parts of Surrey, and but a few miles distant from the Thames, lies the ancestral home of Lord Champney, known as Champney Mere. The house itself is a grand old mansion, with a magnificent facade, and presents a most imposing appearance. It is flanked by stone terraces, with atone steps, and low, carved balustrades, and it is approached by a wide, lime-shaded avenue at the foot of which is the great gateway, guarded by a picturesque stone lodge. There are stately gardens, fine parks and sunny lawns belonging to Champney Mere, and all these were kept in immaculate order, although Lord Champney had paid the place but flying visits for many years, and although his wife had not been here since the early days of her marriage. The mere, from which the place took its name, lay to the eastward of the house, and in full sight of its long east windows. It was a fine, clear sheet of water, covering about fifty acres and its borders were fringed with pollard willows, whose drooping branches trailed on the water, and cast a host of tremulous shadows.

A host of memories thronged into her mind as she sat there, and held her silent. She had come to Champney Mere a bride, fresh from the marriage altar. These had been her bridal rooms. Sidney had fitted them up for her before her marriage. She remembered that he had chosen the pale blue satin upholstery, be- cause, as he had said, it contrasted so perfectly with her dazzling complexion and hair of pure pale gold. How everything had changed since then! Mrs. Bisset, solicitous for her lady's satisfaction, hastened to say:

"1 nave taken care of these rooms myself, my lady, sinte you were here. The rooms have been kept dark, and the fuiniture hasn't faded. But I suppose your ladyship will fit up your rooms in modern style ?" "I dare say," -said the baroness, carelessly. "Yet I like them as they are. . What is that noise, Mrs. Bisset? Wheels?

Upon that day, in the latter part of June, which Lord Champney had appointed for his return to the Mere with his wife, the place presented a scene of rare festivity and gladness—such as, indeed, it had not witnessed since the baron had brought home his bride, eighteen years before. The day was lovely. Not a stick, stone or leaf marred the cleanliness of the wide avenues and walks or the smooth-shaven lawns. The mere lay in the glad sunlight, within its fringe of encircling willows, like a glittering and gigantic diamond. The hoirse itself wore a festal air. Although the house-steward had had but two days' warning of the home-coming, the plate glass windows glittered like jewels, and were shaded by gay Venetian awnings, fresh from London. A flag fluttered from a staff on the topmostlurret. The entrance doors were open, and the wiffe, great hall and the grand portico outside were all wreathed with flowers and branches of spicy, odorous pines. The tenants of the baron, of whom there were at least thirty, had gathered, with, their families, to do honour to the return of their landlord. The house servants, who had been attached to the Champney family all their lives, had gotten up this impromptu reception of their master, who, they fondly hoped, had come back to the Mere to spend the remainder of his days; and the tenants had joined in with them with hearty accord, for the, baron was one of those persons who are ever considerate of the rights and wishes of ,those inferior to himself in point of wealth and station. At about three o'clock in the afternoon the tenants had assembled on the lawn in gala attire, the house steward moving about among them and doing the honours of the occasion with a beaming expression on his portly, rubicund countenance. "This begins to look like it, Mr. Hodges," he exclaimed, clapping a stout miller familiarly on the shoulder. "We're going to have the old times back again. My lord has done with them heathenish furrin courts, and is going to live at home with my lady like a Christian. You'll see gay doings now, mark my words. Company from London, excursions to abbeys, to the Tema, to where not, and riding and hunting parties, and feasting and jollity--oh 1 it all seems too good to be true 1' "So it do, Mr. Lefties— so it do ! " returned the miller, half growling, half approvingly. "The way I look at it is this: When a nobleman has a handsome propitty, clear an un'cumbered, I take it it's his duty to stay 't home on it, and not go gal- livanting off to heathen counjries, as my lord has done. Why, I hear strange stories of them Ger- mans, and no good of 'ern, except that they are good at drinking beer, which, I take it, is time best thing you can say about 'em. Furriners are heathens, anyhow you take 'em. There 's no dif- ference between 'em, only some eat frogs, and some don't."
The housekeeper went to the front window. "It's the trunks, my lady," she said. "I will order them to be brought up." She hastened to do so.
CHAPTER XXXI. AT CHAMPNEY MERE.

The Lady Barabara went into her dressing-room and lay down upon a couch. What thoughts occu- pied her mind no one could know, but the tears dropped softly on the cushions pillowing her head, and her lips quivered in a mortal grief. An hour later she arose and began her toilet, her maid having arrived in the waggon with the trunks.

"I have tried pleadings and prostestations with Sidney," thought the wife, bitterly, as her toilet progressed, "and all is over between us. Yet I would like to show him that, though he rejects me through jealousy, he must yet admire me. And, Heaven knows' if I cannot have his love, I would like to compel his admiration I" She debated the momentous question of what she should wear. Having settled it at last, she arrayed herself for dinner.

Her dress was simple enough, as it seemed, when she had finished, but it was in exquisite taste and exquisitely becoming. It was of white tulle, over white silk, all puffs and fleecy folds, cut with a graceful train. The white silk corsage was cut low, and the tulle softly veiled the sloping shoulders and the white, rounded arms, enhancing their beauty by the half-pretence of concealment. An elaborate white sash lent its charm to the toilet, and a handful of water lilies from the mere clus- tered at the lady's throat. "Sidney will like me in this," she thought, with a half smile. "Ho always liked to see me in white."

At the dinner hour she descended alone to the dining-hall. Lord Champney was there already, and met her at the door, giving her his arm and leading her to the table. The room was stately, and just now irradiated by the glowing sunset rays. The glitter of silver and crystal, and the soft glimmer of dainty porce- lain upon the snowy damask, made a brilliant centre to the grand old room. The me_al went on, the baron doing his part courteously, and the Lady Barbara exerting her- self to keep up her reputation for wit and bril- liancy. More than once she caught an admiring glance from her husband's eyes, and those inter- cepted glances wete like draughts of wine to a fainting person. The dinner over, Lord Champney gave his wife his arm and conducted her to the drawing-room. "The merry-makers have all gone home," he said. "We are left to ourselves at last. The Mere will seem dull to you after the gaiety of Saltair, and I begin to fear you will be home-sick." "I think not," replied her ladyship, carelessly, "as long as I have books, a piano, needles, and drawing materials. I am a woman of considerable resources, and am never at a lose to entertain my- self."

The house steward was about to reply to this piece of profound wisdom, when the children and young people set up a great shout of joyous wel- come. The carriage was coming! Mr. Lefties retreated to the house' in the main ball of which the servants were drawn up in phalanx, and placed himself at their head with an expression of the severest dignity on his portly face.
The carriage had been sent to the station to meet the travellers, who had come on from Lou- don, having left Saltair on the previous day, and having spent the night in town, stopping at a hotel, _

'You are foitunate," said the baron, moving restlessly back and forth. "Ada Gower is in town, selecting her wedding finery, and you and I, 13).rbara, are two loveless persons shut up to- gether here, caring nothing for each other, and about to be moped to death. I declare I half envied Willard Ames and Ada :this morning, as they sat together at Mrs. Estways, planning their happy future. I wonder if Ames's life will turn out like mine!'
Presently the carriage approached the great gates, which swung open, amid shouts and cries of welcome, and wheeled slowly up the avenue.

Flowers, singly and in bouquets, were showered upon the new-comers, and rained into the open carriage, and the Lady Barbara bowed and smiled right and left, and Lord Champney, pale still from illness and mental pain, took off his hat and waved it in smiling, courteous acknowledgment of the hearty greetings. "How happy they are !" said little Mrs. Hodges, the miller's wife, discontentedly. See the white plume on tne bonnet flutter. It's plain that my lord dotes on my lady, and that she has everything that heart can wish for, and not a care in the world. What a difference there is between rich and poor and high and low, to be sure 1 It's the way of the world, I suppose." The carriage bowled on, its occupants still bow- ing and smiling. What a farce it all was to the baron and the Lady Barbara 1 They happy, and without a care? They had not interchanged a word since they had left Saltair Manor Oh the previous day. They had oc- cupied different apartments at the London hotel, and were farther apart at this moment in heart than if their bodies were at the opposite poles. The carriage drew up at the portico, and Lord Champney alighted and gave his hand to the Lady Barbara. The two ascended the steps together. A moment was given in the hall to greetings of old f, mily servants, and then the noble couple nassed into the drawing-room. Lefties and the hoasekeeper followed.

" linpos•dble ! " said Lady Champney. " Wil- lard Ames will commence his marrieddife with an implicit trust in his wife." "And so I began mine !" returned the baron, his lips curling. "But he who pins his trust to a woman's constancy writes is name on the sand, where the next wave will kweep it away. He had better rot marry ; but, marrying, he should provide his wife with a duenna!" Lady Barbara's face glowed redly, but she did not reply. She was beginning to grow patient with her husband's weakness.

"Shall I sing to you, Sidney?" she asked. "If you will. It is years since I heard your voice in song 1" The wife sat down at the grand piano, and played and sang some of the songs she had sung in that room years before, and her tears dropped silently on the keys, while her voice thrilled through some of the quaint old ballads Lord Champney loved. When she arose and returned to her seat, she saw that he was weeping silently, his eye shaded by his hand. With a sudden impulse she went to him, and laid her hand on his forehead.
He trembled under her touch. He looked up at her with a sudden and passionate devotion. "0, Barbara !" he exclaimed, with a moaning cry. "If I could only wake up and find it all a hideous dream !"

" Leffles," said his lordship, with a ghastly smile, "I have been ill, as you see. lam even now fitter to be in bed that out of it. Let the tenants be properly entertained with cakes and ale, and what- ever else they want. Let them have a good time, and a dance on the lawn, if they like. And say to them that Lady Champney and I properly appreciate their cordial and kindly reception, and shall hope to see them all here at a latter period." Lefties bowed, and withdrew on his errand.

"If it only Were !" sighed the wife. "But the past can never come back, Sidney. We can never be more to each other than strangers. How vividly this couiing back to the Mere bangs it all back--our happy early married days. Ah • She started back abruptly, as if a serpent had bitten her.
"What is it, Barbara ? " cried the baron, in alarm. _
The housekeeper, a p-riM-litile-Woman in a black silk gown, brought herself under the Lady Barbara's uotice.

She faced him, pale, stern, and anxious. Then she slowly retreated to the further window, shiver- ing as with an ague. "Never mind me, Sidney," she answered, in an altered voice, and without an indication of feeling. "Only let me alone. There should be no sentiment between us."

" by, Mrs. Bisset," said her ladyship, extend- ing her hand with a smile. "You are still house- keeper, as you were eighteen years ago. How little you have changed.' "And I may say the same to yourself, my lady," replied Mrs. Bisset, much flattered. "You are looking as young and fair as you did when you came here a bride. And handsomer, my lady! " she added, enthusiastically. "You look like a queer); Ah, it's easy to see that you are happy." The Lady Barbara's fair face shadowed a little. She toyed with her glove fastenings, bending her head so that her countenance might not be seen. " Yes, Bisset," said Lord Charnpney, with an odd laugh, "her ladyship's very happy. And so am I. You haven't complimented me on my bright looks. But about the rooms. Are they ready ?" The housekeeper looked puzzled as she responded, with a courtesy : " Yes, my lord, but I thought Leffles must have made some mistake. He said your lordship ordered the east rooms to be got ready for my lady, and ordered for your own use a suite in the west wing. And though I thought Ltffles must have misunder- stood the letter, the rooms are all ready—" "Quite right," interposed the baron, cutting her explanations short. "There was no mistake. I know the way to my old rooms, and shall not need attend wee to them. Bisset, you may show Lady Champney to her own apartments, and be kind enough to attend upon her until the arrival of her maid, who will be here with the luggage soon." As he concluded, he went out hastily, and sought out his own apartments. • There was a compassionate look in the house- keeper's eyes that touched the pride of the wrong- fully suspected wife. " You may lead the way upstairs, Mrs. Bisset," she said calmly, yet with burning cheeks. "I will go to my rooms." Mrs. Bisset obeyed. _ _ _
Lord Champney regarded her in amazement. She seemed suddenly to have withdrawn herself far from him.
At the same moment the sight that had so dis- turbed the baroness appeared again, blanching her cheek.
It was only the figure of a man sauntering under the polla.rd willows by the mere. But the man was her enemy—Colonel Effingham!
CHAPTER XXXII. COMING TO AN UNDERSTANDING.

- i There was something n the appears...Jos e Felix Warner that impressed the Narrs str vly and unpleasantly, as he strode into the little parlour of their hired cottage at Chiswick, Pliter his visit to the chamber of the imprisoned Dora. Jack Narr was sitting alone in the dark by the open window, almost within view of the young Squire Weir, who remained perched in the tree out- side Dora's window, but totally oblivious of the young man's proximity. He arose as Warner and Mrs. Narr entered, the latter bearing a light, and hastily shut down the window, coming forward with a beaming face and unsteady gait. Despite her uneasiness in regard to her guest, Mrs. Narr scrutinised her husband sharply, and demanded, as she sat down the candle: "Have you been out of the house since Mr. Warner and I went upstairs ?" Jack's flushed face grew redder. He answered, huskily: "Only round the corner for the candles and meat —that's all."

" Well, I should tbinl.: you'd been drinking, if I didn't know you haven't any money," said Mrs. Narr. "And I believe you have, too," she added. "Needn't say nothing. You drink, too," said Jack, sulkily; the truth being that he had regaled himself on his favourite beverage out of the money with which Dora had brihod him-
The "east rooms" were situated directly over the drawing-room, and overlooked the mere. They consisted of three or four apartments, con- nected by sliding doors, and comprising boudoir.
KAMINER, NOVEMBER" 23g 1696
Zrart-Siiiired-at the insinuation, and turned her attention to Warner, who was still standing, and who was regarding the couple with a gaze that both felt to be uncomfortable.

"Is there anything wrong, Mr. Warner ?" de- manded Mrs. Narr, uneasily. "Anything up ?" asked Narr, jauntily, and with a certain air of consequence due to his recent libation. "Girl horty and set up?" "She utterly refused my proi osals," said War- ner, in a tone of ill-humour. She rejected all my 'overtures with indignatiop." "She did ?" ejaculated Narr, in a jaunty sort of surprise. " Strange ! You ought to have made your proposals such ,as she could listen to them. Miss Dora aint one to tamely submit to an insult. Old saying's a true one: 'Blood will tell—'"

" Jack !" cried his wife, warningly, "you have been drinking. Hush up !" "Hush up yourself, retorted Narr, with a brave assumption of marital authority. "A wo- man's place is to hush up. Man's privilege is to talk, and I'm going to exercise the privilege—banged if I don't. You are always telling me to shut up, just as if I wasn't head of the family. Mr. Warner," he added, defiantly, turning to his guest, "I have said it, and I repeat it, and I don't know as it'll hurt anybody. if 1 say it the third time. 'Blood will tell.' That girl upstairs is the equal of anybody, if I do say it !"

- Warner pushed a chair into the gloomy space beyond the circle of light and sat down. Mrs. Narr whispered a hasty warning to her husband to be more discreet, and Warner caught her concluding words, "penal servitude for life 1" Narr seemed sobered a little, and sat down also. " It is time we understood each other thoroughly," said Warner, after a pause, watching the two with furtive keenness. "I have this evening made to Dora a proposal of marriage. I have offered to make her my wife, and to take her to Champney Mere and introduce her to my noble kinsman; but •she has refused me 1"

"She may think better of her refusal," said Mrs. Narr, cautiously. "She will not. She cannot pardon the advan- tage I took of her changed and desolate con- diticu me her that other proposal. She has all tha fine and haughty instinct of her ra—of a true woman, and she will never willingly marry me ! "
"You will give her up, then ? " asked Mrs. Narr.
"Wish he would," said Jack Narr, jauntily. "Know how to make a big pile of money out of her ! Girl 's a fortune to us 1"

"I will not give her up," said Mr. Warner, pay- ing no heed to Narr. "She shall be mine—my wife —whether she will or no! You, Mrs. Narr, must bring the necessary screws to bear, and compel her to accept me ! " There was a tone of authority in Warner's voice that struck the woman with a vague sense of anx- iety and increased uneasiness. "I'll see what I can do," she said. Of course we will be well paid ?" "I will recompense you according to your de- serts," returned Warner, coolly. "Before we go any further, we may as well understand each other. I have already a claim on your cupidity, but, from a chance word of Narr's I see that you have con- sidered the possibility of making a larger specula- tion out of another than me. Nov mark me. I am the only safe person for you to deal with, and it is for your interest to be true to me. Under- stand ?"

"What do you mean 7" demanded Mrs. Narr. "I mean that I can send ou both to penal servi- tude for life !" replied Warner, coolly. Narr half bounded from his chair. Mrs. Narr grew ghastly pale, and her features hardened themselves to the likeness of stone. "You have said so much, Mr. Warner," she said,. in a strange voice, "that you'd better go on!"
There was a desperate gleam in her eyes that enforced the suggestion. Warner eyed the startled pair with the air of a master.

"You are anxious to have me unbosom myself, eh ?" he asked. "Very well. This girl upstairs—. this slender, graceful, dainty young creature, known as Dora Chessom—is not your daughter ?" Mrs. Di arr uttered a strange ejaculation—half terror, half menace.
"Not our daughter " exclaimed Narr, half sobered. "Who told you 2" -

Mrs. Narr put up her hand feebly. The shock of Warner's announcement seemed almost to para- lyze her. "What do you mean, Mr. Warner ?" she asked, huskily, mechanically using the same words she had used before.
"I mean," responded \Varner, "that the girl upstairs is not of your blood, but that she is, in reality, Barbara, the only chila and heiress of Lord Champney of Champuey Mere."

Narr uttered a shrill cry. "it is not so l" she gasped. "It is so I" asserted Warner, raising his voice. "Let me tell you the story, and revive your memory. Twenty years ago, you, Catherine Narr, were a wait- ing maid, or nurse, in the family of Sir Graham Gallagher—then plain Doctor Gallagher—in Lon- don. You left his service to marry the tenant of a small dairy farm. in Surrey. About three years later—just seventeen years ago—you had a child born, a daughter—" _ _

" Yes, Dora I" 'whispered Mrs. Narr, her haggard black eyes fixed in a burning gaze on Warner. "Not Dora! At about the same time Lady Champney gave birth to a daughter. Doctor Gal- lagher was her ladyship's attendant. For weeks thereafter her ladyship was too ill even to hear the presence of the child, and by the advice of the doctor, your former employer, the child was taken to you and left in your charge." That's all so," muttered Narr—" Only the girl wasn't Miss Dora."
A slow, strange smile curled Warner's lips.

"Shall I go " he asked, looking from one to the other of the blanched faces and trembling fig- ures. "Shall I recall the forgery committed by idle, drunken, dissolute Jack Narr ? Shall I tell you how, to avoid the consequences of his crime and to enjoy its fruits, a flight was determined on? Shall I recall to you how, a day or two before your flight, your child—your own offspring—was taken ill with some infantile disease and died? You remember all this?"
Catherine Narr looked at Warner dumbly, a haggard fear staring from her eyes. "It wasn't our child that died," she whispered, "It was the other." _

"it was your child. The fact is patent. Look at your husbandts face woman. Is not the truth plainly written there?" Mrs. Narr slowly turned her head and looted at her husband. He was completely sobered, and was cowering in his chair, the picture of an object and absolute terror. "You see l" said Warner. "That man's looks declare his guilt. Do you still intend to brave out your denial of the girl's identity? Now listen to me. I know that your child was buried as your nursling, and that when you fled from the Surrey farm you took the little heiress with you as your own child, probably with the idea that, at some future period you might reap a handsome sum by restoring her to her parents. Afterward, finding the child an encumbrance, and not daring to open negotiations with Lady Champney, and his lord- ship having gone abroad, you sold the little child to a rich Sussex squire, whose wife bad taken a fancy to the little one. With the money thus ob- tained, you two went to America, from which you have recently returned, to take up the game where you left it. Deny this if you can." The Narrs made no attempt to deny it. Pale and stupified, they sat like criminals awaiting sen- tence. Even the woman's bravado had forsaken her now.

"You came back," said Warner, "and separat- ing at Chester, where you had friends, I presume, Mrs. Narr went on alone to Ch.essom Grange as a widow, expecting to receive a large sum of hush- money from the old squire, who idolized his dar- ling. The squire's death, and his son's avario, put a new aspect on the face of affairs. You took the girl and came on to London, rejoicing in her beauty, and resolved to make money out of her in some way. You fancied you had in her a fortune. You thought you would make her support you by teaching. You thought to make money by selling her to me. And, at times, you have thought of revealing the secret to Lord and Lady Charnpney, having first made a bargain with them for your own safety and a liberal sum of money. You see how much I know, and how well I read you." Narr groaned heavily. ills wife breathed hr rd, and clenched her hands nervously and spasmodi- cally. "Now let me show you just where you are,". said the triumphant Warner. " That old forgery business is still hanging over you, Jock N.,rr. I've been to your old Su, rev farm to-day, ;001 searchA out the whole matter. The map whose name ca forged has got the idea that, you Ir,ve ronrned to the country, and has set a detective on y;air track. This detective is like a blood-hound circl ig on your trail, and at every lessening circle he drcvs nearer to you. Jack Narr, you are on the brink of arrest

Mr. John O'Leary is a unique Personality among Irish politicians. He came back to Dublin, after his long banishment, with some French tastes and with all the generous simplicity of a youth, quite unsoured by his long exile. Nothing could be further removed from the vulgar conception of the Irish patriot than this gentle, refined Fenian. His politics are, perhaps,not exactly practical. but that is no bar to the affectionate regard in which he is held by many who belong to a later political gener- ation, and who cannot see their way to'adopt his uncompromising attitude. One of his friends has sketched him eagerly leaning forward, with eyes ablaze,and exclaiming," I'd lead an attack myself," That is John O'Leary ; but where is the, Saxon who ever chatted with him over a cup of cafe noir after the five o'clock meal who did not vow that it was a delightful experience?

Miss Mildred Beresford Hope was a devotee of dogs. But it seems a pity to enshrine in last wills and testaments those lighter sentiments and wishes which, spoken by word of mouth, surviving rela- tives would be certain to respect. Miss Hope, how- ever, besides leaving to d friend the "locket con- taining the hair of her dog Quiz," has bequeathed to her brother Philip (till lately proprietor of the "Saturday Review ") £lOO to keep the said dog's grave green at Bedgebury, with its monument " whole and undestroyed." A leisurely relative could easily have been trusted with these little commissions, one would suppose—or a trustworthy uncle, for instance, such as Miss Hope possessed, in the Marquis of Salisbury !

The rumour that the.Uovernment are proposing to deal with the Sugar question is now confirmed by an official announcement that a Commission of Inquiry is to be at once appointed to inquire into the condition of the sugar industry, and the semi- official statement which is added, to the effect that the Commission will be instructed to report within a month. The significant point of this is that the Government will then have a report,in their hands in ample time to promote legislation based upon it during the coming session. The session will not be dull if a battle for Free Trade is added to the battle for the schools.

The narrowness of some of the Anglican clergy is proverbial, but seldom has there arisen a more marked instance than is to be found in a case which has just been before Chancellor Dibdin. A Mr. Moody lately lost his wife, and be bad a monument prepared for erection over her grave in a church- yard of North Devon. At the last moment the in- cumbent, the Rev. Mr. Germon, objected to a line in the inscription which said of the deceased that she was "born again at Barnet 21st of June, 1863." For this be refused to allow the monument to be erected. The Bishop was applied to, and ultimately the Chancellor held a special cot rt to determine whether the words were admissible. The incum- bent's legal adviser argued the case, the point of the objection being that the words were intended to exclude or contradict the idea of baptism being a part of or essential to being "born again." The Chancellor, however, held that the words must stand; and he quoted the opinions of the late Arch- bishop Sumner and the present Bishop of Exeter to show that the words objected to did not convey or suggest erroneous teaching. He therefore granted a faculty for the erection of the monument, and read the parson a lecture upon the desirableness of consulting as far as possible the feelings of parish- iooers in matters of this kind.

• There is a growing feeling among Irish politicians of the more liberal stamp both in this country and in Ireland of the necessity of maintaining an ac- tive policy in Parliament. It is seen in the prompt response from all parts of Ireland to a recent sug- gestion of a Tipperary priest that an independent Parliamentary fund should be organised for the purpose of maintaining at Westminster those mem- bers of the Irish Parliamentary party who are per- sonal supporters of Mr. T. M. Healy. and who have hitherto been dependent on the Parliamentary fund of the party. Up to to;day,l hear, some six hun- dred pounds has been subscribed,in amounts rising from ös. upwards; and the movement is being taken up in London as well as in Dublin. This movement is to many a revelation of the extent of Mr. Pealy's following in Ireland,especially as many of the subscribers are men who have not hitherto been identified with the party divisions. Mr.ll‘ealy is as desirous of keeping in touch with the English Liberal party as Mr. Dillon himself. A competition in Parliamentary zeal between Dillonites and Healy- ites will probably stimulate both sections to better attendance at Westminster, and thus there is promise of plenty of interest in the forthcoming sessian.

Three of the series of the interesting exhibitions, which Mr. Chamberlain has been the means of bringing together at the rooms of the London Chamber of Commerce, with the view of illustrat- ing the character of the foreign competition which British manufacturers have to meet in the colonies have now come to an end, and are beginning a long provincial tour, such as I suggested should be un- dertaken when the first of the series opened. Beginning at Liverpool, the tour will proceed through all the large industrial centres, and it will be seen, that we are beaten, not so much by the de- fects of our working men's part in British produc- tion, as by the shortcomings of the managers or employers of our great industries. A comparison of the way in which Continental goods and British goods are made up for the market will show this at a glance. It is quite true that, in other respects the low and sweating rate of wages, and the long hours of work, on the Continent, account for much of the underselling by foreign producers, or for the production of cheap rubbish. But it is better to leave the cheap rnbbish to the foreigner than to de- grade the condition of the English artisan.l

----- The statement that some sensational correspon- dence between Lord Rosebery Rnd Sir W.Harcourt is about to be published is generally discredited. It is not believed that there is any important corres- pondence in existence,and even if there is,it would he repugnant to all the traditional conventionali- ties of English public life to publish it at the pre- sent juncture. It is needless to say that Lord Rose- bery is the last man to be suspected of contemplat- ing any breach of the unwritten laws which regu- late the confidential relations of public men.

There is some satisfaction amongst advanced Liberals that the resolutions to be submitted to the committee of the National Liberal Federation at Liverpool are not more aggr4.,siv and definite. It is stated that both on the subject of Armenia and e of education there is a very general desire amongst the Liberal rank and file for 0.3 formulation of some definite demands. It is a matter of dicussion whether these shou:d come from the leaders of the party or from the Federation, and the answer is almost invariably, " From the Federation." As a matter of party tactics it is admitted that it is the duty of the Opposition " to oppose," and that the leaders of the Opposition in Parliament are wise to confine theniselves to that function. But the men who are attempting to organise and educate the electorate in the constituencies in preparation for the next appeal to the country affirm the necessity of a united and affirmative policy, and they think that the Federation might well give them this, and could do it without embarrassing in any way the Parliamentary Opposition.

It is probable that the split in the Conservative ranks over questions ot South African policy will show itself in the House of 'Commons early next session. It is Stated to be the intention of the malcontents to raise a discussion on Mr Chamber- lain's action in regard to South African affairs either on the Address or the moion for the re-appointment of the Select Committee. In all probability they wilt directly oppose the reappointment of the Com- mittee. The dissatisfaction is a great deal more widespread thaq is generally understood, and it is certainly by no means confined to the few members who have hitherto sided openly with Mr. Maclean. It is now pretty evident that the inquiry will he of as thorough and searching a character as the Liberals on the Committee, at all events, can make it. Quite apart, too, from the merits of the Transvaal question, there will be no reluctance in certain quarters to have a dig at Mr. Chamberlain personally. h will not he long, probably, before we shall hear something about the now obvious failure of his attempt to lure the colonies into an Imperial zollverein. Mr. Chamberlain himself has frankly recognised that he went too far in the matter,, hut no confession on his part will prevent his critics from making things as unpleasant as they can for the Colonial Secretary.

11.-rr's shrill wail rang through the room, and the man fell on his knees, pleading for protection and mercy at the hand of Warner. "Save me!" 111 pleaded. "Save me. I Will devote my life to you. Oh, if hadn't come back to England Save me, Mr. Warner, and I will be your slave." "I will see," said Warner, calmly. "I can save you, and perhaps I will. Mrs. Narr, you have laid yourself open to a life-long punishment on the charge of kidnapping Lord Champney's child, and of substituting for it your own dead off- spring—"

"Yu can't prove that Dora is the Champney child," interposed Mrs. Narr, flushing suddenly through the pallor of her despair. "I can prove it. Sir Graham Gallagher, the physician, and Lord Champney, the father, as well as the nurse who attended Lady Champney, can all swear to the fact that on the arm of the baby heiress was a birth-mark—a scarlet, irregular cross, of peculiar shape and vividness. That cross I have seen to-night upon the arm of Dora Chessom."
Mrs. Narr was staggered. The -sullen flush faded flom her face.
A pause followed, during which the branches of the tree against the window brushed the panes as if the were in violent agitation. The occupants of the parlom neither heard or heeded the sound.
"What are you going to do with us 2" asked Mrs. Narr, at last, in a stifled voice.

"That depends upon yourself," was the response. "How ? Will you give us a chance yet ?" "Yes. This girl stands between me and one of the fairest inheritances in England. I love her madly. If I marry her this week, she will bring me immediately all the grandeurs and glories I should otherwise be compelled to wait years for, if I got them at all, now that she is in my way, for Lord Champney would bestow upon his daughter a princely dowry. I am tired of being the humble secretary—the poor relation—the hanger-on of a great man. I want to be rich on my own account, with estates and rent-rolls and gervants and honours. And all these the Lady Barbara Champ- ney upstairs—the young Lady Barbara—can bring me. Now I'll make a compact with you. Make the girl marry. me, and I'll not only protect you both from the law, but will settle on you the sum of five hundred pounds a year. Jack Narr immediately ascended from the depths of despair to the heights of hope and bliss. Mrs. Narr's gloom lightened a little. " How are we to force her to marry you, Mr. Warner?" she asked.

" How ? Why, she believes you to be her own parents. Shut her up in the cellar, if need be, to break her spirit. Feed her on bread ana water. Try oppression and cruelty. Make her fear you. And if she she hold out still, there are drugs, I have heard, which paralyse a person's will, and render them as submissive and pliable and gentle as a wax image. I'll try them, if other means fail. What do you say? Are you willing to work for me, heart and soul ?" The Narrs assented with feverish haste. The way out of their peril seemed to them delightfully easy. __

"We will obey you, Mr. Warner," said Mrs. Narr, humbly enough. "We are willing to do in everything as you say. And, in return, you will protect us 7" "Yes, I promise it. And when the girl becomes ray wife, and I take her to her parents, and cause them to acknowledge hr, then I will pay you the handsome reward I have promised—five hundred pounds down, and the same sum yearly, as long as you live." Mrs. Narr's haggard eyes began to glow with re- viving hope and cupidity. Warner arose and walked slowly to and fro the room, giving his instructions as he proceeded. Finally, as he became thoughtful, Narr asked, tremblingly: "Are we to stay here in the Black Cottage, Mr. Warner? Won't the detective find me here 7"
"He will if you stay. I 'ye got a place in my mind's eye for you to go to. You must abandon the name of Narr and begin anew. Hark! What's that?"
- He halted, listening, as again the branches of tht tree swept the window pane. The next moment, with a wild look, he bounded to the door and sprang out on the porch.
The Narrs flew-aftei They were just in time to see Dora dropping from the lowest branch of the tree into the arras ot the young Squire Weir. (To be continued.)

The abuse warrants a vigor- ous protest from those whose principles prompt them to gain a livelihood by fair trading and hot by selling worthless substitutes for or imitations of, genuine articles of repute. Latterly a preparation known as " Syrup of Figs," manufactured by a scientific process known only to the California Fig Syrup Company, LISS been receives' with unqualified favour. This successful remedy—at once so pl&tsant and so beneficial—is hp- mediately imitated in name, and substitutes are offered in order to profit by the reputation gained by the Cali- fornia Fig Syrup Company; unscrupulous traders con- coct imitations and substitutes in which the world "Figs "is made to play the principal part ; everywhere, in fact, something or other is offered to intending purchasers as "just as good," or" the same thing "as the original California Syrup Figs. div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.

MY DEAR NELLIE, , In the fashions for young folks there really seems quite an epidemic of scarlet cloth about. I have seen many capes, cloaks, and even whole costumes of bright red, and very becoming they look. Some Suitable for little girls of ages varying from fiVe to 11 years might be in thick beaver or zibelline cloth, cheviot, serge or any of the warmer materials. A garment intended for quite a little girl from four to eight years of ,age is very easily made; the paletot being cut in three parts only, back and two fronts, and set on a square yoke of astrachan or caracul, slightly pointed at back and front. The box-pleats must be well wrapped, and taped on the inside nearly to the bottom to keep them in place; and if a thin cloth., accssitating a lining, this must be cut out with the material, and both pleated together. The sleeves are in a modified gigot shape, pleated on the shoulder, with neat turn-down collar and gauntlet Cuffs .are, of. astrachan. The hat may be of felt matching the cloth, bound with velvet', and trimmed with a twist of velvet round the crown, and small bow with three quills at the side. i •

A becoming dress for a young lady for attending parties should be made of a fanciful material, and made with a box-pleat down the centre of the front, and is buttoned with &double row of velvet buttons, the sleeves are wrinkled to the wrist, and velvet buttons again put in their appearance in the front of the skirt.

A black astrachan coat has a vest and inner collar of ermine, and this is lined through with rich white satin. Many people do not care to wear fur coats, but are glad of the warmth of a deep collarette or small cape of fur, and some exceptionally pretty ones have been designed in this style.

A very nice coat in black cloth needs to be very well-cut, and finished with the new tabbed collar. The hat worn with this is of black velvet trimmed with black ostrich plumes and a steel ornament. 4 can be designed in any colour. A very smart coat is of bright red cheviot serge matching the shirt, worn with a plain cream flannel shirt and exhibiting the very latest scarf which should be of black satin, made in one with the neckband, that hooks at the back, lined with silk, and very , slightly wadded down the front to make it set nicely. ' • The white boat-shaped felt is far less seen than when early October was with us. King Fog laid his grimy fingers upon its snowy serenity, and Jo! its charms had gone never to return. Its red-toned rival, with a cluster of black toque feathers and a band of black satin ribbon, has ousted it from service, and its place is not likely to know it again this winter.

A very elegant bat with a fancy brim Of moss. green velvet, and a high crown, which is covered with rich satin brocade. A bow of green velvet appears in front, with a handsonee paste button in the centre, and above this there are white ostrich tips, which curl over towards the front. Rosettes of ribbon appear under the brim on either side, and there are black velvet strings to tie under the chin. -

--- --- The latest idea of Pari3 is to drape the skirts very slightly on the hips with two or three small folds. This seems to indicate an inclination to bring draped skirts into fashion again, but as the same sort of thing was attempted once before, soon after the umbrella skirt came into fashion, without much success, we may still hope to have the pleasure of wearing plain skirts for some time to come. A charming little cape in sealskin is edged with a flounce of chinchilla, which also forms a deep roll collar,- and this dainty garment is worn with a chinchilla muff. The same idea might be . carried out in black velours and chinchilla, or the fluted frill might be of mink. A very elegant little coat, with two gored Watteau pleats hanging from the shoulders at the back, has a flouuce of mink round the bottom, and fluted epaulettes of the same fur on the shoulders. A full roll collar and flat cuffs complete this smart model.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The Prince of Wale., according to presentAarrange- ments will leave Elieland early in the Sprirg for the Riviera, but it is probable that his Royal Highness will not enjoy so long a holiday as he did this year for, in view of the Queen's sextennial commemoration, there are countless matters to be put in order, which must command his personal attention. When the official programme of the rejoicinga is pub- lished next year, it will be found that in every way possible, Her Majesty has been relieved of oneroas du- ties. The Queen is so anxious to. give Pleasure to her people, and her relatives, that she would try and under- take things well nigh impracticable, and it is this reso- lute desire to act up to her convictions which hinders the perfect accord just now between the Soverign and officialism. The splendid reign of the Queen has made the edi`or of a queer little women's paper in America come to the conclusion, that one of cur sex would prove an equally good President of the United States, in 1901! There is, however, one item the editor (a woman of course) over- looks, viz : that Her Majesty has been trained in state- craft all her life, a thing to which no woman in the United States can lay claim. It is understood that Her Majesty has settled the Bal- moral domain so that it will pass with the Crown, being desirous that the place should tecome the Scotch resi- dence of all future Sovereigns. Balmoral was bought by Prince Albert from the late Lord Fife's trustees for £31,500, but the castle has been over and over again en- larged with a view to its affording adequate accommoda- tion for any Court. Nothing could exceed the length to which the prin- cipal American papers have lately- gone, to" cover "the Blenheim entertainments. Half-a-dozen special corres- pondents and as many women" fashion and society specials,"2 accompanied bv the artists, were installed at Woodstock, and one New York paper arranged to have an entire page of reports cabled to it every day during the festivities. That the magnificent ball could not take place was of course a great disappointment, but on the whole, the new American Duchess, with her many dollars, has.scored a brilliant success in the social world. _ _ _ .

- Speaking of balls, when one is given at the Court of the German Emperor, all the rooms are perfumed by means of a specially prepared scent, which is poured upon red hot iron plates.—These are carried about the apartments *before the guests le.gin to arrive. All the rooms are then brilliantly lighted up, the scent of amber fills the warm air, the soldiers in parade uniform, and the lacqueye in gala, are at their posts, and the scenery of the coming festivity is complete. The rage for scented violets seems to increase every year. and since the visit of the Empress of Russia they appear everywhere and with every colour. At a concert the other afternoon I espied a tall, graceful woman, not too tall—the women of the moment are too tall, they are just a little alarming—wearing a red felt trimmed with red ribbon and an erection of market bunches of purple and white violets at one side. Another pretty girl, sitting just in front of me, had donned a white felt bat, trimmed with black glace ribbon,and huge bunches of shaded violets at the left side as well as beneath the brim behind. The scent from them was delicious. There is no doubt that Russian leaders of fashion are much disappointed at the plain dressing of their Im- perial mistress, who Li certainly not ambitious of earn- ing the reputation of being" the most splendidly dressed woman its Europe." This is neither understood nor ap- preciated by Russian ladies of fashions and the circum- stance is the more noticed, as the Dowager Empress fur- nished a strong contrast in her halcyon days, being con- sidered the best dressed woman at Court. With regard to sleeves one of our leading London dressmakers was telling me the other day that she had had more trouble with her clientele since the introduc- tion of smaller specimens, than it was possible to des- cribe. It mattered not, she went on to say, how elabor- ately the bodice was otherwise trimmed, the cry was always the same "It looks mean"—ln one instance she merely took out the existing sleeves, and replaced them by others of larger dimensions, and the result, so far as her customer was concerned, was an overwhelming suc- cess. It seems then, as if we are not even vet prepared to part with our huge sleeves, without one final stsuggle. The best built skirts are decidedly narrower than we have had them during the past few months, but at present no one need be anxious, or meditate" altera- tions." Still, the day of narrow skirts will arrive again is a fact that should be taken into consideration, by those of as who do not revel in many naw gowns in the course of the year. It is to be hoped, however, that we shall have the.good sense (leaving out the question ef decency) to stop short of the skin-tight models we in- dulged in some years ago. Gentlemen, with an income of £39 or £4O a year, who would gladly keep out of the industrial market if they could live with any decency in a country cottage, and obthin additional comforts for themselves by their garden produce, will be glad to know that on the sug- gestion of Miss Campbell Smith one or two wealthy ladies of title are taking the matter up. Miss Smith her- self, is doing most useful work in providing homes for women where they can live in refinement and comfort on a small income. In Gloucestershire, one of her ten- ants has a tiny furnished cottage with two rooms,a little scullery, and a pretty garden, for £l2 a year, and as the rent of the cottage is under £3 it will be seen that Miss Smith places her enterorise on a sound commercial basis. The motor-cars, unless one is distinctly fond of the odour of oil,fare rather things to be avoided at present. I have only, so far, had the misfortune to come very near them once, and that was on the celebrated 14th day of Ws month, but my one impression of the "start," was " oil "and " ugliness." 'rho old fashioned omni- bus dragged along in the usual way may not ue the most luxurious conveyance in the world, but at any rate it is preferable to the motor car of the moment. Apropos, it is annually noticeable in the autumn that omnibusses, which in the hot weather seat six or seven with a merely sardine squeeze, become as winter draws DO, exceedingly uncomfortable for the first four of the six, who are wedged to their seats by the last two. The explanation of this probably is that folks wear more clothes, and overcoats in winter, and consequeetly take up more room, and not, as a truly scientific person sug- gested recently, that omnibusses obey the univeral law of nature of expanding in heat and contracting in cold! It is well-known that some children require more sleep than others and it is as well to extend to those who are usually least willing to get pp in the morning any little indulgence which does not unreasonably interfere with the routine of the day, ll'here is also little doubt grown up people may, if circumstances permit, claim the same con-ideration with no less advantage, both physically and mentally. Dr. Talcott,the superintendent of a New York asylum, and who is said to ,be one of the most eminent specialists in the world, on insanity, has lately been adding his testimony to the theory that early rising is a most prolific cause of the disease. In support of this assertion Dr. Talcott points out the higher percentage of lunacy in the country districts where most people are early risers. He says "the early morning Lours, when everything is still are peculiarly fitted for sleep, and it is a gross violation of all the laws of nature to tear huitnan brains out of the sound rest they enjoy at this time." Probably the vast majority of us find little difficulty in agreeing with this opinion, sleep' is like wealth and everything else, many could do better with a little more. and others would be equally as well with perhaps a little less. There is not much that carries conviction in the early rising lunacy theory, but there is no doubt what- ever that a little 'relaxation of rigid rules is often bene- ficial to growing children.
" MADGE."

Nothing could come of this but increasing weakness, and it wasn't long before it was all he could do to sum- mon strength to walk about. M for working on his farm,that to be sure was not to be thought of. He had a-doctor attending him, as we should expect. If the services of a learned medical man are ever needed they must be in such a case—when nature seems to be all broken up,and the machinery runs slow, as our family clocks do when we have forgotten to wind them at the

usual hour. Well, Mr. Legate took the prescribed medicines, but got no better. He asked the doctor why that was, ani ho appeared to be puzzled for an answer at first. Natur- ally enough a doctor doesn't like to admit that his medi- cines are doing no good,because he expects to be paid for them, and then there is his professional pride, be- sides.

However, he finally said, "If my medicines fail to make you better it is owing to your age." That idea was plain as a pikestaff.and if the patient had never got any better afterwards, why, who could dispute what the doctor said P Nobody, of course. It would look just as though Mr. Leggate were really going to pieces from old age. But something subsequently happened which spoils that easy theory of the case. What it was he tells us in a letter dated February 3rd, 1893. "After doctoring several months without receiving any benefit, I determined to try Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. I got a bottle front Mr. G. H. Hanson,Chemist, New Bolingbroke. After taking the Syrup for a week I was much better. I had a good appetite and what I ate digested and strengthened me;' and by the time I had taken two bottles I was well and strong as ever. You may publish this statement if you think proper.(Signed) Richard Leggate." So it proved, after all, that Mr. Leggate was not suf- fering from old age (at seventy ! Nonsense !), but from indigestion and dyspepsia. When Mother Seigel's great discovery routed that. he felt " well and strong as ever."
Now for the moral : It is not Father Time who mows people down thus early in life; it is the Demon Dyspep- sia.. Keep him away, and—barring accidents—you may live a century.

div.head: 'TUE EXAMIN.ER, SAT ciRDAY, .17sOVEMBEI 1896.
div.p: 'TUE EXAMIN.ER, SAT ciRDAY, .17sOVEMBEI 1896.
!WHY NOT LTV A CENTURY?

"1w the coming time," said a fam3us English poet, "a man or a woman eighty or one hlndred years old, will be more beautiful than the youth' or maiden of twenty, as the ripe fruit is more beautiful and fragrant than the green. These ripe men and women will have no wrinkles on the brow, no grey hair, no bent and feeble bodies. On the contrary they will have perfect hearing, clear eyesight, sound teeth, elastic step, and mental vigour." Does this sound ab3ord and impossible a Why should it ? People over one hundred years old are frequently met with in these days, as they have been as far as human records go back. A man is of no real value un- til he is past fifty and gained control of his passions and acquired some practical wis lom. After that he ought to have from fifty to seventy-five working years before him. Whoso dies short of one hundred (bar violence) dies of his own folly ortha•t of his ancest,ora. One chief thing, however, we must learn. What is It? Take an illustration—such as we see multitudes of on every side. .

Mr. Richard Leggate of New Bolingbroke, near Boston, I Lincolnshire, is a man now somewhat over seventy. He ' is a farmer, well known and highly respected in his dis- trict. In the spring of 1891 he had an attack of influenza from which he never fully recuperated. The severe symptoms passed away, of course, but he remained weak. No doubt food would have built him up, pro- vided he could have eaten and digested it. Yet here was the trouble, his appetite was poor, and what little be took, as a matter of necessity rather than of relish, seemed to act 'wrong with him. Instead of giving him strength it actually produced pain and distress in the sides, chest and stomach. Then again—which is a common experience—he would feel a craving for something to eat ; yet on sitting down Ito a meal, in the hope to enjoy it, the stomach would suddenly rebel against the proceeding, and he would turn from the table without having'swallowed a mouth- ful.

He told the Committee then that they were quite ready to go on, and ascer- tained some particulars from the Committee which he had previously been unable to get. He wrote to the owner of the property, who came to seen him and sail he was sorry it had happened then because he was offer- ing the property for auction. They started with the work and he had written to the builders to say that they were to go on and finish it in accordance with the request of the Corporation. Mr. Green added that he was extremely anxious to do all he could to promote the health, welfare, and comfort of those people living in property placed under his care. The cost of the work was nearly £l5O and was a serious matter. He thought the bench would be justified in dismissing the case. Councillor Roberts (who is deputy-chairman of the Health Committee) said he was not adjudicating in the case but the allegations made against the committeelby Mr. Green were not strictly correct. div.head: INSANITARY PROPERTY IN WARRINGTON.
div.p: INSANITARY PROPERTY IN WARRINGTON.
A TOWN COUNCILLOR SUNIMONED.

On Friday morning at the Warrington Borough Police Court before Alderman Harrison (chairman), Alderman Wright, Councillor Roberts, Mr John White, and Mr. S. Wright. Mr. Joseph Shaw Green was sumitoned under a complaint on the 10th November for tha premises 2,4, 6, Mottram's-yard, and 1,3, 5,2, 4,6, Glasshouse-yard, off Scotland- road on the ground that tho.following nuisances existed and were a nuisance and injurious to health :—Defective floors, walls, ceilings, outside brickwork, spouting, roofs, yards, w,at of slop- stones and pipes,and inadequate closet accommoda- tion. The summons was issued under the Public Health Act, 1875. Mr. Green said he admitted that the nuisance existed. The property was now being renovated and made good. He asked the bench to dismiss the 'summons on the ground that the work was now proceeding and had been for some time. _ .

Alderman Harrison : Is your contention that the work has been dene ? Mr. Green : No sir, it is going on. Inspector Norman stated that he made an inspection of the property last July by order of the Medical Officer of Health, and made a detailed report upon it. This waz recorded in the journal and placed before the Health Committee. The committee pissed a resolution that no- tice should be served upon the owner to abate th, nuis- ances, and a notice was served on the 23rd July last. The nuisance consisted of broken floors, broken walls, decayed Waster, unpaved yards, and inadequate closet accammodation. Where one person had been living about a fortnight previously there were many a hundred pieces of broken flag. and the place was not fit for thing to live in. The only thing he had Seen done at them was that new spouting, had been put tip. He visited the buildings that morning and there was no one working there. Dr. Gomel], medical officer of health, said he felt at some disadvantage as the bench seemed to accent Mr. Green's statement that work was going on. He was only watching the case from the public health poiat of view. What Mr. Norman had stisted was perfectly true, and for years they had been trying to get the property made better and they had failed. He might say that on thel(Ph September Mr. Green appeared before the Health Committee, a most unusral course— he (Dr. Gornall) supposed because he was a member of the Town Coun- cil. He was listened to very attentively and he promised that the Drop .rty should be put in a satisfactory londi- don. He was allowed a • month and he had not yet carried out the behests of the cammittee, and the pro- perty to-day was in an insanitary condition and unfit for any human being to live in. Under the Public Health Act he asked for an order to close the houses until they were pot in a proper and habitable condition. Mr. Green said he had no questions to ask Dr. Gornall. Eta then went on to say that the Dr. had referred to his visit to the committee. He (Mr. Green) was treated on that occasion in a manner that he did not think any in- dividual in the town ought to have beeli treated. For some time he had been endeavouring to ascertain what would satisfy the committee to put the property in a sanitary'Condition. He had written to the Town Clerk that the owners of it were prepared to do what the com- mittee asked. He had tried te ascertain what would satisfy them. The owners were anxious to put the pro- perty in a proper condition. When he got the summons it took him by surprise. It was a proceeding which; 'he was bound to say,ought never to have taken place, be- cause if the customary notice had been sent to him stating that a summons would be taken out if be did not proceed with the work,he would have gone to the Town Hall to ascertain what to do, and it would have been done. He complained to the Health Corrdnittee that the summons was taken out without eiving him the custom-

;try notice that a summons would 13;; issued. On the Friday prior to the Wednesday on which the summons was issued he saw Inspector Norman and asked him what was to he done with the Scotland-road cottages. He said he would go over them with him (Mr. Green). They did not go• though the speaker was prepared to

Mr. Green: Certainly not. I only want to do that which is right. Inspector Norman: The summondes were both under the Public Health Act. Mr. Green: I have at this moment this work pro- ze-ding. Alderman Harrison : Mr. Norman has been there this morning and there is nobody working there. Dr. Gornall : We have been there so often that lam afraid some of the inhabitants of Scotland-road will think we live there. I have made up my mind I will not go there again. I have no confidence in the owner carrying out the improvements unless I have the order. Alderman Harrison : Then we make an order that it be closed until it is put in proper condition. FARM FIRE AT RISLEY. OR Sunday morning shorly before seven o'clock news came to the Warrington Fire Station that a fire bad broken out in the stackyard of Messrs. J. and J. C. Warburton, Parket's Farm, Risley. The brigade, under the direction of Superintendent Tnrner. promptly turned out with the fire engine Major, and proceede4 to the scene of the conflagra- tion, which is four miles and a half distant. On their itlrrival they found that a large stack of 30 tons of hay—one of a row of six— was in flames. The efforts of the brigade were directed to preventing the fire from spreading. In this they were success- ful, and also in saving a portion of the burning stsok itself. The damage which is estimated at £l2O. is covered by insurance. The brigade re- turned to Warrington late in the afternoon. P.S. A, AT THE Y.M.C. A. The open meeting of this society on Sunday last was well attended, Mr. William Roberts presiding. Mr. James Evans delivered a good address, and it was made evident that he is a favourite with the members. Mr. Levi Richardson was in good form with his two solos and his fine rendition of " Come unto Me " pill be long remembered. Mr. Hurst and Mr. Gregson assisted in the service which was concluded with the hearty singing of the hymn Saviour. again to Thy dear name we raise," &c.

_ TEE NEW ASYLUM AT WINWICS. A blue-book published on Monday contains a supplement to the report of the Commissioners in Lunacy iring particulars of the new Lancashire asylum to be erected at Winwick. The new bandit in will accommodate 2.000 patients of the chronic class in equal numbers of the sexes, to be drafted to it. from the four existing asylums for the county. The architects are gessrs. H. Crisp and Oakley, and W. S. Skinner, of Bristol, whose plans were AP- preyed by the Secretary of State on the 16th September of laqt year. The quantity of land purchased amounts to 206 ac---.

" I take great pleasure in giving you this report of my children, and the benefit they have derived from Scott's Emulsion. Our little boy was very ill about the end of September last. Our medical attendant advised US to give him Scott's Emulsion, as he said he was a weakly child from birth, and was quite rickety. We purchased a bottle. It was quite surprising how .well he got on. He is now nearly able to walk alone; he has got upstairs several times by himself, and he is as lively as possible, and is much fatter.
