div.head: V.-nGIERS.
div.p: V.-nGIERS.
S.S. Midnight Sun
When we left Granada the sky, which had been per-
fectly clear since we landed at Lib ,n was veiled with
gray cloud, portending the autumn rains. The railway

, down to. 'liobadilta -runs botween b)ld reddish hills seamed aad scarred with saw-like riligy out-lines. It Looked like a land over which a confl4gration had passed Here and there we saw a green belt of trees, or a mile or

two of ;olive-yard. Acacias and horse-chestnuts, white with the dust of the long drought, grew about the vil- lages through which we passed. In the valleys now and then we saw a little green glen where figs and pome- granates mingied oddly with English bramble and yellow groundsel. The forms of the mountains were exceedingly bold and grand, huge wedge-lika peaks half- swathed in cloud, and olive gardens sloping down into the plain. Now and again we passed parties of laden mules and donkeys, with red saddles, in charge of men in blue cotton suits, red sashes and sombreros,and gipsy like women with bright handkerchiefs bound over their black hair.
Nothing can equal the stately deliberation of a Span-

ish express train, unless it be that of a Spanish hotel waiter. At a little station just above Bodadilla we stopped so long that it was supposed they had tele- graphed up to the stationmaster to keep us there until they had got our coffee ready. We were quite ready for that same coffee when we reached BadadillA June-

tion between four and five. On the platforin were a number of Murillo beggar boys, and a crowd of women and girls,smiling and friendly. They held up their babies for inspection, and one delightful black-eyed infant.in a lace cap, submitted so happily to be nursed by the Eng- lish _ ladies, that one of them was with difficulty re- _ _ . _
strained from taking it on as part of her personal-lug:-

gage. We arrived at Malaga with inexpected punctuality, soon after eight, and had a long drive to the quav,along the immensely wide boulevards. It was too dark, un- fortunately, to see anything of the town. At the har- bour we were lighted to our place of embarkation by the _ _ _ _

glare of pieces of tarred rope, and in spite of this -fitful illumination, and the excitement of getting off some six score people in small boats, reached our floating home without any mishap, and sailed away for North Africa. The Day of Rest was doubly welcome after the excite- ment of the past few and we were glad, after morning
service days, on deck, to sit about- under the awnings, comparing experiences, and tramping (inetaphoricallv)

with latticed windows and arabesques over the doorways n green and violet and red and blue, peeped at us over hedges of cactus and aloe and wild g.ranium. Far in the distance lay the mighty range of Atlas,with the ver- dant and smiling Metidj t between. We drove by El Bier to Bonzarea, with magnificent views for nearly the whole way, and returned past the huge Hospice of Les Petites Qceurs des Pamres, by a zag road that tried the springs of our carriages, to the bottom of a wild gorge, with white, flat-topped houses perched on cliffs here and there, and pine and ilex cling- ing to the side of the red crags. At the bottom of The ravine is a dry river bed. spanned by stone bridges, and probably a raging torrent in the rainy season. We lunched on the ship, and in the afternoon started again for the Botanical Gardens, the chief curiosity of which are the enormous india-rubber trees. There is an avenue of them there, as large as en ordinary avenue of pines. Then we went on to the Ravin du Femme Sauvage, so called from a sore, of Moorish hermitess,who is said to have lived here at the time of the French con- quest. Here we revelled in the luxuriance of the vege- tation after the bare hills of Spain, pines on the heights and in the valleys, figs and sycam )res with a rich under growth of rhododendrons and bamboos. Comparing Tangier, which in climate and beauty ()- situation almost equals Algiers,with the city we had just visited,we could not help congratulating our neighbours across the channel on what they had made of this ancient nest of pirates. The gaiety and grace of Al- gerine life as we saw it, the unsurpassed quaintness of the Mohammedan quarter, and the picturesque medley of every conceivable garb and tongue in the palm-shaded squares and boulevards, all these are now among the treasures of memory.
on the prostrate forms of those who had' not veatured tO join in invading the Peninsula. In the afternoon we

assembled in the smoking-rootn to hear Sir Lambert Playfair's last lecture, introduced by a few words from Mr. Justice Ross, who carried the whole assembly with him when he spoke of the gratitude and goodwill which our distinguished fellow-passegger had earned irom us all, and of the earnest good wishes which will accom-
'pany .him into his retirement, when he returns to Scot-

land next year. Before beginning his lecture,Sir Lambert playfully ad- vised the ladies to supply themselves with extra pocket- handkerchiefs, and in all seriousness, if ever " tears to human suffering were due," they are called for by the victims of the pirates of Algiers. Christian slavery in North Africa was the subject of the address, which dealt briefly with the rise of Mohammedan power in North Africa, the establishment of the Saracens in Sicily and Spain,and the deeds of the Mediterranean pirates who sallied forth from their fortresses at Tunis, Tangier, and above all Algiers' to harass and capture merchaut vessels of every nation, dooming crew and passengers to hope- less captivity. The most disgraceful part of the busi- ness was that although anyone of the European Powers could easily, at any time, have brought the Dey of Al- giers to reason their mutual jealousy would not permit of this solution, and the pirate state was flattered and ca- joled by each of the Christian nations in succession; as it Fe?med likely to be a foil in the side of a neighbour. This obvious anolop,y with the state of things ironically termed "the Concert of Europe," was noted with great appreciation by the audience. A certain proportion of Christian slaves in every cap- ture were allotted to the Dey, the remainder sold to pri- vate purchasers or sent to the public works.where they toiled half clothed and half fed, with chains on their limbs, and often subjected to conditions too horrible for description. Yet, as the lecturer pointed out, their lot was no worse than that of many of the Christian subjects of his mos: Christian Majesty, Louis XtV. of France, and the Huguenot victims of the galleys and the dragonade might almost envy the slaves of the Aigerine pirates . With all this in our minds' the first glimpse of Algiers was hailed with very special interest. The rain, which had been threatening for the last day or two, was falling in sheets; but even under these disadvantages we could admire the fine sweep of the Bay, and the fair city with its domes and minarets, crowned with the old Moorish citadels and gleaming white out of its garden graves. There is a civilised and progressive atmosphere about this delightful town, compared with other spots which we had visited in our wanderings which impressed us immediately on landing, and the Cheerful impression was not entirely removed even by the ordeal of having to call at the post office for an important registered letter, and producing two witnesses to one's identity before it could be wrested from the tcnacious grasp of French officialdom. The Boulevarde de la Republique, with its handsome blocks of offices, skirts the quay, and behind this is the Bab-el-Azoun, with some really nice shops, and crowds of Arabs in all the colours of the rainbow, rubbing shoulders with sober-tinted Europeans. This leads us into the ?lace de Gouvernement, spacious and palm-shaded, with the glaring white dome of the New Mosque facing the sea. Here .we en- gaged an Arab youth, red-turbaned, red-slippered, and for the rest, an indescribable bundle of yellow rags, to convey us through the Moor-

_ ish quarter. There is a sharp division between the ancient and the modern town of Algiers, marked by the Rue de la Lyre, which runs parallel with the quay. Crossing this you find yourself in another woeld. There are no streets, strictly speaking, only passages of endless stairs, hemmed in an either side by high houses, with narrow barred windows and projecting balconies,almost shutting Out the sky. Many of these houses are solidly built, with massive oaken doors.carved in elaborate pat- terns, and with a little grated window at the top. These are the residences of the wealthier Arabs. Up and down these s'airs, in the shadow of the nodding balconies, streams a continual succession of picturesque figures— some draped from head to foot in the folds of the white burnous, others in haike of crimson or blue, lined with another colour and richly embroidered ; uthers, again,in white full vests and baggy trousers, with a crimson sash and yellow or blue embroidered jacket; and among them women looking like mere white bundles, and veiled up to the eyes, some holding little black-eyea Moors by the hand, some with immense brown water-jars on their heads. The shops were merely dark caves formed by the taking away of the ground flocir front, and here the Arab squats among his goods, and conducts endless di- plomatic intrigues over the disposal of a brass tray or a piece of embroidery. The traveller must make up his mind to be taxed heavily in his Eastern shopping, either in money or time. ,If he can afford to spend an hour and a half over each purchase,he may succeed in bring- ing down the price to something iike the real value of the article. If not, he must submit to be mulcted con- siderably by the sons of Islam. Several of these gloomy recesses were cafes,where the clientele was sitting about on strips of matting, drinking black coffee in tiny cups, and playing at cards and dominoes. Out Of breath with climbing, we finally emerged on the platform at the top of the hill, at the gate of the ancient kasbah, or citadel,now used as barracks. There is a clumsy-looking salmon-pink tower at the corner, with a projecting green turret. And here took place the famous episode, when the last Dey, on some'remon- stranee from the French ambassador, struck him in the face With hi fan, thus furnishing a pretext for the French occupation. ,Opposite is a transmuted mosque. now a Christian chapel and convent school. We went into thelchapel—a plain whitewashed building, with the usual daubs on the wall,representing the Stations of the Cross. Two squads of brown-skinned children—boys and girls—under the guidance of the Sisters, were chanting the " Salve Regina." It was a pretty, touch- ing sight, particularly when one remembered what within the last hundred years might have been the fate of Christian boys and girls almost on that very spot. Then we went on to study the devotees] of the Pro- phet in the grand mosque. Rue de la Marine the oldest ' in Algeria. It, is a cool,colonnaded, white-walled place, spread with carpets of varying patterns. A few of the faithful in white burnouses, were kneeling in rows, kis- sing the grout.' at intervals, rising and bowing three times to Mecca, and then kneeling. We were in- debted to the French Government for the unusual privi- lege of entering, as they, made it one of the articles of capitulation that the mosque should be open. An ancient attendant sits on the threshold with a supply of im- mense red slinnere,which you slip on over your walking shoes,and shuffi a about in during your Fitay in the sacred enclosure. The mosque is built round a court with a picturesque fountain, at which certain of the faithful were scrubbing their faces, hands, and teeth with much energy. If anpthing could dams!) the ardour of a British travel- ler it would be the downpour of rain that we had on the previous day. To-day, however, the sky was brilliantly clear, and the sea of the true Mediterranean colour. At breakfast Mr. Pernwne announced the arrangements for the day, we sorted ourselves as directed into parties of fonr,and found our carriages waiting for us at the quay. It involved some time and trouble on all these occasion ; on the part of Mr. Perowne, Mr. Lunn, and their able lieutenants, to see that all were comfortably settled and that no straggler was left behind; but that being accom- plished, off we went through Mustapha Suporieure, the French residential suburb of Algiers, up a steep hill,past the villa of the Governor with its lovely garden, and out into the open country. The air,coolel by the!rain of the day before, was exhilarating as champagpe, and every turn of the road gave us a fresh view of the Bay,and the intense sapphire blue of the open sea. Curious little "villas "and " campagnes," half French, half Moorish,

div.head: PROFESSIONAL PRAISE.
div.p: PROFESSIONAL PRAISE.

If proof were needed of the high therapeutic value of that ever-popular and never-failing remedy Warner's Safe Cure, one has only to glance at a few of the un- solicited written encomiums which have been heaped upon it by prominent medical men in England, France and Germany. If medical men make personal use of a patent medicine, it speaks volumes for the faith they have in its curative powers. Dr, Fischer. the Govern- ment Physician of Neuenbuerg,Germany, has written to Messrs. Warner a m3st gratifying letter, stating the pleasure he feels in testifying to the rapid and complete cure of a lady patient who was suffering from Bright's disease of the kidneys, by a timely use of the famous remedy. Many patent medicines have made their ap- pearance during recent years, and the advent of many more is only a question of time; be let them be as pre- tentious as they may, the public faith will remain un- saken in a remedy which has been tested in every pos- sible manner, and has never been known to fail. Warner's Safe Cure is one of those few old remedies to which we cling, and however keen the competition, however euphonious the titles of future specifics, the household words Safe Cure will never be eliminated from the home,be that home prince's palace or peasant's cot.

UNSOUND SIEAT PROSECUTION AT WARRINGTON. A BUTCHER HEAVILY FINED. John Henry Bradbury, butcher, 5, Scott-street, was summoned at the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday morning, before Mr. Monks (in the chair), and other magistrates, for being in possession on the 11th November of one fore quarter and one hind quarter of beef, one heart, and eighteen other pieces of beef, which were unsound and unwholesome, and unfit for human food, and also with being in possession of 201 b. of beef deposited in a yard adjoining his dwelling-house, 5, Scott-street. The Town Clerk appeared for the prosecution and Mr. J. W. Knowles for the defendant. A plea of not guilty was put in and by agreement the two cases were taken as one. The Town Clerk briefly stated that defendant was charged with being in the posßession of meat unfit for human food. With regard to the second case the meat was concealed and covered over. He did not allege that it was diseased, but unwholesome and unfit for food.

Mr. Monks: What is technically known as "slinker ?' The Town Clerk; Yes. Mr. R. Norman, inspector of nuisances, stated that on Wednesday week he visited the defendant's shcp, 41, Winwick-road, and found hanging on the side rail in the shop a hind quarter and a fore quarter of beef. He also found on the benches 18 other pieces and one heart, Having collected them he examined them, and found they were very soft,wet,and appeared to have come from a beast that had been a very old one, and in his opinion unfit for human food. The defendant's father was in charge of this shop, and witness asked him where he got the side of beef from. The father led him to believe that he was the owner until late in the afternoon. He said he got the beef from Lymm and had given 303. for the two quarters. When asked did the meat belong to him be said "Yes." Witness told him he should seize it and convey it to the Town Hall for the Medical Officer of Health, who would certify whether it was fit or unfit for food. The Medical Officer examined the pieces very carefully, and certified they were unsound and unfit for food. About half-past one on the day mentioned the defendant's father came to his office and asked him if he would allow those two quarcers to remain there that day, as a numbar of butchers were coming to see them. He went away, hut they did not come, and witness waited till three o'clock. Then de- fendant's father told him that Mr. Shawcros3 was coin- ing to make an examination. Mr. Shawcross came at half-past five. The defendant's father told him that the meat did not belong to him, but to his son. Witness asked his son's name, and he said "John Henry Brad- btiry." In the second na,se he went at 11 o'clock the fol- lowing forenoon, the 12th November, and visited some property in Scott-street. Witness was in a yard next to the defendant's yard, and sew something hanging trom a hook which turned out to be a piece of beef weighing about 201 b. By Mr. Knowles : He made ten minutes to a quarter of an hour's examinatinn of the meat. He lead never been in the " butchery " business. He had had twenty years' experipnce RS Nuisance Inspector. He had had no training. He believed the meat was unfit for human food,land be would not care to eat it. In fact it was not fit for a doe. It appeared to have Come from an ordin- ary cow and not a small one. He knew that good meat could be bought in Manchester abbatoirs at 2d. a lb. and the best meat at 4d. a lb. Defendant said he gave 2d. a lb. for the meat. Dr. J. H. Gornalt,medical officer of health,said he was at the Town Hall on the day in question when the meat arrived. He examined it,and the two quarters appeared to have belonged to an animal that had been ill-fed and aged. The meat was soft and unhealthy. The muscular spaces were like jelly. Toe flesh was of a very dark purple colour. It was snit, inelastic, and easily torn,and the cellular tissues coptained a mucilaginous fluid. He came to the opinion diet the meat was in the early stages of putrefaction, and unfit for human food. Mr. Knowles: Was it first, second, third, fourth, or fifth rate meat? Dr. Gornall: Fourth or fifth rate meat, and unfit for human food. Mr. Knowles : Would you call Silver-st. and neigh- bourhoed a fourth or fifth rate aristocratic neighbour- hood? Dr. Gornall : I should say it was a democratic neigh bourhood. (Laughter.) Mr. Knowles : Then this is democratic beef? (Laugh- Dr. Gomel! : I think the working classes should have as goad food as I have. Dr. J. Guest (Jornall, deposed to examiring the 201bs of meat. He described it awe said he had no hesitation in saying it was unfit for human food. One of the Corp )ration clsrks stated that Mr. Shaw- :tress and Mr. Bradbury examined the beef at the Toni Hall about 5 p Mr. Knowles, for the defence, pointed out that there were all sorts and conditions of mankind who lived on various kinds of meat. He cont i nded that the meat was fit for food. H sdid not say that it was fit for food for Dr. Gornall. It was fit food for the poor people of the neighbourhood. It was second-rate meat and quite wholesome. They Would not co:npell tee poor to come to the leading shops and pay a high price for their meat. Mr. Monks : It ii our business to protect the poor and see that they are provid with good meat. I know from my exnerienee on the Stnitare Committee in this past, the diffiaulty there was in detecting the sale of "slinker" i meat. Mr. Knowles said it was good cheap meat and came from a sound animal. Re concluded by appealing to the bench, if they c nivicted, to deal leniently with defend. ant as he was youeg, had several sisters dependant upon him, and had only just started in business. He wets doing well and a conviction would boa serious thing to With regard to the case in Scott-street. Mr. Knowles said defendant's lather would swear that the meat was for home consumptiou, and there was an end to the matter. The Town Clerk said he must press for a conviction in the case, John Bradbury,father of defendant,sald he bought the meat at Lynam for a little over 2d. a lb. It was "sound as a bell f brass," and was sold for poor people who if thep had 61 to spsnd would spier' I 41. in ale and 2d. in beef. The meat in 8(•0t-St., he said, was for consump- tion by the family. In answer to the Town Clerk he said he told his family to keep an account one week and from Sunday to Thursday they ate 321bs of meat. Arthur Snawcrose, veteriaary surgeon, stated that he had had 3 years eeperienee in public abbatoirs. He examined the mea- at the Town Hall and considered it sound meat. It was not dal le purple and putrefying,. There was no question about it being fit for the food of man. .

The Clerk : Do you consider yourself competent to say whether •t was fit for the food of man ? Witnegs I do. After a short ConsultatiOn with his brother magis. trates the Chairman said they found defcnciant guilty, And inflicted a peno„ty of 403. and costs, (£3 193. Od. in , all).

SATURDAY, biOVEM.BER 28. b, 1896

THE Government is credited in Some Proposed Legislation, various quarters with the inten- tion to legislate during the coming session of Parliament upon two important questions. In each instance the legislation, if it is brought forward, will touch in a very direct manner the interests of a large number of people. The. Government intend—so it is reported—to pro- mote a Savingsßanksßill for the purpose of reduc- ing the interest paid on deposits in the Post Office Savings Bank from 24 to two per cent. Now, as everybody knows, the investors in the Post Office Savings Bank are comparatively poor people. They are, as a rule, people who are on;y able to save at all by the cultivation of provident and thrifty habits. This being so, it may well be asked, why the Government should go out of its way to discourage this class of investors above all others, for there be no doubt that the lessening of the amount of interest upon these post office deposits by one-fifth will act its a very serious discouragement. It is because the Post Office Sav- ings Bank does not pay its way, now that money is more "cheap and plentiful" than it used to be? Even if that question co Ad be answered in the affirmative, we do not know that it would be a conclusive reason for any such change as is con- templated. We take it, that the primary object of the Post Office Savings Bank is not the making of profit, but the encouraging of habits of thrift amongst the masses of tne people. It might. be argued that the accomplishment of that object would be worth a little sacrifice on the part of the imperial Treasury. As a matter of fact the Post Office Savings Bank is, even whilst paying its 2 per cent., a profitable institution. According to official figures, it annually shows a balance on the right side of setnething like 1:80,000,and this sum is, of course, utilised in lieu of taxation to that amount. If the interest were reduced from 2i- to two per cent. there will, it is said, be an addi- tional profit of i:800,000 a year. In other: words, ' the thrifty poor of the co,ntry are to be de- prived of nearly a million peunds a year which is at present distriuuted amongst them in the shape of interest upon deposits in the Post Office Savings Bank. It is clear, therefore, that the projected charge can not be justified on the ground that the Post 'Office Savings Bank does not pay its way. The explanation must be sought in some other direction that that. As a matter-- of-fact it is roundly stated that the real object of this legislation, should it tailio shape in a parlia- mentary Bill, will be to relieve the rich at the expense of the poor. It will be another piece of class legislation of exactly the same character as the Land Rating Bill of last session. At the pre- sent time the law prescribes that post office sav- ings bank funds must be invested in consols, and the result is that consols are an extremely high- priced security. This is no doubt a great incon- venience to many wealthy people and to bankers in particular,and probably the influential though, comparatively speaking, not numerous section of he community is bringing great pressure to bear on the Government. The present Government is, as every one now knows, very easily moved to. ctio on behalf of the "classes," though all it

Promised benefits for the " masses " have yet to eerae. It is, however, in every way likely that the Present scheme, if it ever takes a definite shape, Will be met with a very strenuous and probably Successful resistance. The spectacle of a Govern- reent, influential members of .which have, when in ePPosition, advocated old-age pensions, deliber- ately proposing to rob the thrifty poor of what they are entitled to, both on grounds of policy and of justice, will, we should think,be a trifle too exasperating even for the most asinine of " Tory Workingmen." The other subject of legislation which, it is said, the Government have in contemplation is a duty of one kind or another upon sugar, all article that is consumed in every house- hold, rich and poor. The sugar planters of tho West Indies complain that their business is depressed by the system of bounties paid by the Governments of Germany, Austria and France, Upon the beet sugar which is exported from those countries, and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN has notified his Intention to send a Commission to inquire into the state of the sugar industry in the West Indies. This seems to indicate that if the Commission reports in favour of protection for the West Indian planters there will be an attempt to raise the price of sugar. But, as Lord FARRER pointed out at the meeting of the Cobden Club on Tues- day, cheap sugar has been one of the greatest boons to the poor people of this country. In ad- dition to that a great system of industries has been built up in this country upon cheap sugar. The British people have,says Lord _ ARRER,beCOMO "the confectioners of the world." These import- ant industries will be ruined by the imposition of a protective duty upon sugar. In the case of this legislation, if it ever comes to anything, as in that relating to saving bank deposits, the result will be the benefiting of the few at the expense of the many. It will, in a word, be class legislation of the very worst kind, and as such it should be re- slstei to the uttermost.

OYSTERS have been suspected for Oysters and Disease, some years past of being a medi- um for the propagation of certain infectious diseases, and therefore a report upon the subject which has been issued by the Local Government Boatd will be read with some inter- est, especially by those who confess to a liking for this particular bivalve. This report does not, it may at once be said, contain anything of a sensa- tional or alarming character. Its distinguishing note is that of scientific caution. It is stated that eases of cholera have occurred on the eastern coast in the neighbourhood of Grimsby and Cleethorpes Which were suspected to be due to the eating of oysters by the infected persons. The oyster has therefore for a year or two past been under the Close examination of certain experts of the Local Government 80ar3.. This trial has not resulted in a very decided verdict either way. Dr. Thorne states that "every skilled observer whose investi- gations have gone to show that certain oysters have served as the medium for conveying disease to man has admitted that the risk is by no means a great one." It is even said that the particular germs which are the cause of cholera and enteric fever do not thrive in the oyster. They may get between the two shells when the oyster beds are Contaminated by sewage, but when once there the "cholera vibrio tends soon to lose its physiological Properties." That, we take it, is the learned way Of saying that the cholera microbe is deprived by the oyster of its power of doing mischief. At the same time it is quite evident that a good deal too much sewage has access to some of the oyster layings on the English coasts. These contamin- ated spots are specified in the report alluded to al:k1 their owners will act wisely if they take seri- °Us notice of the .criticisms of the Local Govern- Inent Board's experts.

div.head: NOTES AND NEWS.
div.p: NOTES AND NEWS.

One result of the China-Japanese war has been (says the " Chronicle ") to create new conditions in the ].ktikado's dominions which may censiderably modify the Internal life of his subjects. Thus, as the direct result Of that war, the people have taken to eating meat, the habit having been formed by the soldiers, who were served with a meat ration every day. The expense of this form of food is such that the old wages are no longer adequate, and the price of labour has gone up, although it is still far from the European standard. Thus a carpenter's daily wage amounts to 55 sen a day, or about is. 41., the sen being the equivalent of a cent or halfpenny, although the depreciation in silver has lessened this by nearly a half. Plasterers, painters and bricklayers each earn 65 sen a clay, w— ha ne paperhangers, upholsterers, and tinsmiths are paid at the rate of 60 son, Tile-layers are paid 50 sen, but stonemasons, Shingle-layers, and engravers make 75 sen, and cabinet- Makers receive 70. The gardeners, however, to whose labour so much of the peculiar beauty of Japan is due, Only receive 40 sen. The tailors and the laundrymen are the plutocratic employes, for they in one yen, Which is equivalent to a dollar worth, n the depreciated currency of the country, about 2s. 2d. Labourers,how- evet, who do the rough work, such as carrying sand,&9,, receive only 35 sen a day. House servants are paid by the moo h; instead of by the day, and a cook receives Item 15 to 20 yen a month, and man-servant 12 to 15 Yen, and an ordinary servant from 7 to 10, while a nurse can be procured for from 10 to 15 yen.
The Pendleton Bistressed Armenians Aid Society has aent,through the treasurer of the Grosvenor House Fund, a first instalnaent of £lOO towards the relief of the Rufferers.

A bill was introduced into the Alabama State Assembly ori Saturday for the regulation of the costumes of Women. It is proposed to make it unlawful to Fear Shirt-waists, tight-fitting Jerseys, bloomers, and divided skirts. Nor must they appear in stockings which visibly fasten above the knees. another sentence in the mea- suVe deals with evening dress, and proposes to render it !inlawful for the top of any bodice to be mere than three Inches below the junction of the chin and throat. Kin- ally, the measure declares that no article of clothing wors by men shall be worn by women. There is a pros- Peet that the bill will pass in some form.

When did influenza first make its appearance in Wes- tern. Europe ? It would soem (says the " Daily News " Paris correspondent) in 1400. A parchment bearing the Beal of the Grand Chamber of Parliament, with the date Qf 26th April, 1400, has been found in the National Li- brary. it is to this effect :—"This day all the lords of Parliament were laid up by colds and fevers together by the pestilence that flies through the atr, and which had triad* the lords cough hard at their last sitting and the Registrar so ill and weak that he c ould hardly record anything. May it please the gracious God to help thent through their illness." In the following month there died of the cold and fever illness a nun at St. Denis. She bad undertaken to suffer vicariouqly for the sins of the *Queen Isabeau of Bavaria, "to the Queen's great con- tentment." Her death was looked upon at Court as a disaster, as she was held to be a saint. The Queen used or her sake to lavish elite on the convent.

Elison has made a remarkable statement to the cffeet that by the use of the Rontgen rays the blind may be able to see' the only condition being that the optic rve must be intact. Esrriments have been made at "is laboratory, apparently to SOIRP extent successfully, and Mr. Edison prophesies that within three years they 'will be able to restore sight to the blind.

Birmingham continues to go a-head, and we, says : Science Siftings," recommend other cities to Mllow her example. It has now been decided by the Ilealth Committee to infAitute an exhaustive inquiry 113 to the question whether boracic acid should be per- lalitted as an antiseptic or preservative in various food 44bstances. Dr. Hill has made a statement, which we '9notsd recently, to the effect that the proportion of ,oracic acid in butter is from sixteen to twenty grains the pound. Boracic acid, he says, is essentially a 7,ruz when put into foodstuffs, and when taken day .71ter I:lay it is injurious to the constitution. It sets up :41iZestion and diartbeea, and depresses the nervous Yttern. In the opinion of Sir Andrvw Clark, and other a"nlnent physicians, many diseases, the origin of which "troy; are unable to trace, are attributable to such an- illePtics as boracic acid and salicylic acid.
RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
Sr. MICHAEL'S CHURCH, RUNCORN.

The anniversary services on behalf of Newtown Mission Day School were held in St. Michael's Church, Runcorn, on Sunday. The preachers were—Morning, the Rev. J. Holden, vicar of Antrobus ; afternoon, chil- dren's service, the Rev. H. B. Firth ; and evening, the Rev. IL C. Moyle. The collections were on behalf of Newtown Day School. ST. EDWARD'S CATFIOLIC CFLURCIZ, RUNCORN. On Sunday the feast of St. Cecilia, patron saint of music, was celebrated at this church. In the morning a capital rendering of " Gounod's " illissa de Sancta Cecilia" was given by the ciaoir. At the evening service Murphy's benediction service (No. 1) was performed, the offertory piece being Mercadante's " Salve Maria," which was finely rendered by Mr. J. W. Dockrey, the choirmaster. Mr. W. Grounds presided at the organ. Collections were made on behalf of the choir. The offi- ciating priest at both services was the Rev. Father Gore, who is in charge of the Mission during the temporaty absence of the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi on a well-earned brief holiday.

On Monday evening in the schoolroom a social evens ing was held. A large number sat down to tea. Tras. - had been generously given by a number of the congre- gation. A meeting was afterAards held, the Rev. It. J. Cliftcn opening the proceedings ,Fith prayer. Mr. P. Speakman, J.P., C.A., presided, and was supported on the platform by the Revs. T. Brackenbury, W. George, and R. J. Clifton, Messrs. F. J. Norman, J.P., T. Simister, J. Bazley, R. Posnett, and J. Harrison. A statement of the trust of accounts was given by Mr. Bazley,which was considered very fair. A resolution moved by Mr. J.Bazley, and se- conded by Mr,Speakman,and c rdially carried ,expressed sympathy with Mr. S. C. Beckett (the treasurer) and regret at his absence. The proceeds (not including the Sunday collections) amounted to about £l3, and are to be handed over to the trust fund to defray the expenses incurred by sanitary improve- ments.

div.head: BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IIiPROVEMENT SOCIETY.
div.p: BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IIiPROVEMENT SOCIETY.

On Wednesday evening a ladies' meeting was held in connection with the above Society in the Brunswick- st. Schoolroom. There was a large attendatne. Mr. T. Sinister occupied the chair. The evening's entertain- ment was opened by the company present singing a hymn, followed by prayer. Miss A. Taylor contributed the song " Butter,flies." " Two merry hearts" (duet) was splendidly rendered by the Misses Birkett and A. Jones. A paper entitled "Women's rights" was read by Miss A. Jones. During her paper she put forth some strong remarks on the rights of women. She contended that women when employed in place of men, should receive the same remuneration. She strongly argued this point. A discussion followed. The second part of the programme consisted of duet by Mrs. T. Leach and Miss Simkin ; a reading by Miss Spearing ; song, Miss A. Taylor; song, "The Ballad Singer," Miss Simkin ; read ing, "Miss Amelia's Young Man," by Miss Clayden ; re- citation, Miss Baker; song, Miss Clara Taylor; song, "Love's old sweet song," by Mrs. T. Leach; glee, " greodnight," by the lady members. Miss J. Crosby kindly acted as the accompanist. Refreshments were provided by the lady members. A most enjoyable even- ing was brought to a close by the singing of the Doxology. FUNERAL OF A WELL-KNOWN RIINCORNIAN. _ .

On Wednesday the remains of Mr. John Powell Newby, of Bentinck-st., Runcorn, were laid to rest in the Run- corn Cemetery. The deceased, who was in his fiftieth year, contracted a cold sense time ago, and this was fol- lowed by an attack of pneumonia, to which he suc- cumbed on Saturday. Deceased was widely known by the officials and workmen of the canal, who showed their respect by attending the funeral in large numbers. A procession formed by Captain Heasley, Dr. McKenzie, Messrs. J. Ayers, S. Hardy. J. R. Hardy, W. McKenzie, J. R. Hill, A.Haining, Gregson,W. Durham,A.Lawis, H. Hughes, T. Davies, W. Johnson.W.Gregson,J.Wade, J. Derbyshire, F. Derbyahtre, S. Battersby, H. Smaithan, T. Evans, H Jevnson, G. Finney, C. Bowyer, D. Heeds, W. Crabb, W. Aspey, &c. ,headed the hearse. RUNCORN TENNIS CLUB.

The members held their first social of the season in Bethesda Lecture Hall on Friday night, and it proved to be one of the most successful functions that has taken place in connection with the club since its formation. The room had been elaborately and beautifully decor- ated for the occasion. Tne credit of this work is due to the members of the committee and friends, who were congratulated on their successful efforts- There was a very numerous attendance, and besides an excellent pro- gramme of dances, songs were rendered by Messrs. A. Grounds and J. Booth. Mr. J. H. Taylor admirably carried out the duties of M.C., and Mr. W. Grounds provided the music. Suitable refreshments were pro- vided by Miss Spearing. A most enjoyable time was spent, and it was not until the early hours of the morn- ing that the gathering broke up. The BETHESDA TEACHERS' AND ELDER SCHOLARS' SOCIkL
EVENING.

The first of a series of social evenings which it is in- tended to hold during the winter months was held on Wednesday is the Lecture Hall,High-street. Mr. James Taylor presided in the absence of the pastor the Rev. J. S. Simpson who is suffering from indisposition. An at- tractive programme was submittee, and Mr. C. Temple opened the evening's entertainment by a comic song, entitled "I've just come away from the inquest." The Misses Heathrington gave a duet " The minute gun at sea." Mr. W. Smith pleased his hearers by giving the (violin solo) " Village Wedding." Miss Cartwright dis- played her abilities on the piano by giving a solo. Mr. C. C. Le Couteur was applauded for his work on the piano. Mr. R. Wright delighted the audience by sing- ing the comic song " Ours is a happy home," and in re- sponse to the call gavt " Can't change it." Mr. A. Senior was encored for his recitation. Mr. W. Lacy proposed a vote of thank to the chairman and artistes. Mr. T Stanway seconded, and it was cordially carried. The singing of the doxology brought a pl aunt evening to a close. Light refreshment's were provided during the evening. A collection was made to defray the ex- penses.
SAD DROWNING MYSTERY AT RUNCORN.

On Saturday the body of Herbert Leyland, aged eight years, son of Thomas Leyland, of Porter-street, was re- moved from the Bridgewater Canal, opposite the crane, Halton-road. The deceased was last seen alive in the vicinity of the waterway, and not returning home dur- ing the night, dragging operations were commenced with the result named. How he got into the canal is unknown. Mr. J.E. Worsley held an inquest on the body on Monday afternoon at the Police Station, Runcorn.— Margaret Fendley, sister, said deceased livid with her. About 5-45 p.m. n Friday he left the house, and said he was going to meet his brother who worked on a boat. Witness told him not to do so, as her brother would not be home until 11 o'clock. Their house was about three minutes walk from the canal, and about five minutes walk from where his body was picked up.—Alice Bon- field said deceased and another boy called at her house on Friday night with a basket of groceries at about 20 minutes to seven. She did not see him again.—John Howard, 10, Water-street, deposed to recovering the body from the Bridgewater Canal on Saturday last.— P.C. Gregory said there were no marks with the excep- tion of a few scratches on the body. The body was fully dressed. Witness examined the bank in company with the last witness. There were finger marks in the soft clay on the banks, as of scmeone having fallen into the 'rater, and attempted to get out. The marks were quite clear. The jury returned a verdict of "Found Drowned," The Coroner remarked that it was a very sad case. The father of deceased said the lad had been many times in the canal and he could not get hint to keep away. ST. JOHNS' PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH, RUNCORN.

On Wednesday a social evening was held in the school room, Victoria-road, Runcorn. A large number were present and a capital programme was submitted. The Proceedings were opened by a selection from "National Airs" rendereSby a string band. Mr. T. Johnson gave "I fear no foe." The " Toilers" contributed by lliss S. P. Hayes was well received. A recitation was given by Mr. W. G. Jackson from Scott's " Lady of the lake." Mr. Greenwood was encored for his cornet solo. The "Holy City "was beautifully rendered by Mr. J. Leath- wood, who has attained a grand reputation in his native town—Runcorn—as a tenor singer. He was enthusias- tically received, and was loudly encored. In response to the call he gave a comic song and kept his hearers in good humour all through. At the interval a short meet- ing was held, Mr. James Pritchard (chairman of the Runcorn School Board) presiding. In a brief but en• couraging address, he spoke on the object of their meet- ing that evening which was to raise funds to wipe off the debt now existing on the choir. The choir members he said, had worked hard for the cause and had secured £l5 amongst themselves. This was their first appeal to the congregation, and be hoped it would be met with a hearty response. (Applause.) Refreshments were then provided by Mrs. Timperley, Miss Hayes Miss Hough, Miss A. Dobson, Miss E. Dsb- son, Miss M. Bowl], kiss M. Jones, and other members of the choir. The second part of the programme was then continued. The Misses Warburton rendered a mandoline duet with piano accompaniment in grand style. The song "The Old Soldier," sung by Mr. A. Povah, caused much amusement and was encored. Mrs. Timperley's song "Angus McDonald "was well received. " Very suspicious" (duet) proved very amusing and caused much laughter." Mr. M. Thomas contributed "You can't thirk of everything.' He was loudly clieered and in response to the call sang" Polly,the cow is in the corn." This proved even more amusing than his first, and when he left the stage he was loudly clapped. Miss Warburton (Runcorn) and Miss Wailing (Widnes) were the accompanists. Games, Stc., were then freely indulged in, and the evening's entertainment was brought to a close by the singing of the" Doxology." The proceeds are to be handed over to the organ fund.
CHURCH CONFERENCE AT RUNCORN.

On Monday the annual chapter and conference of the Rural Deanery of Frodsham took place at Runcorn. At the chapter in the chancel of the Parish Church the sub- ject "The seventh question and answer in the ordering ef priests" was opened by the Rev. Dr. Cogmell, And afterwards discussed. The conference was held in the Seaman's Institute under the piesidency cf the Rev. Canon Wood. The 'question of "Church Fin- anee " was introduced by Mr. John White, of Warring- ton, and discussed. The Rev. F. E. Powell, vicar of Over, Winsford, a representative of the Church Worm League, gave an address on " Is disestablishment ones- sary before the Church can obtain any measußt of reform ?" He argued that the measure of disestablish- ment was sure to include a considerable degree of dis- endowment. He spoke of the necessity for reform is the Church of England from the fact that she was aboutthe only institution which during the present century bad not been thoroughly reformed. To maintain much longer an oligarchic institution in the midst of a people accus- tomed te democratic principles was impossible. The Chairman led off the discussion, and remarked that in any great society such as the Church of England there must be occasions when something required to be re- arranged. If Churchmen would bricg pressure to bear an the Government something might be done. Other clergymen and laity considered that reforms were abso- lutely necessary, and the .Rev. G. D. Wray thought if these could not be brought about without disestablish- meat he was ready to go in for it wholesale. The Chairman referred to the pressing question—this federa- tion of schools—and suggested the formation of a com- mittee. On the motion of the Rev.G.D.Wray, seconded by Mr. White (Helsby), it was resolved that the follow- ing gentlemen form a committee to consider the matter with their rural dean :—Messrs. G. Egerton Warburton, James White, A. Horton, and John Littler, the Revs. Canon Hohme, H. B. Blogg, L. J. T. Darweli, and T. W. Sturges.

RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

Wood ward ,J. M. Williams, T. Wright,E. Aaron, J. L,wis, J. Weir, J. Parr,C. Royl- ance.W. Bradfmrd,C. W. Davenport, J. L. Jones, G. Pil- ling,T. Darlisgton; Mr. J. Ashton (clerk),Mr. G. Ashton (deputy clerk), Mr. Farrington (nuisance inspector), Messrs. Diggle and Swinton (surveyors). MEDICAL OFFICIR'S REPORT. . . . .

Dr. Adams reported on the outbreak ot diphtheria at Sutton, where there had been seven cases, with three deaths,and the disease originated in his opinion from the drinking of impure water,tho use of which had discon- tinued after analysis. The water supply now obtained was said to be of a good' quality. He visited the dis- trict the previous day,and found only one case left, in a condition of convalescence, and he had every confidence that the outbreak was now ended. THE RE-APPOINTMENT OF HR. A letter was re:t(i from the Local Goyanment Board sanctioaing the re-appointment of Mr. James Farring- ton,as inspector of nuisances, at a yearly .salary of £l4O a year. TETE ELECTION OF RURAL DISTRICT COUNCILLORS OF

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
( BY A CORRESPONDENT.)

We noted in our issue of last week that the steamship Valde Travers collided with the pierhead at Runcorn docks, and had to proceed to Manches- ter to be overhauled. This again shows the neces- sity of having a graving dock in the vicinity,where boats and ships which have come to grief on the Ship Canal could be repaired,instead of having to go to Birkenhead,Manchester and other distant places. The movement mooted some time ago by Mr. Branch that a basin at Weston Point, coutd be easily and without great expense converted into a graving dock for the repairing of vessels, would, if carried cut,be of greitt advantage to this port;aud would re- quire a large amount of labour. The matter was placed before the Weaver Trustees, who are the owners of the dock in question, but nothing has been heard since. The question is an important one for Runcorn, and should not be allowed to rest.

The result of the four days' bazaar held last week in aid of the Seamen's Mission did not realise as much as was anticipated, but when everything is taken into account it may be considered that the sum realised is a very handsome one. At Friday's proceedings Mr. J. W. Lightburn cangratulated the workers on the success of the bazlar considering the" depressed state or trade." Mr. Lightburn, as well as many other public men, has severely criticised the action of the townspeople in " crying down" the town,yet Mr. Lightburn uses the phrase "depressed state of trade,"which tends to show that it is not the townsfolk but the public men who are "crying down "the town. He referred to the col- lision at the Runcorn docks pierhead,an d its inser- tion in the newspapers. He considered it wap not worthy of notice, as such paragraphs in the news- papers tended very much to the injury of the town. But are the representatives of the press to let such things pass without taking a note? The press would be just as ready to report the progression of trade in the town, as it is to report a depression.

The question of educating the workhouse children outside the house has been the chief subject before the Board of Guardians for the past six months. On Tuesday the discussion again arose, but the Clerk read a letter from the education authorities in Lon- don stating that the Dutton Echool Board were jus- tified in refusing the children,on account of insuffi- cient accommodation. The Guardians felt strongly on the matter of having the children educated out- side,but now there is an end to that proposal—at any rate for the present. They came to the conclu- sion on Tuesday to advertise for a school-mistress for the workhouse. One member made the remark that they would have to wait until the new Educa- tion Bill was passed to see what position they were in.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

What jubilation existed in Runcorn last S.atur- day when the premier team knocked the lights out of their Stockport brothers ! Considerable interest was taken in the meeting, as both teams are Cheshire clubs and are also cracks in the Lancae hire section of the Northern Rugby Union.

Stockport arrived in Runcprn with a strong team in which were included some noted aliens. Run- corn, like Warrington, stick to their own towns- men, and will stand or fall by that determination. The form of both these teams has been watched by football enthusiasts with some interest since the opening of the season, and the result of the meeting on Saturdaywas anxiously awaited by the suppor- ters of both clubs.

Runcorn were without several of their players, whose places had to be filled by A team men. This drawback did not seem to matter a toss to Run- corn, for they played up manfully and ran out win- ners by a penalty goal, tw) tries to Stockport nil. To-day's encounter between the Cup-winners-- and the Runners-up (Oldham) in the Northern Rugby Union last year, will be the chief match in the table this week. Both clubs have played the same number of matches—nine—but Runcorn are five points below the Oldhamites. But with the same team that showed such good football form on Saturday, there's no reason to doubt that to-day's battle will be a stiff one, and the winners—no mat- ter who they may be will have to earn their victory.

div.head: TRADE OF RUNCORN.
div.p: THE TRADE OF RUNCORN.

PROPOSED NEW WORKS. We understand that the directors of the United Alkali Company have decided to erect plant, &c., at the Old Quay Works Runcorn, which will bring in- to the town an entirely new industry and employ a great number of hands. There if also every pros- pect of a soap works being erected at Weston Point in connection with the Costner Kellner Chemical Co., in the near future. Extensive alterations and improvements are to be carried on at the Camden Works of the United Alkali Company, and it is ex- pected that when these are finished, more decided developments will be effected.
