Smith (Widnes), touch judges G. Skidmore (Broughton Rangers) and J. Graham (St. Helens) ; St. Helens v. Swinton, leferee W. Dillon (Warrington), touch judges J. T. Knowles (Warrington) and J. Quirk, (Leigh) ; Tyl- desley v. Wigan ,referee Priestley( Broughton Rangers), touch judges F.W.Smith(VVidnes)and T.Barn6s(Warring ton) Stockport v.Widnes,referee F.Turner (Warrington), touch judges J. Tyrer (St. Helens) and J. Hope (Tyldes Icy) ; nuncnrn v. Leigh, referee J. Underwood (Wigan), touch judges J. Edwards (St. Helens) and R. S. Davies (Broughton Rangers) : Salford v.Morecambe, referee W. ll,lPCutcheon (Oldham),touch judges J.E.Farrell (Widnes) and T. Hancock (Runcorn. ROCLIDALE HORNETS' GROUND AGAIN SUSPENDED.

There was a meeting of the Lancashire Section of the Northern Union in Manchester on Thursday night, when tho Roqhdalo Hornets' spectators again became the sub- ject of inquiry, Mr. J. Priestley (Broughton Rangers). the referee in the match against Wigan last Saturday, having reported them for assaulting him. The official in question,with Messrs. J. T. Knowles Warrington) and G. Wainwrillit, (Runcorn), touch judges, gave evidence and after a long discussion it was decided to suspen,d the ground until December 31. This is a serious blow, as the Hornets will lose four home matches—Warrington, Broughton Rangers. Stockport, and Crompton. The Hornets were granted permission to play the matches L during suspension on their opponents' ground.

div.head: GIJARDIANS.
div.p: GIJARDIANS.

_ Mr. J. Wilson, clerk to the Croydon Rural District Council, wrote with reference to a proposal to petition Parliament to amend the Local Government Act 1894. So far as it provided that the district councillors for any parish in a Rural District should also act as Guardians. It said that in that and other large rural districts, the members appointed found the joint duties too numer- ous and onerous, and that such duties took up more time than business men could conveniently spare. He therefore asked the Runcorn Council to consider the matter and state its views on the subject, and say sviaether it would be prepared to petition in favour of such an !amendment of the Act as would render it pos- sible for Rural District Councillors and Guardians to be separately elected as in the case of Urban Districts.—No I discussion took place and the letter was laid aside.

div.head: COMPLAINT FROM SUTTON.
div.p: A COMPLAINT FROM SUTTON.

Mr. Thomas Yarwo,,d, Sutton, drew attention to the defective sanitary matters at Sutton dock, where the drainage was blocked. As diptheria had been raging, and was Still so, and he having buried one child,and had aeother now attacked, after the house had been disin- fected, he thought it was high time that something was done, tctrovide the houses with a water scheme and !Wove the block to the drainage.—Mr. Farrington (inspector) said the outbreak of diptheria was not at- tributable to the drainage at all. No doubt the drain- age was a little defective, and he had written to the nent upon the matter. The writer of tho letter had no gravid of complaint whatever, as it was well-known that there was a scheme now in operation, and when it was carried out his house would be well supplied. Mr. Yarwood knew all about the house and the drainage, and also the water supply when he took it. He (the inspector) kttributed the outbreak of disease, to his en- terie the house whilst it was in a damp state, and the damp atmosphere that prevailed recently,—The subject was then dropned.

div.head: TRE APPLETON PARIM COUNCIL
div.p: TRE APPLETON PARIM COUNCIL

Mr, Ellison, Chairman of the Appleton Parish Council, forwarded the following copy of a resolution adopted •by the authority :—" That the clerk write to the Rural District Council of Runcorn asking them to lay the drain, fill the ditch,and repair the footpath behind the London Bridge Inn garden, in the parish of Appleton."—The clerk pointed out tikat this was a matter for the Parish Council and the County Council jointly, it being outside the jurisdiction of the District Council. This concluded the business.

div.head: LHE NAUTICAL BAZAAR AT RUNCORN.
div.p: LHE NAUTICAL BAZAAR AT RUNCORN.

The bazaar in aid of the fund for liquidating the debt on th, Seamen's Institute was continued in the Public Hall, Runcorn, on Friday and Saturday afternoons. The proceedings on Friday were opened by Mr. J. W. Lightburn, J.P.,chairman of the Urban District Council, who said he was exceedingly glad to be present that afternoon to as let an undertaking which everyone ought to have at heart. He supposed that they had heard a great deal about bazaars in general, and they had heard for the last three days of the Seamen's In- stitute bazaar. Some people objected to bazaars, but he thought that they Were the best known method by which money could be readily got for such good causes. He remarked that the Mersey Mission was of a twofold character. It had a recreation room and a place for public worship. The more they considered the com- bination the more they appreciated it. The institute existed for the benefit of seamen, of whom they were all proud. The life of a sailor was one of extreme isola- tion. When on a voyage he saw the same men, the same sight—the sky and the water—from day to day and week to week, and when he reached a port he hastened ashore to seek and make acquaintances. There was, therefore, need for a recreation room where these men could meet. [he seamen also met in Runcorn an admir- able missionary. (Hear, hear.) When they got the men into the recreation room they were eaVily induced to enter the place of worsinp. He was glad to see so many present, who had corn,. that afternoon to benefit that noble institution—the Seamen's Mission. Dr. McKenzie proposed a vote of thanks to. Mr. Light- burn, and said that from experience he knew sailors were delighted to have such an institute as the one at Runcorn to visit when in town. If they had no seamen's mission, the meeting house for sailors would be the pub- lic-house. They might get fifty people, but not another Mr. Shaw. (Loud applause.) Mr. J. Taylor seconded the proposition. Mr. W. Shaw, in submitting the motion, said great help had been given to the Institute by Mr. Lightburn, who had attended to the enjoyment of the sailors, by providing a bagatelle cable which had proved a source of amusement. Mr. Lightburn said he was very thankful for the very cordial way in which he had been received. He con- gratulatei the wurkers upon their efforts in making the bazarr a success. They had been long sufferers,not only from depression, but to some extent from partial mis- representation—they had their troubles magnified in a remarkable degree. They saw in the papers the previous day that a ship had come to terrible damage. fie was sorry to s(e it, because the Bridgewater interest and that of the town were identical. He thought, as he had said publicly before, it did the town immense injury to be constantly crying it down. If the little mishap had occurred in Liverpool,it would not have been noted, for the b )at was not damaged. He raised a protest against such proceedings and he hoped the reporters would give publicity to it. The proceedings were then declared open. The bazaar was again opened on Saturday after- noon.

Captain Heasley, in calling upon Mrs. Dig,ges, the wife ' of their secretary, to perform the opening ceremony, spoke of the indefatigable way in which she and her husband had laboured to bring the project to a success- ful issue. He stated that he (Captain Heasley) had been brought up to a sailor's life, and had climbed from the position of cabin bey to that of captain, end he could as- sure them that the work of seamen was very bad in- deed. He also alluded to the value of such an institute as the one provided by the Mersey Mission to Seamen for such a class of men, and it was gratifying to see the use made of the one at Runcorn. The object was one deserving liberal support. Mrs. Dieg,es said she felt gratified at being asked to cpeet the bazaar. She had willingly put forth her efforts on behalf of the object for which the undertaking was being held, and she earnestly trusted that as a result of the bazaar the debt would be liquidated. She under- stood that already £240 had been realised,and she hoped that sum would he greatly augmented during that evening. She had much pleasure in declaring the bazaar open. Mr. H. Grounds proposed a vote ter thanks to Mrs. Digg,es fer her services, which was seconded by Mr. Darlington. Each speaker wished the event to be at- tended with great success. The vote having been carried, Miss Cook presented to Mrs. Digees a very beautiful bouquet. Mr. Diewes, in responding, said the work performed by himself and wife had proved a pleasure to both of them. Their efforts had been put forth on behalf of what to them was a useful and valuable institution. They had already succeeded in considerably reducing I - the debt, and he hoped ere the proceedings closed that the sum raised would be augmented. During each evening a variety of entertaiments was given. The captain of the luggage boat was Mrs. Shaw, and chief officers, Mrs. Lockett and Mrs. Hol- ford. The cloak room was in charge of Miss N. Douglas and Miss E. Mack ; and the parcel office was officered by Mrs.W.Marsh and Miss F. Temple. The name of Mr. Darlinuton also, did not appear among the members of the committee given last week. On Saturday night, on the takings being counted, it was found that the total armour t, with the balance in hand and donations, reached £265.—0n the motion of Mr. Crosby, seconded by Mr William Shaw, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to those who had laboured in connectien with the undertaking.—A compli- ment was paid to Mr. J. K. Digges, the secretary,for his indefatigable exertions, on the proposition of Captain Heasley, seconded by Mr. Shaw.—ln responding, Mr. Digges submitted a vote of thanks to Mr. Shaw and the ' committee, which was seconded by Dr. McKenzie, and unanimously adopted.

div.head: W ESTON.
div.p: W ESTON.

THE SUDDEN DEATH OF IN OLD MAN.—OH Friday afternoon Mr. J. E. Woreley held an inquest on the bod; of Fdward Duncalf, aged 70 years, of Heath-road Weston,who died suddenly at noon on the previous day, The evidence was tp the effect that the deceased was en. gaged repairing a clock in the bedroom of his daughter'- house, where he resided, when he fell and immediately expired. He had suffered from a weak heart for some time. A verdict of death from natural causes was re- turned.
RUNCORN BOARD OF GUA.RDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was held on Tuesday in the Board room at the Dutton Workhouse. Mr. J. Brandreth presided, and there were also present the Rev. Canon Wood, Messrs.& Taylor, J.P., C.C., A. R. Norman, and T. Lea, as well as the members of the Rural District Council, and Mr. J. Ashton (clerk), and Mr. G. F. Ashton (assistant clerk).

div.head: HOUSE COMMITTEE.
div.p: HOUSE COMMITTEE.

This Committee recommended that votes of thanks be given to Mrs. Rigby, and Are. Rogers and party, for their recent concert to the Workhouse inmates. The Committee also recommended that "Bell" light lamps be provided for the house. It was also recommended that the usual Christmas dinner and supper be provided on the 25thfprox.,the dinner to censist of roast beef,plum pudding and half A pint of beer to each adult, and half a pint of milk to each child. For supper the food sug- gested was bread and cheese and half a pint of • beer for adults, and half a pint of milk for each child.—Admiral Parry proposed, and Mr. J. M. Williams seconded.—Mr. Darbyshire moved an amendment that the minutes be passed with the exception of the beer. He did not like Christmas as it was kept in England. It was a day when people indulged in this excessive eating and drink- ing. He thought half a pint of beer was too much for many of the inmates, and he was positively sure that it would be injurious to them. He proposed that the beer be struck out of the bill of fare. He thought tea.coffee, Ice., would do as well and would certainly do more good, and he spoke against the drink in the strongest terms.— The Chairman: The beer is only given to those who care to have it.—Mr. Williams: The inmates are not forced to take beer and can refuse it if they like.—The ori- ginal motion was passed.

div.head: DRAUGHTS IN THE WORILEIGUIE.
div.p: DRAUGHTS IN THE WORILEIGUIE.

The Local Government Board,in reply to the enquiry as to the powers of the Guardians of the Runcorn Union to incur certain expenses in providing. draughts, dom- inoes, &c., for the male inmates of the house said that the Board would not think it necessary to object to such expenditure.—Mr. Heywood proposed that a alny of the letter be given to the Ladies' Committee who had made the above suggestion, and he thought they ought to carry it out. The expenditure should not exceed £5 Mr. Parr said he had suggested billiard, tables to be pro- vided when the matter was up last.. ea war now willing to give £1 as subscripti®n towards• providing such a game.—The expenditure was then limited to £3.

div.head: EDUCATION DIFFICULTY.
div.p: THE EDUCATION DIFFICULTY.

The Education Dvartment writing on the 11th inst . in answer to a communication of the 26th ult., stated that it appeared from the last returns in their Lordship's possession that there was no vacant accommodation at ftlle Dutton Schools. So long as there was not room is the school for the children their lordships would not con- sider their exclusion unreasonable under Article 78 of the code.—Mr. Heywood thought that they would now have to settle down and wait until after the New Edu- cation Bill had teen passed. He proposed that a school mistress be advertised for at the rate of £3O a year.— Mr. Rylance seconded.—Mr. Woody ard said he hoped the matter would not be dropped. Ile was net satisfied with the children being educated in the house.—Mr. Roylance asked if the Local Government Board were informed of the matter would they take any steps Mr. Woodward said most of the children in the house ' were Runcorn children, but they were (whilst in the house) considered inhabitants of Dutton. He thought if some means could be devised to enlarge the Dutton Board school it would be better.—lt was unanimously decided to advertise for a schoolmistress. This was all the tusiness.

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT AT BANK QUAY
div.p: FATAL ACCIDENT AT BANK QUAY
STATION.

An inquiry was conducted at the Patten Arms Hotel, Warrington, on Monday evening, relative to the death of William Ritchie Haycraft, of Lower Hall Farm, Manley, who met with his death at Bank Quay Railway btation the previous Friday evening. Mr. Fenna, solicitor, was present on behalf of the L. and N.-W. Railway Com- pany, and Mr. H. Woods (Ashton and Woods) appeared on behalf of the relatives.

Walter Haycraft, brother of the deceased, gave evid- ence of identification. He said the deceased was 54 years of age. He last saw him alive on Friday morning, when he drove him to Dunham Hill Station, in order that he might go to Manchester. The deceased was in the habit of travelling from Bank Quay station on Tuesdays and Fridays, and always by the same train. Charles Moseley Williams,solicitor, practising in Man- chester,and residing at Helsby, stated that on Friday he travelled with the deceased by the 5.10 p.m. train from Exchange Station, Manchester. At Warrington station deceased suggested that they should change into a smoking compartment. They had been travelling in a second class carriage. As they were walking along the platform deceased suggested that they should obtain some refreshment. Witness said he had no objection, provided there was time. Deceased replied that there was ample time. They accordingly went into the re- freshment room together, and deceased ordered some whiskey and a split potash. The attendant of the bar stated that she had not a large potash, and she served them with two small pnes,which required unwiring. She filled the glass nearest to the deceased, and he took it a little before his (witness's) was filled. As the train was not staying in the station F; long as it sometimes did, owing, he supposedito there not being as much luggage as usual, deceased loft the room immediately he had drunk his whiskey, and witness followed close behind. He noticed that deceased turned to the h ft, presumably to go to a smoking carriage. Just opposite the refresh- ment room door there was a latticed milk truck, and behind that there was a North-Western coach. The train was just gettiog in motion as he (witness) was leaving the refreshment room. Witness not ob- serving deceased thought he had got into a second-class compartment, and he decided that he would get into the nearest carriage and join the deceased at Daresbury. He consequently jumped into a third-class compartment. As soon as he got in he heard shouts and the train was immediately stopped. Deceased was found between the platform and the rails. Winless jumped on the rails and raised the de- ceased's head and asked him if he were hurt, but he did not reply. Witness believed deceased was then dead. His body was removed to a waiting-room. A doctor ar- rived and pronounced life extinct. Deceased was in the habit of travelling by that train, and he (witness) al- most invariably travelled with him. The train was timed to step two minutes, but it very often stepped four or five minutes, owing to the milk traffic. The train was barely moving when he got in.—By a Juror: Deceased was a fairly active man.—ln reply to nix. Fenna, witness said he heard nobody call put that the train was going. He would not swear that no one did she it. He did not know which vehicle passed over deceased.—Witness, replying to a juror as to whether the deceased was of temperate habits, said he had known him for five years, and he had never known him to be intoxicated. - - - -

Elizabeth Clench, attendant at the Bank Quay Station 1 refreshment-room, said on the day in question deceased 1 asked for a Scotch wh'skey and a split potash, with which she served him. She left him to speak to the manageress, and he and his friend went out of the room. Deceased was sober. She could not say whether the train was then moving or n )t. Deceased had been to the refreshment room on two or three former occasions, I and she had never seen him otherwise than sober. Edwin Mitchell, parcel porter, said the train came in from Manchester on Friday night about five minutes past six, and departed at ten past six. He got out the parcels for Warrington and put others in, and as he was going along the platform with a truck deceased passed him as the train was moving. Witness shouted to him that he must not get in. He, however, made a dash for the guard's van, and in trying to get on the step missed his footing and fell on to the platform. He did not see deceased's friend get into the train. There was a Great Western Railway fish truck and five other coaches be- hind the guard's van. When the train started the guard's van was about ten yards past the refreshment room door. When the train was brought to a standstill it was found that deceased had been killed.—ln reply to Mr. Fenna, witness said he rushed to de- ceased, and endeavoured to pull him away from the train, but being a heavy men he was beyond his (witness's) power.—lf he (witness)had stuck to deceased he would have been dragged in also. Mr.Fenna : You did youi best to assist him P— Witness : Yes, but he was too far down for me to get him back.—You are quite sure you called to hire before he get to the van ?—Yes. —How long had you been on duty P—l had just come on.—ln reply to Mr. Woods, witness said the guard was not in the van. It was a Great Western Railway van. Be could not tell whether Great Western vans' foot- boards were not so near to the platform as those of the London and North-Weste n Railway. Decea3ed en- deavoured to jump on to the higher step, not the foot- board, and fell into the space between the end of the van and the next truck. nugh Thomas Williams, the guard of the train, was 1 called, and examined by Mr. Herbert Woods. He said the train came in at 0.3, and commenced to leave the station at 6.5, and it was stopped immediately. The door of the van was at the end. This was always the case with four-wheel vans. He did not know of any difference between the footboards of the Great Western vans and those of .the London and North-Western Rail way. 'The jury returned a verdict of" Accidental death," and exonerated the railway company's officials from blame.

div.head: I GENEROUS ACTION BY CHOIR-BOYS.
div.p: I GENEROUS ACTION BY CHOIR-BOYS.

A very generous action by the choristers of the cathe- dral church of St. Nicholas, Newcastle, has jest come to light, and deserves to be noticed. It appears that the choir-boys of the tensporary church at Weston, which is a large village in the great parit h of Runcorn, have be- stirred themselves to do what they can in helping to build a proper church, and in addition to giving liberally out of their own pockets they have been writing to other choir-boys asking for their assistance. The appeal to the Newcastle lads was sent just before the sth of November, and moved by the zeal and self-sacrifice of the 'Weston lads the Newdastle choristers voted that the money which had been collected for them to spend in fireworks should he sent instead to help in building the church at Weston. It was a beautiful act of self-denial. —" Guardian."
THE P.S.A. MOVEMENT IN
WARRINGTON,
ANNUAL TEA MEETINGS.

Wycliffe F.S.A. Society's annual tea meeting was held on Monday evening, and as has been the case in previ- ous years, was a great success. Tea was provided in Wycliffe Hall, but owing to the large number present, it was impossible to accommodate them all at one sitting, and consequently two sittings were held which some- what prolonged the proceedings. The tables were pre- sided over by the following ladies :—Mesdames R. At- kinson, John Atkinson, W. Travis, F. G. Gleave, T. Gibson, T. Wallington, G. J. Brown, Yonge, W. C. Bris- tow, Robins, L. Crook, J. Brown, Greenhaves, Misses Blease, E. A. Knowles, raul, Porritt, Ada Wom,lsley, L. Wallington, M. rickavance, E. Kershaw, F. Beswick, Cowap, A. Taylor, Shepherd, and were ably waited upon by a number of young men from the two first classes of the Sunday school. During the interval before the commencement of the subsequent proceedings, Lia adjournment was made to the church where an organ recital was given._

Mr. WILLIAM OWE), J.P., presided at the entertain- ment, and in the course of a short address he said he had a thorough-going sympathy with the P.S.A. move- ment. He had a thorough appreciation of a happy Sabbath ,and would do anything to help others to have the same. He did not think there was any workman who dropped his tools on Saturday with greater alac- rity than himselfr and it was a perfect delight to look forward to some rest on the Sabbath. If the P.S.A. meetings gave the members an hour's pleasure,he should say hold them. He had to congratulate them on the great success of the P.S.A. at Wycliffe Church. He re- membered some time back when he was asked to pre- side, the members were only about half what they had now reached. (Applause.) There was another satisfac- tory feature of the rnovement,and that was that it was fairly well self-supporting. It was always a great plea- sure to help those who helped themselves. That was one of the chief reasons he came amongst them to carry out the society's ewn motto, "to lend a, helping hand." (Applause.) Referring to the president -of the society and his recent illn,s3,he said there were Churchmen who had a thorough-going sympathy with all those who were working on parallel lines -a themselves. He was taught that parallel lines would not meet, but he hoped they were running on lines which would converge at the goal which they all wished ta reach. (Applause.)' Whilst con- gratulating them on their self-dependence, they must not forget that they did depend to some extent on the President, and those who Sunday after Sunday engaged in the work connected with it. Their dependence upon them was a matter of great pleasure, and they ought to be grateful to those who helped them to make the meetings so successful. (Applause.) The entertainment was then proceeded with. The first item was a selection by the Wycliffe Orchestral Band who creditably rendered a march under the conductorship of Mr. William Brown. Mr. Arthur Griffiths next sang a solo in his usual acceptable manner. Mr. Furness provoked the audience to laughter by his humorous recitations, and Miss Furness, his daughter, recited "The Curfew." Mrs. R. H. Pearson gave a very effective rendering of" Kathleen Mavourneen," and mtit with a hearty reception. The instrumental selections, in addition to another performance by the band, included a trombone solo " The Death of Nelson," per- formed by Mr. Smith, a selection on the fairy bells by Mr. Sandal!, and a violin solo by Mr. R. H. Pearson ; all of which were given in a praiseworthy manner. A song by Mr. W. H. Wallington brought a pleasant evening's entertainment to a close. Mr. W. H. Payton fulfilled the duties of accompanist. _

A vote of thanks to the Chairman and those who had in any way assisted to the evening's enjoyment was pro- posed by Mr. Hickman, seconded by Mr. B. Farrar. In supporting it, the Rev. John Yonge said he wished to keep the society's unsectarian character distinctly before the people of Warrington. It was started on undenemr inational lines, and he thought they had been loyal to that ides. They had associated with that P.S.A., men belonging to almost every religious denomination in the town, and some attached to none at all, and they had great reason to be thankful for the splendid meetings toy had bad. He hoped that institution had come to stay, as the Americans said, and if it had, lie believed the town of Warrington would be the better for it. (Applause). He wished they could have an experience meeting so that the members might tell them of the good they had derived by attending the meetings. Ho felt certain there were many who had been strengthened in their desire to do right, and had felt assistance in do- ing so, through the P.S.A. (Applause.) The Chairman having replied the meeting terminated.

div.head: Y.M.C.A. SOCIETY.
div.p: THE Y.M.C.A. SOCIETY.

The annual tea and concert in cDnnection with this society was held on Tuesday evening. Over 100 per- sons sat down to tea and did justice to the viands prc- vided by Mrs. Haywi rd. The after-proceedings were presided over by Mr. Th omas Morris, F.G.S. In the course of a short address he said it was very evident from the number present that the Pleasant Sunday Afternoon movement had come to stay with them. (Ap- plause.) It was also an evidence that some good was being done. In fact, he failed to see where any harm could come in. When he considered that the whole of the sixty minutes were taken up by reading the scrip- tures, singing hymns or 5010.% or both, prayers, and a suitable address, it seemed a hard matter to find fault with the ..moventent. That evil-disposed and jealous man did exist, no one could doubt; but why these people taxed their ingenuity to find a screw loose where- by they might, with their fingers and thumb, lake one out and so retard the movement was beyond his compre- hension. Latterly, he bad looked upon these people with, more charity than he used to do, because no i matter what the movement might be, there always was and he supposed there always would be some one to find fault. Even the Sunday school movement had its op- ponents. He would like to ask what would have been the state of attendance at the various places of worship had it not been for the influence of the Sabbath school. The pioneers of that P.S.A. movement had got cause for congratulation as to the number of members. It was not to be expected that all men could if they would, or would if they cceild, join them. Some men preferred staying at home with their wives and family on Sunday afternoon. If there was any compulsion as te attend- ance at the meetings the people would rail, and have just cause to do so and use their vile pens against the movement. (Applause.) It was the other side of the question that presented difficulties to him at first, that ,of finding people to sing and address the meetings. But this difficulty had'been got over, and there was ne lack of old talent, and plenty of new talent continually coming forward. (Applause.) The programme piovided was of a miscellaneous des- cription, and the various items were given in,,a manner that delighted the audience. The vocalists were :—Mrs, R. H. Pearson, Miss F. Booth, Mr. A. Griffiths, and Mr. W. H. Wallinkton. Each vocalist contributed two items to the programme which were well received. For Mr. Wallington's capital rendering of "I would I were a king," the audience demanded an encore, to which he complied. The humour of the evening was suppled by Mr. G. Carter,and Mr. H. M. Ashton, and both received enc ores. The former was very successful in his humor- ous sengs,and Mr. Ashton was again to the fore with his readings. Mr. R. H. Pearson well deserved the plau- dits he received for his musicianly treatment of several violin solos, viz." Ave Maria," " Rondo Perputus " and " Tarentella." Drum-Major Riches, and Mr. F. and Miss Hickman also added to the success of the concert by the performance of instrumental selections. Mr. W. H. Payton accompanied on the piano. During the latter part of the programme, the chair was occupied by Mr. William Roberts. Great praise is due to Mr. Kent, the president of the society, Mr. Hickman, the organist, and the committee for the satisfactory arrangements made.
FAILURE OF CLIESIIIR-E FA.MILERS.-11FITY LIABILITIES. _

A meeting was field on Tuesday afternoon in Manchester of the creditors of George Percival and John Percival, of Parkside Farm, Preston Brook, Cheshire,who traded there and at Bolton under the style of" G. and J. Percival," and who traded at Bolton as hay, straw, and potata dealers, under the style of the " Cheshire Farmers' Supply Stores," and at Greenway-road, Runcorn, as cream and milk dealers. Mr. A. B. Potter,assistant official receiver, who presided over the meeting, stated that the un- secured liabilities which had been disclosed amounted to £11,790 19s. 9d., and the assets, after the deduction of preference claims,te £1,979. The debtors gave as the cause of their insolvency want of capital,low prices of produce,loss by fire in I%larch 1895, loss of stock through disease, dry summers during the last two years, excessive rains dering the past two months, and bad debts in connection with the Bolton business. In reply to a question,it was stated that the debtors were not in a position to make any offer to tne creditors. Mr. Thomas S. Lamb,cbartered accountant,2o Castle-street, Liver- pool,was appointed trustee,with a committee of in- spection.

div.head: NATION'S HEALTH.
div.p: THE NATION'S HEALTH.

It is becoming more and more evident year by year to those who minutely observe the current of internal events and especially the health of the British nation that we are faAt becoming a nation of Dyspeptics. The malady of dyspepsia has spread its effects not only over our own nation, but it is the prevailing malady of civi- lised life. There is no diseaae more prevalent or more difficult to cure. It is a disease of the stomach and as- sumes a variety of different forms in parts of the body far removed from the seat of the disease. Dyspepsia is only another name for the, effects of indigestion and the different forms it assumes as its effects are known by various names, according to the different symptons it presents, as dyspepsia flatulence, heartburn, sick head- ache, pains in the stomach, palpitation of the heart, heart diseases,colic, dysentery, diarrhma, &c. All these and even apoplexy aud paralysis and nine tenths of the cases of convulsions-in children have their source in that defective nutrition to which the term indigestion has been applied. Other causes are worry, anxiety,over work, emotion, stimulants, narcotics. Many persons overload and over- tax the digestive organs which impairstheir powers and renders them incapable of performing their proper film. tions. Constant overworking of the stomach must pro- duce disease of that organ. More nutriment is furnished to the tissues of the body by a small quantity of food well digested, than by a large quantity half digested. The only trustworthy and permanent remedy is Gwilym Evans's Quinine Bitters. rhe Vegetable Tonic, which, acting upon the digestive organs, strengthens them and stimulates them to healthy action, and gives tone to the whole stomach imparting new life, hope, strength and happiness. A HORRIBLE EfOI7SEHOLD AT WARRINGTON.-SIX MONTHS
FOR A NEGLECTFUL MOTHER.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday morning. before Mr. Monks (in the chair), Alderman Harrison, and Mr. J. W. Hayward, Ann Owen,a widow, residing at 23, Dolman's-lane, was charged with having on the 16th inst. and at divers other times during the past six months neglected her children, Zillah twelve years,Arthur nine,William seven,and Anne three,in such a manner as to cause them unnecessary suffering.—la- epector WAteer,N.S.P.C.C., prosecuted,and stated that on the 16th of this month he went to defendant's house in company withlSergeant Smith. They found defendant and two children at home, Arthur and Anne. They were all in a filthy and deplorable condition. The child's body was literally alive with vermin. Arthur was dressed in a few old rags, and his body was in the same condition as that of the younger child. The vermin walked over the outside of his clothes. Witness and Ser- geant Smith went upstairs, and in a corner of the front room found a mattress lying on the\boards. Here there Slept George, aged 15, and two other children. The mat- tress was "black as black could be," and saturated With filth. In another corner of the room was another mattress in the same condition,and on it lay the defend- ant's sister, an imbecile woman of 43 years of age. She was nearly naked, and had no bed covering. Dr. BEM- den subsequently visited the house. There was no im- provement in the condition of the children, and as this was one of the worst cases which had come under his notice since he had been in Warrington he askedfor a conviction. On Sunday night he visited the house and found defendant drunk. She did not know what she was doing. It was almost impossible to enter the house owing to the stench. —P.C. Bell deposed to seeing defendant drunk and find ing the house as described. —Sergeant Smith corrobo- rated as to the first visit. He had never seen a worse case since he came ti Warrington.—Dr. Bowden deposed to visiting the house of the defendant accompanied by Inspector McAteer. He saw the c ildren Arthur and Anne. They were very dirty, and also their clothing,on which he saw vermin. The house was also in a dirty condition. Dr. Bowden described the condition of the mattresses, one of which, he said, fell to pieces whon it was touched.—Defendant: I am very sorry. I have never had anything coming in except what I get from the parish. lam quite willing to work.—Alderman Harrison: You cannot urge anything in mitigation of the accusation against the woman ?—Dr. Bowden: It is a clear case of neglect.—The Inspector, in answer to the Chairman, said he must press for a conviction, as he censidered this to be a very bad case.—The Bench sent the defendant to prison for six months, and ordered that the children and the imbecile be sent to the Workhouse. THE ASSAULT WITH A STEEL BAR AT A WARRINGTON WIRE WORKS.

On Thursday morning before Alderman Sutton (chair- man) Mr. W. Owen, and Mr. S. Wright. at the War- rington Borough Court, John Whitfield, aged 14, was charged with assaulting Thomas Bertram Allen aged 19, at Smith and Sons Wire Works on Wednesday the 11th inst.by striking him on the head with a steel bar;a cress summons charged Allen with assaulting Whitfiald.—Mr F. R. Roberts prosecuted and Mr. Browne defended.— Mr. Roberts stated that the case was adjourned from a fornight ago to enable Allen to attend as he was confined In the Infirmary. The charge was originally one of grievous bodily harm and they now substituted one of common assault only. The bo) s worked at Smith's Wire Weeks, and on the 11th inst. at 6 o'clock, both were on the premises. Allen was going to work overtime, and defendant coming away. As the bell rang. defendant Whitfield rushed to get his coat and fell over Allen's foot This seemed to have irritated defendant and he rushed at Complainant to strike him. Complainant pushed hini away and he fell into the arms of another boy named Pictoc, and then them seemed to have pushed him aboul between them. He lost his temper and picking upa steel bar he struck prosecutor on the head with it just as the latter stumbled on his knees. Prosecutor fell un- conscious and was taken to the Infirmary where he was found to have a wound on the head and a fractured skull. If defendant was pushed about by the other boys and did something in self-defence the-law emphati- cally was that in defending himself no greater violence than was necessary for protection must be used. A steel bar was not necessary in self-defence when defend- ant was only pushed about in fun.—Thomas Bertram Allen, corroborated Mr. Rolants' statement. In answer to Mr. Browne he denied tripping defendant up. Ho admitted attempting to thrash him after the blow With the bar, but he swoomd away. He also denied baying made disparaging use of defendant's sister's name.—David Percival,a workmate of Allen's supborted the latter's evidence. Allen did not put his foot out. The pushing was done in fun—John Henry Picton also corroborated.—Mr. Browne said defendant had teceiv( d great provocation. He complained that he was con- Venally bullied by prosecutor and his mats and on the es—fling in question they forcibly prevented him leav- jut, the works. Allen thumped him and kicked him behind the ear. Ho had been °medically attended ever since.—Dr. Kisby deposed to seeing de- fendant on the 12th and finding a swelling behind his ear and bruises on his iface. They might either have been caused by a kick or blow.—Defendant corrobor- ated Mr. Browne. He said he hit Allen to stop him ill- usinglim.—Complainant denied kicking defendant and said he had lost £2 through being off work.—The Chair- man said the whole thing was the result of a lark and brought about through the boy losing his temper after great provocation. They could not however admit that he wasi right in using a weapon such as the steel bar and fined him the costs and ordered him to pay com- plainant 103, compensation.

MONDAY.—Before Messrs. A. Thernas and G. L. Davies. A RUNCORK PUBLICAN DRUNK ON HIS LICENSED PREMISES. —Samuel Brown, landlord pf the Welsh Harp, Cooper st.. Runcorn, was summoned foe being drunk on his licensed premises on the 17th inst. The defendant was represented by Mr Arthur Browne. of Warrington.—S, rgeant Lee said that on the date named about 10.33 p.m he and P.C. Butler visited the Welsh Harp, and found defendant sitting in the bar-parlour. Witness spoke to him, and then Browne got up and staggered across the room He said he had t urned his housekeeper out of the house and wouldn't have her any longer bee use she had been drinking with the lodgers. (Laughter) Brown left the house to go to the Town Hall (police station) presumably with the idea of proving his sobriety. The defendant staggered along for some distance, and when in Church-street he met P.C. Lakin, then he refused to go any Luther saying if they got him into the police station that they would look him up. He retu wed to his house and after witness had given him some advice, de- tendant closed the house.—By Mr. Browne: He did not think he was exced ding his duty when he advised the de- fendant to close his house.—P.O. Butler and Lakin gave corroborative evidence.—Mr. Browne in addressing the court en behalf of the defendant, explained that his client had kept the beerhouse in question for eleven years without any complaint. On the night named he went at the iuyi- tation of two of his lodgwrs, to a neighbouring fully-licensed house for a whiskey. He had not touched beer for two mouths, and he was not in the habit of taking spirits. He contended that the police evidence was exaggerated, as de- fendant declared he was not drunk, and was capable of , taking eare of himself.—The magistrates thought the case proved, and fined defendant ss. and 11s. 6d. costs. A SAD CASE OF MARRIED LIFE.-11'nrp PollaTd. 14, Manchester-road, Middleton, tanner, was summoned at the Instance of his wife. Ann Pollard, Spark-lane. Halton, for persistent cruelty and neglecting her and her three children. aged 11. 12 and 13 years.—Dr. Carruthers, Halton, said he had known Mrs. Pollard for a greet many years. In 1891, she was suffering from extreme feebleness and general prostra- tion., He attended her for that complaint. She was broken down bodily and mentally. and was unfit for work. Food was given to her by her father. He thought her condition was due to persistent neglect.--Complainant said she was married to the defendant in 1884. She had received from him when in employment 14s. to £1 a week. I atterly she had not rfd, eiverl anything. Her husband had often struck and threatened her. One night at about 10.30 in the month of June. he came to her house and threatened to murder her children. She had to call in P.C. Juett in consequence of his language. Sin^e he had been in his present employrrent. which he got about nine months ago, he had onlw sent her £1 18s. He had struck h r continually during her married life, and she had often to leave the house ow ng to his violence. If it had not been for her friends she w mild have had to go into the work- house.—P.C. Juett and Alice Bllen Dunbabin gave evidence in support of complainant's case.—Walter Gerrard stated that defendant earned 30s. to 355. a week —Defendant said the only cause of the home being in the condition named, was neilectfal wife. If she had acted differently their married life would have been much happier.—The magistrates granted a separation order, and ordered defendant to contribute 12s. a week for the maintenance of his wife and children, as well as the costs.

The exploits of the" Diamond Gang" are providing the penple ef Burnley with some little sensation. Three lads of highly respectable parentage who are believed to he memhers of the " gang " were brought up at the Burnley County Police Court on Tuesday under the fnl- jawing circumstances. A. CONSTABLE AND Co.—Et valuable addition to I biographical works is a new "Boswell's Life of Samuel Johnson," which is to be complete in six 21 volumes. Three of the volumes have already been issued, and are reagable productions of some 300 pages each. An% introduction- to the work is from shoen 'of Mr. Augustine Birrell who relates the his- . torY of the biography in a characteristic and pleas- I ant manner. He does not attempt to vie in erudi- tion with Malone or Dr. Birkheck Hill, and avows his object as being simply to increase the number of Boswell's readers. "The number of persons," lib says, "who have never read 'Boswell's Johnson', and who yet are capable of enjoying it to the tips 0! their fingers, is enormous and yearly increases. . . . There is no book in the whole range of Fnglish literature so richly endowed with those qualities of interest, charm, humour, and life which go to make up enjoymeat as Boswells Life of Johnson. '"Such a word of praise, added to the general public knowledge of the merits of Boswell's' work, ought to go far towards making that acces- sion• to its readers, which is Mr. Birrell's aim. Volume 1 gives as frontispiece a beautiful reproduc- tion of Dr. Johnson's portrait in the National Gallery, and the second and third volumes contain etchings of Lichfield (she birthplace of Johnson), and Lichfield Cathedral. respectively.—A three shillings and sixpenny volume from the same pub- lishers contains "A Sturdy Beggar," and " Lady Bramber's Ghost," two stories by Charles Carring- ton. Both are original in character and make good reading. The first is decidedly unique in that it chronicles the life of a madman, ends up by making a lunatic of the chronicler, and finally installs a subservient personage in the story as chronicler of the chronicler. All this sounds problematical and puzzling, but a perusal of " A Sturdy Beggar" repays itself. There is manifest care in the struc- ture of the tale, some humorous incidents, and clever narrative. " Lady Bramber's Ghost," tells of a being who is first introduced to the reader as a literary thief, a purloiner of another writer's work. Lady Bramber is a novelist and playwright almost worshipped for her genius, and her "ghost," turns out to be the so-called literary thief. Instead of following this disreputable calling, the "ghost," is in reality the creator of Lady Bramber's master-' piece's, and while allowing her the glamour and fame and profit of his work, he contents himself with a pittance which is sufficient to keep him I supplied with what are, in his estimation, the luxuries of life. The cause of this false compact is explained ingeniously by the author, who has a third character in a newspaper-writer with a bent for interviewing.—A novelist who bids fair to at- tain the highest literary honours is Fioha Macleod, I a lady writer who has already made a mark in IHighland literature. Her five books previously published have met with profuse eulogy, and I Miss Macleod is beginning to be recognised as I a writer with a genuis for Pourtraying natural I charms. In an article in the "Academy" Mr. George Cotterell says " It is impossible to read and not to feel that some magic in her touch has made the sun seem brighter,the, grass greener, and the world more wonderful," while Mr. Grant Allen thinks her vocabulary astonishing. The latest work from her pen is" Green Fire," a 6s. volume worth every penny of its price. In no book could the truth of Mr.Cotterell's remark be made more fit,- ting,for the talented authoress clothes her rapsodies on the beauties of nature with such a delicate charm that, the world really does seem more won- derful. For local colouring, insight into character, and power of treatment "Green Fire" is remark- able. Not a page can be reasonably " skipped," and what might be padding in some books is here but an artistic enhancement of the whole. The story is mainly pitched in Brittany, but there is a sojourn in the Highlands which adds .to the Celtic flavour of the writing. As a novel too "Green Fire," is unusually clever and gives full seope to Miss Macleod's power of expressing human sympathies and passions. There is nothing commonplace from one end of the book to the other, but instead, originality of the most striking kind —" Songs for Little People." by Norman Gale,is a delightful little volume of poetry. The author has designed the book for a position between such extremes as the frankly babyish song books. and Stevenson's exquisite memorials of a child by no means typical. Children up to the ages of fifteen are those he wishes,—and has succeeded —to attract. Many of the songs and poems tell of the country's joys and treasures,and about all there is a healthy, joyous tone which must be grateful to their readers. Altogether there are 108 little pieces of poetry. and ts each a most appropriate illustration is supplied by Miss debars Stratton. Miss Stratton seems to have just caught the meaning and requirements of the verses, and pictures them faithfully and skilfully. The publisher, too, has done much to make the book attractive, and the combination between author,artist,and publisher is most marked • Six shillings is the high-class price for this high- class work.—This month a very handsome edition of "The Western Avernus," or toil and travel in further North Americo, by Morley Roberts, has been published. The author in his preface says the book was originally published in 1887. He adds "Though his volume is nsually spoken of as a book of travel, I might prefer to regard it as autobi- ography, seeing that it contains few references to spots nor now well within the range of the mere tourist. It is primarily the story of peculiar per- sonal experience.which many have endured but few recorded." Mr. Roberts has a happy way of relat- ing his exp-riences, and withal eminently descrip- tive, which makes the work interesting reading in stead of resembling a geographical school book. There is no lack of incia.ent and fun and readers of the book will only have one regret, and that is that they were denied the pleasure of its perusal ten years earlier. The illustrations by A.D. McCormick are really splendid, and in keeping with the smartness Of the volume. Other pictures equally pleasing, are from photographs, and altogether there is a gratifying quanity of excellent pictor• ial mattor. The book is priced 7s. 6d.—A special winter number of" The Arrist "is just out. It is a consideration of the art .of Frederick Sandys, and the editor announces that the special edition is issued primarily because Frederick Sandys is an artist whose work has hitherto been unpublished. The chief concern of the publishers is with Sandys the painter, rather than with the illustrator. The half-tone reproductions and photographs which adorn every page are beautifully worked, and the whole number IS 80 goad as to ;lustily the depar- ture the publishers have made in issuing a special number.

MACMILLAN AND CO.—Now that Christmas time is approaching,fathers and mothers will be looking round for suitable presents for the young hopefuls. A book proves often an acceptable gift and there have just been issued three half-crown stories, prettily bound, which are sure to delight the jure- nile mind. Two of them." The Carved Lions," and "Sheila's Mystery," are by Mrs. Molesworth, and the third," Eric, prince of Lorlonia," by the Coun- tess of Jersey. Mrs. Molesworth's work is too well known to need commenting upon here, and it will suffice to say that to those nhildren who have not yet read the two stories mentioned, they will be if not"a joy for ever,"certainly a sourceof pleasure for some time to come.Both'contain;several illustrations by L. Leslie Brooke. The Countess of Jersey's book is dedicated to Beatrice and Arthur. It is a fairy tale of the days of chivalry, and of quite the ap- pcoved kind.. The marvels of the Valley of Wishes forafits base and the story is simple and entertaining.—A new adaptation of Mr. Ruclyard Kipling's works is seen in the Kipling Birthday Book, compiled by Joseph Finn. All the days of the year have a prose and verse quotation selected from Kipling's works, and the usual space for the signature of the person born on each parti- cular day. Most of the quotations are suitable for either a male or female, and they not infrequently prove very apt. It's very peculi- arity makes it a more than ordinarily interesting birthday book. A neat binding encloses the whole.—" Pic George Trssiady," the novel by Mrs. Humphrey Ward. which recently ran through the " Century "magazine has since become a most famous work. Reviewers have devoted columes to praising it highly,and now the same periodical has secured a story by F. Marion Crawford. Thern open- ing chapters. are given in the current number. It is called " A Rose of Yesterday," and will run for six months The story opens in Lucerne,and while it is entirely separate in interest, some of the per- sonages that appear in it will be familiar to readers of " Don Orsino." It is wholly romantic in character.

CASSELL AND Co.—This month's " Quiver " is the first part of a new volume. Particulars of the winter programme have been given in this column, and we will only say now that part 1 fulfils all ex- pectations.—" Cassell's Magazine "will be perman- ently enlarged next month.—The first number of "The Church of England," a history for the people, has just been issued. It is written by the Very Rev. H. D. M. Spence, Dean of Gloucester, and is well illustrated. With this number is pre-

sented a large reproduction plate of " Cranmer at the Traitors' Gate," from the painting by Frederick Goodall, R.A. Each part will be 7d.—A sixpenny monthly edition of "Electricity in the service of man," a popular and practical treatise on the appli- cations of electricity ill modern life, by R. Wormell, D. Sc. div.head: WARRINGTON v.: WIDN,ES
div.p: WARRINGTON v.: WIDN,ES

This return match between the above clubs was played on the Wilderspoel enclosure on Saturday in good weather. There were fully 7,000 spectators on the ground,including a hundred or two from Widnes. Both teams turned out strongly, the only alteration being Jolley in place of Taylor (Warrington) who took his 'place in the front rank of the County team. The players were : Warrington, full back ; Lawless, Cross, Barber, and Moores, threequarters ; Houghton and Higgin- , bottom, half-backs ; Nevins, Hill, Scholtze,Swift, Jolley, Roby, Thornton, and Barratt. forwards. Widnes, Baty, full back; Peters, Rispan, Nevitt, and Brennan, three- quarters; Drummsnd, and Alford, half-backs ; Emery, Donnelly, Handley, Johnson, J. Acton, T. Acton, Hemp- son, and Hunt. forwards. Widnes kicked off against the wind, and the ball go- ing in touch it was ruled back. After exchange kicking play settled down in Warrington quarters and the homesters had to defend. A penalty kick gave n 3 re- lief as Baty returned well, and Drummond getting possession also kicked for touch. • Houghton charged down and gathering the ball up raped along the field and passing to Higginbottom that plas3er" kicked like scoring, but his kick sent the ball dead. This sudden relief seemed to freshen the homesters up and both Higginbottom and Houghton kicked with good judg- ment. Baty failed to return smartly and the homesters struggled bard on the line. Houghton transferred to Lawless who kicked into Baty's hands, and again the visitcrs' full back failed to make use of It. Passing movements between Higginbottoni, Hoifghtoo, and Moores were very useful and Hill finished up well by finding touch at the cerner. Widnes were again penial- ised, and Thornton failed at goal. Nevins charged a kick down and a score seemed certain, but Baty luckily got his foot under the ball and put it in touch near the line. Play was very fast, and the visitors were hard put to it to keep their lines intact. Another.strong dash was made by Barber, and Lawless relieving him of the ball had hard lines in being pulled up. All this pressure could not but result in something,and at length Eloughton took the initiative and stepping from behind the scrimmage dropped a neat goal amidstloud cheering. Drummond restarted and 'Nevins was soon on the way but was grassed at the 25. Houghton gained ground by a fine kick, and getting possession again he passed to Cross. The latter dodged the opposing backs, and running from near the half way line, he passed to Barber, who raced round and put the finish to a brilliant effort by grounding near the posts. Lawless made a very good attempt to convert. Immediately the game was in full swing again Warring- ton assumed the aggressive. A kick from Heesom sailed towards the Widnes goal. Rispin missed the ball and it rolled between his legs over the line, where Baty was luckily at hand to save. A moment later half-time ar- rived with the home team leading by seven points to nil.

Hill set the ball rolling again and Nevins was soon in possession. With a lengthy punt he put his side well an the aggressive. Widnes, however, showed more deter- mination. and Drummond relieved splendidly. Baty returned Houghton's kiole from the scrimmage, and Bar- ber landed the leather close to the Widnes line again. The visitors' forwards got away strongly but Thornton fell on the ball. Still the game travelled to the home half and Rispan dropped unsuccessfully at goal. A couple of!good marks were made by Baty but neither came to anything. A pass went wide out to Lawless who raced to the Widnes 25 before being tackled. Another kick reached Baty who this time dropped at goal,but could not emulate his feat of three weeks ago. Moores returned and by a smart follow tackled Brennan before he could kick. Widnes now pressed strongly but showed no combination in their efforts. Nevitt gained headway by kicking and Higginbottom relieved by a run and kick. More forward dribbling was checked in plucky fashion by Moores. Lawless accepted a pass and made a fine sprint but was ruled back for off side. The homesters now repelled the attack energetically and a tricky run by Higginbattom along the touch line caused Widnes to defend. A neat bout of passing between the home backs showed Barber and Lawless prominently but no score was effected. The referee,a substitute,blew the whistle a little before time owing to the darkness. War- rington thus won by one dropped goal one try k 7 points) to nil.

RUNCORN v. S COMPORT. The encounter between these twe Cheshire organiie- . tions created a vast amount of interest, the matches played by them being of a most popular character. The game was awaited with more than ordinary anxiety, seeing that the visitors hitherto had net sustained a single defeat during the present season. The home team were short of the services of Richardson, who is on the injured list, and the vacancy was filled by Nickson. Stockport turned out as selected, so that their best avail- able team did duty, they being desirous to keep their escutcheon unsullied. The weather was fine, but dull, • and the ground was in good condition. There was also a large attendance, the enclosure being surrounded by fully 4,000 spectators, many of whom are followers of the visiting players. On stepping into the field, it was found that the following was the composition of the teams :—Runcorn Houghton, back ; Warder, Myers, Bntterworth, and Nickson, three-quarters; G. Robinson and J. Faulkner, haif backs; W. Faulkner, Walker, Farmer, Langley, Shepherd, Liehtfoot, Reece, and Gay- ter, forwards. Stockport : Saville, back ; Bailey, Sands,; Worsley, and Robinson, three-qu trters ; Mien and Booth half-backs ; Gareidci Roberts, Milligan, Mottershead, Speet, Gibson, King,`and Wrigley, forwards. Saville started for -:tockport, and J. Faulkner made a poor return into touch. Houghton immediately after made his Mark and punted to Saville, who put in a good return. Runcorn got to the centre, and Warder broke away but was collared. A free kick to the home team was taken by'W. Faulkner, who sent the ball in touch in the Stockport half. Houghton was now conspicuous with a fine kick, which Saville returned feebly into touch. The visitors got to midfield, where toe home contingent engaged in passing, but a knock on spoilt the chance. W. Faulkner got possession and passed to Robinson, who gained ground by running. Stockport now get away with dribbling, but Houghton gat posses sinn and cent into touch. After scrummaging in th- centre J. Faulkner dribbled away and Saville was col- lared before he could return. A free kick to Runcorn saw Warder place a splendid goa The referee ruled it back, however, and on trying a second time the ball I went outside. On restarting the visitors a tto the cell- ' tre, where Warder a moment afterwards placed a splen- did goal from a free kick. Runcorn pressed. Robinson. of the visitors, got away, but Butterworth collared him in fine fashion. The home forwards now put in some splendid dribbling, Walker kicking the ball over the Stockport line, and Geyter rushed up and scored. T. Warder took the kirk at goal, and had extremely hard lines, the ball striking the upright ann beunding back again. On the resumption Bailey got away, but Butterworth stopped his career. 4nother bout of passim: by Runcorn put Stockport on the defensive. J. Faalkner received the oval from Lightfoot, and,dodging the visiting backs,scored a grand try. Warder took the kick at goal, which was charged down. Play now Bet- ted in the visiting half. Saville made his mark, but did not gain much by the kick. Half time—Runcorn, one penalty goal two tries ; Stockport, nil. After the inter- val W.Faulkner started for Runcorn, R)hineon returned to Butterworth, who in turn kicked to Bailey. and the latter put in a grand kick, and the Stockport forwards dribbled away into the home half, but Houghton and Butterworth stopped the prog,rese. W Faulkner got away with a grand run and passed to Robinson, who failed to take the pass.and a scrummage ensiled. Stock- port now get near the Runcorn line, but J. Faulkner received from a scrummage and put a grand kick into touch. Stockport again pressed, forcing Houehtnn to kick dead. On resuming Sands put in a fine return, and a moment later Robinson and Sands engaged in passing but did not get past the centre. After a scrummage Nickson get,away and passed to Butterworth, who knocked on and later Robinson for Stockport inter- cepted and got away. He kicked to lieu ihtein, who dodged through several men amid laud applause. But- terworth took up the play, and looked like a scorer, after making a brilliant run, but Saville brought him down close on the line. The closing play was very ex- eiting,and of a keen and interesting description. Run- corn.however.held their own,and won a fine open game, the result reading Runcorn, one goal, two tries ; Stok- port, nothing. WARRINGTON ST. MARY'S v. LEIGH " 4 "TEAM.— Played on St. Marc's ground on Saturday. Leigh win- ning the toss, Celiiwell started, no return being made. The Saints made a determined rush to the Leigh lines, but the Leigh forwards worked the ball to half-way, and then pressed for a time, but Roughley relieved with a good kick to half-way. Jackson, of Leigh, almost landed a goal from half-way, the bill hitting the up- rights. From the kick off the Saints immediately began to press,and Rnughley's kick at goal was charged down, and after a series of scrimmages Gregory got away, but only a minor resulted. The juniors again got in the visitors' qu4rters, when half-time arrived with no score.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

WARRINGTON V. MANCHESTER WANDERERS—On Satur- day Warrington journeyed to Manchester with only ten men. Connor,losing the toss,kicked off against a strong wind,and three minutes' play yielded the first point to Warrington, E. Pierpoint sewing with a beautiful drop- ping shot which fell just underneath the bar. This was followed quickly by a goal from Williamson, who shot through from a partial clearance of the home goal- keeper's. The visitors, having once scored, kept the Mancunians busy,and after a fine run by Connor on the left Carroll netted the third from a beautiful centre by his captain. This roused the home Vasa to a sense of their responsibility,and after several vain attempts they beat Webster with a grand shot. The game slowed down considerably,and nothing further was scored until the interval ; score 3-1. On re-starting, with the wind in their favour,Warrington press.3d immediately, but tile , Manchester halves playing very smartly prevented anY scoring for some time. Warrington having obtained a good lead, took matters somewhat easily until about quarter of an hour off time, when they put on a spurt, and goals were seored by Jewkes and Carroll. After the kick-off Connor dribbled half the length of the field, and Williamson put the finish to the fine effort by banging the ball into the net. Just as the call of time Connor scored 'again, and the whistle sounded leaving Warring- ton the winners.l2,y seven gnats to one. Warrington teard :—Webster.loiroughall, Marshall,R. Connor, Carter, Pierpoint, Jewkes, Carroll, Williams, and E. Coonor Kpaptain). PENKETEI v. WARRINGTON N.E.—This match was played at Penketh on Saturday, and turned out to be a much better game than was anticipated by the Dome team and supporters. The bill was set in motion at 3 15 p.m.' the visitors having the advantage of playing down the hill. Notwithst ending this Penketh at once made for the visitors' goal, and within a few minutes scored the first point. Half time was reached with the scare—Penketh, four goals; Warrington, ii. Shortly before half 'line, Warburton, the home riget fullback, had the misfortune to strain his knee, and was disabled for the rest of the game. In spite of a capital defence and plucky play by the visitors ranketh still kept up pressure, and before the call of time had added two more to the score, so that at the finish the hortie team were victorious by six goals to nil. Of the six eals E. Davies scored twice in good style, G.Plumpton (who was a decided success at centre-forward) twice,F. Siogleton , once, and E. Dumbell once.

STOCKTON HEATS TEMPERANCE V. DARESBURY..--"Played at Daresbury in fine weather. Risky started for the visitors, who were soon pressing. From a good pass, Banks opened the scoring account for the Heathens, and before the whistle blew for half-time Risley had Put two goals through, thus at half-time the visitors were lead- ing by three to none. Leech started down-hill for Dares- bery, but good passing by the Temperance forwards, the leather was soon in the home quarters, aod Ranks again scored for the visitors. After the restart Risley and Robin scored. Daresbury afterwards pressed strongly but they were unable to pierce the defence of the Heathens. Daresbury were next penalized again Risley again shot through from a corner taken by Robin. When the whistle blew for time, the score read—TedlPorance seven goals to Diresbury nil. WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT LEM:ME.

PRASLEY CROSS V. RUNCORN kssocrwrion.--This match was played at S. Helens on Saturday. Runcorn arrived with nine players only, but the services of two good substitutes were secured, and the Blues team was as follows : Goal, Rough; full backs, Stoneley and Timpsrley ; half backs, Littler, Jones, and Clarke ; for- wards, Deegan, sub, Mitchison, P. willianss, and sub. T. Cox won the tose and elected to play with a strong wind behind him. Mizchison started and the ball was soon taken near the home goal,and it looked very riuch like leading to a score. For about ten minutes the visi- tors kept up the pressure, but were at last cleared out by a lo og kick by Moss. and Taylor and Co. were soon Peppering away at the Blues' goal, but the defence of Stoneley and his partner was sound, the ball being well cleared several times. kt length,however,Taylor found an opening and scored with a good shot. The home team now played brilliantly forcing several corners, and the score was rapidly increased, half time arriving with the home team five goals ahead. The second half was finely contested, and the Blues had exceedingly hard lines in not scoring on two or three occasions, shots be- ing sent in from all directions. The homesters were again able to pierce the Blues' defence through a blun- der by one of the backs, and the game ended with the score Peasley Cross, 6 goals; Runcorn, nil:

div.head: COMMON DISEASES. 4.-THE LIVER.
div.p: COMMON DISEASES. 4.-THE LIVER.

The liver is the largest organ in the body,and has mul- tifarious duties to perform in the internal economy of the digestive system. After tho stomach•it is the most abused of all the digestive organs. It is inflamed and hardened by the abuse of alcohol, and its functions are hindered and impaired by the tannic acid, the outcome of tea drinking. Errors in diet lead to a diminished se- cretion of bile. It becomes torpid and sluggish and the defects react on the blood current—deleterious products are carried into the circulation—the skin becomes muddy and yellow,the tongue furred. Life becomes a burden and the victim says" Life is not worth living." He flie , drugs, blue pill, and other quack nostrums, and finds a temporary relief, and a rebound to a state worse than before ; destroys his digestion by nauseous medicines nod liver pills and wonders why he continuPn dull,languid, cranky and out of sorts. He never pauses to consider the why and the wherefore, but continues to either doctor himself, or is doctored by others into a confirmed melancholy invalid who invariably shuffles off the mortal doil of a miserable life, through making his stomach a receptacle for all the so-called liver cures in the phrmacopeeia. There is only one method- to maintain the liver in good working order, and that is attention to Diet and Exercise. Happy is the man or woman who does not know they have-a liver! Unless this mighty organ duly perfa,rms its principal function of secreting bile, a whole army of troubles arise. , It cannot be done with medicine.

div.head: GIGANTIC WEIEEL AT NEW BRIGHTON.
div.p: THE GIGANTIC WEIEEL AT NEW BRIGHTON.

The fact that no less tnan 11,000,000 people are an- nually carried to and fro by the Wallasey Ferries has at last attracted the attention of capitalists to cater for the enormous crowds visiting the breezy shore of New Brighton. The whole of the prominent and admir- able freehold site on the sea front row occupied by the Palace and tea saloons has been purchased by a syndicate, and the place is to be transformed into a veri- table fairyland. The principal attraction is to be a great wheel which will far exceed in magnitude the wonderful money making wheels at Chicago, Earl's Court, and Blackpool. The marvellous panoramas of shipping in the Mersey should afford a grand spectacle from the top saloon over this wheel which will be about 350 feet above sea level, and will communicate at vari- ous stages with spacious saloons and terraces which may also be reached bY a central lift. A Company has been formed entitled New Brighton Graydon Castle Great Wheel and Towers Co., Ltd., to take over the valuable' estate and to carry out immediately the necessary works which, including ihs freehold, will amount to £130,000. The Palace will be reconstructed and opened next season so that a considerable revenue will be secured during the building of the wheel. The local authorities will construct a handsome promenade along the front, and a Marine Pier is to take the place of the contiguous waste groend and sand dunes. If only 1,500,00 of the 11,000,003 pses,•ngers pay for admission it is estimated that the net profits will be at least 50 per cent. The Company will enjoy a sifbitantial income from rentals of shops and r-.staurants along the front. Messrs. New- by and S m of NI anehes:er, are the architects and Mr. J. E. Tuit, M. Inst. C.E., who was one of the engineers en gaged on the Forth Bridge Works will supervise the erection of the wheel.

div.head: GREAT_SANKRY SCHOOL BOARD
div.p: GREAT_SANKRY SCHOOL BOARD

A meeting of this Board was held on Tuesday evening in the Board School. Mr. T.Halton occupied the chair,- and there were also present 'Messrs. j. Wright,H.Bate,W.D. Jeansjun,(clerk), and G.Clarke kschoolmaster). The CLERK informed the Board that Miss Jordan had written tor the month's salary she had earned. He explained that she had left without giving proper notice, and really ought to forfeit the month's salary and another two months' as well. The Board, however, decided to pay her salary.—Two tenders were received for the coal contract, one from the Warrington Slate Com- pany and the other from Mr. Denham. It was decided to accept Mr. Denham's contract.--The Clerk reported that for the week ending October 31 there were on the books 345. present 336. average 311. 4,fees 123. 61.; week ending November 7, on the books 344, present 322, average 273.1, fees £1 ; week ending November 14, on the books 342, present 315, average 384.4, fee 4 _el 0 81 ; week end- ing November 21, on the books 348. present 324, average 289.9, fees .£1 84. Average for the month 2891,10tal fees £3 13,;. 21. There had been an out- break of measles among the young children at Sankey Bridges, and several had been absent from school. The borough attendance officers took over the children up to Sankey Brook on November 9th. Registers of attendance were forwarded by them to be filled in each week that all absentees might be visited. The chairman had kindly offered prizes for the best attendances for the past year. The schoolmaster prepared a list of the best attenders in each class according to his instruction, and good prizes have beechesen suitable for presentation. The report was ad4ted.--Miss Sykes was appointed assistant mistress at a salary of £45 per year.—This was all the business of importance.

div.head: SHIP QAN AL.
div.p: SHIP QAN AL.

LAST WEEK'S TRAFFIC. During the week ended Friday, Nov. 20, 180 sea-going cargo vessels, with an aggregate net registered tonnage Of 44,086 tons arrived at and cleared from tbe port of Zdanchester, as compared with 139 vessels of 40,086 tons in the corresponding week crf 1895. Thirty-four vessels of 24,454 tons arrived from or cleared for foreign ports, and 146 vessels of 19,632 tons arrived or sailed coastwise. General cargoes were imported from Bordeaux, Copen- hagen'and Stettin, Hamburg, Rouen, Paris, Treport, Eoulogne, Rotterdam, Ghent and Antwerp, and New York ; timber and wood pulp from Gefle, Riga, Cron- tadt Gothenburg, West Bay, Halifax, Shediac, and 'Pe Tormentine ; fruit from Valencia and Nova Scotia, '°tton from New York and Galveston, grain from Riga arid the United States, iron from Sweden,,and bone-ash from the River Plate. Five steamers left for Con- tinental ports, three for the Baltic, and one each for Galveston, the Mediterranean, and Bombay.

A NEW LIGHT.—EXPERIMENTS AT WARRINGTON The number of competitors with coal gas as an illuminant seems to be on the increase, and one of the latest is acetylene gas,which has been described ' as the light of the future. It has recently been in- troduced into this country, and the agent for War- rington and district is Mr. J. S. Garland, Bridge-st. In order to see the new light under various condi- tions a reporter of this journal was invited to visit Mr. Garland's premises. On doing so he found the new light being experimented with by Mr. Taylor, Police Court Missionary, with a magic lantern. 'The new gas gives a brilliant white light—very similar to lime light—and owing to the ease 'and rapidity with which it can be manufactured, it Should prove very popular with lanternists. The generators in which the gas is made are of various sizes. The smallest covers an area of less than one foot, and stands about a foot and a half in height. It consists of an external receptacle provide I at one side with an aperture and tap by which to turn on the gas when needed. Within the external receptacle there is another cylinder, suspended by its upper part and not reaching the bottom of the Outer one, and as the gas is being used, this ascends and reaches its full height when the gas has been Used. In order to make the gas, the consumer has simply to provide himself with the necessary quan- tity of water and cacium carbide and he can make the gas in less than lice minutts. The quantity to be used, varies, of course, according to the size of the generators, but for the smallest size one lb. of the carbide is sufficient. It is supplied in rock forro and is dissolved within the generator by Water. The cost of the lb. of carbide is about seven- Pence, and this will produce a light of 60 candle Power for seven hours. After this period, it will be necessary to recharge the smallest generators, but in the larger ones, the manufacture of the gas can be carried on unintermittently. One of the ad- 'vantages of the light is that it is more cleanly than gas, and will not blacken the ceilings. It can be connected with ordinary gas fittings, and the light regulated according to necessities by different burners. Those who saw the experiments were con- vinced of its usefulness, especially for portraiture, copying, enlarging, and magic lantern purposes. It ould also be a great, ad vantage to people residing In the country districts where coal gas is not ob- tainable.

div.head: LOCAL HOCKEY MATCHES.
div.p: LOCAL HOCKEY MATCHES.

STOCKTON HEATR V. GRAPPENHALL.—The above match Was played at Stockton Heath on Saturday, in perfect Weather,and,after a very tast and exciting game,resulted in a victory for Grappenhall by nine goats to seven. As the score indicates, the attack en each side was better than the defence, the rushes of the Stockton Heath for- Wards, headed by Kirkconnell, repeatedly troubling the Grappenhall rear rank, whilst the passing of the visitors completely baffled the opposing backs. For the home team Kirkconne:l,Gornall,and Richardson were the pick. The goals were scored for Grappenhall by Pearsom (4), Carter (2), Spence, Albinson,and Jenkins one each. PRNKETIL PARK V. CROSSLEV'S--Crossley's (Menthes- tee) played the return match with Penketh on the lat• ~ter's ground on Saturday last. rhe visitors arrived at 0-30, being 3 men short. Substitutes were found and the game commenced shortly before 4 p.m. The Pen- keth team quickly had the upper hand, and pressed hard 11, In were untucky in shooting. Bowyer scored for Pen- Rest!) in the first half. On resuming play after the inter- val it was almost dam, Appleton scoring shortly after the start. Play now became almost impossible, and after tetOminutes the referee closed the game, it being :141Possible to see the ball.—The score was Penketh 2 4°4k, Crossley's nil, Penketh are playing a great deal 'better lately and th)roughly deserved this, their first win.
