div.p: GR A. PHIC ACCOUNT OF A VISIT TO A
mANCHESTER PALACE OF INDUSTRY.

The Press is the most powerful lever of modern civilisation. The pulsations of thought. words. and actions cabled each day, flashed from every quarter of the globe. are conveyed to the human brain by means of the Press. This constitutes the Press the most interesting, the most instructive, and the most fascinating invention and production of the m arch of in- tellect. Kings. Emperors. and Governments have been swept from power by means of the Pres. Both geod and evil ewe naeh to the influence of the Press. The newspaner forms the chief source of delight of interest. and of instruction et the morning breakfast-table. If the newspaper and ?enly ceased to exist, then half the enjoyment on the wo Id would cease also. Even the advertisement columns form a source of pleasure to many readers, The ladies carefully examine their Societe papers for fashions sa'es of milinerr and dress- goods have special interest for the ladies. It. was whilst care- fully noting the heads of different advertisements that I was attracted by the unique announcement of a Gigantie Fur- nishing Establishment at GANTIInRN, Manchester. I determined, after consultation with my wife, to proceed to " The Pantheon." ct Gaythorn. in order to test the aeon- racy of this advertisement. Accordingly we set out, and eventually reached Piccadilly. We made straight for the. " Royal Hotel," at the corner of Mosley-street, and after in- quiry we then took a car bound for Alexandra Park, which' we were informed. passed the very door of "The Pantheon ' at Gaythorn, which is close to the Central Station. We requested the guard to stop the car at " Worslev's." fln arriving there we found that" The Pantheon "was a palatial structure, being nothing less than an Immense Warehouse. with huge plate-glass windows forming a frontage of over 100 feet. We had hardly patience to examine the windows, so great was our anxiety to examine the interior. An' icination is often more enjoyable than realisation. hut in this case rea- lisation altogether overwhelmed our anticipation. Our visit to " The Pantheon" proved to be most enjoyable. Upon examining the windows our attention was riveted noon a magnifiaeat display of Clippendale Furniture, beautifully earved in

BAS-RELIE LP It is the Finest Exhibition of Furniture of this class that I have ever seen The Cabinets are orig'nl.l in design, and from what we learnei afterwards are the very latest— specially drawn and manufactured for Worsley's. I also noticed some very high class Pollard Oak Furniture for the dining-room, magnitlcent specimens of bedroom furniture, besides a miscellaneous collection of household requirements. There were many other specimens of furniture on show ; but we shall now proceed inside the premises and attempt to give a brief description of what we saw there. Coon passing through the entrance we were immediately struck with amazement ty the

(ORGEOIJS DISPLAY. 3- The ground floor of this establishment, we were in- formed. had just been re-modelled and re-furnished. Mv wife immediately expressed astonishment and admiration at the very unique display of the most beautiful and exquisite furnitnre we have ever teen. 111tignificent sneeimens of bed- room fu niture of the very highest, class. at 75, 85, 100. and 150 guineß.s. We saw the most perfect, the most charming. the most delightful bodroom suites in Chippendale mahogany that it has ever been our pleasure to inspect. Their steck is so immense that you can hnv a bedroom suite for £3 155.. or you can per. chase one for 150 guineas. Continuing our insnection of the ground floor, I must meetion that the place is beautifully lighted by electricity. You can, therefore, see everything distinctly. Specimen suites of Oin'tig-room Furniinre in Pollard oak, sp Timen suites of Dining-room Furniture he Chippendale mahoriny of the most delightful design were marked in plain figures at extremely low prices. Our next attraction was the Carpet Showroom upon the same floor. The display did credit to the gentleman who is in charge of this desartment. Rnd was remarkable in some instances for the delicate and artist;c prism tie effect ~ while in other cases they present a goreenus embellishment of de`igiAful hue arid brilliance I noticed that the best productions of the newest patterns for next spring have actually been secured already, and we w.-re given to understand that the next spring's patterns have not yet been shown to any comp... div.head: BIMETALLISM AND BRITISH INDUSTRIES.
div.p: BIMETALLISM AND BRITISH INDUSTRIES.

Sir,—At present, what is the need of all engaged in industry ? All say," Higher prices for produce." How is legislation to bring this about ? Some say, "Restore Protection." But the greatest authorities on agriculture and on the economic and monetary causes of industrial trouble ; the Central Chamber of Agriculture ; all the important members of the present Cabinet; the edu- cated majority of the Bank of England Directors ; every British Professor of Political Economy ; the leaders of the Trade Unions ; an unprecedentedly unanimous array of leaders of every industry and interest ; " every able man who studies the question" ; say, "Restore Bimetallism, and thus correct the insufficient quantity of metallic money and the lost parity (steady exchange value) between the gold and silver monies of the world." The whole United States are unanimous—" seventy millions solid "—for International Bimetallism. Western Europe is only awaiting the lead of Britain. The in- dustrial outlook is very grave. The duty of British citizens is very clear. Bimetallism and its aims and British dangers are vividly shown in Gundry's " Asiatic Peril "and other pamphlets obtainable gratis from me. These pamphlets require serious attention. But the enfranchised citizens of a worldwide Empire, based on commerce and productive industry, can surely, in face of a widespread industrial calamity, with its clearly in- dicted cause, nerve themselves to such slight mental effort and moral self-disciplinesas is shown by every one when young in his mastery of historical and geographi- cal facts. " The price of liberty is eternal vigilance." I am, sir, yours, &c., ELFIIINSTONE V. A. MAITLAND. Edmendsham Tower. Bournemouth.
THF. BOARD OF GUARDIANS AND THE BRABAZON SCHEME.

Sir,—l notice with surprise and regret that the Guar- dians have not only declined to adopt the " Brabazon scheme" but (according to your report) seem unwilling to consider the subject on its real merits, or to tolerate the question in any shape or form ; indeed, only one member of the Board thought it worth while to argue or discuss the matter at all, and his very pertinent speech was altogether in support of the scheme, dismissed with such scant courtesy by an unthinking m...jority. Surely a system that has had the commendation of so many important" Unions "is entitled to more consideration than it has received in Warrington.—Yours,
- J. RYMEti YOUNG. Warringtoa, November 20th, 1896.

Sir,—Will you allow me a short space in your columns to enter a protest against the action of our Guardians as notified in your issue of last Saturday. I write as a business man, as one perhaps quite as deerly interested as a humanitarian, and possibly at least as interested as a ratepayer, as any member of the Board. The paint to which I desire to call public attention is the utter hol- lowness of the arguments advanced against the Brabazon Employment Scheme; in fact so hollow are these argu- ments that it is obvious that the speeches made were concerned rather in veiling the real reason than in ex- pressing them. The question therefore arises what lies behind? Why this hyper-sensitive care that the master and matron should in no way be inconvenienced? Why is this scheme which has succeeded elsewhere so unsuit- able for our workhouse? Why must our poor inmates be denied the kindly services of the charitable that are allowed in other unions? There must be a cause for this. Is it a worthy one? A heavy responsibility rests on those who deny to the old, the penniless, and the in- firm any crumb of comfort that may be offered to their declining years, and the Warrington public is certainly entitled to some better explanation than any which has as yet been forthcoming. In the absence of any fit justi- fication, it surely behoves the electors to remember that the Guardians are appointed by them, and to see, when the next election comes round that justice is done. Of course to the credit of the Board it will be remembered that while upon ten rests the responsibility of its rejec- tion, nine stood up in favour of the scheme—Your obediently, A RATEPAYER. Warrington, November 19th.

Sir,—l venture in a few words to call the attention of your readers to the very SeriOtl9 step recently taken by our Board of Guardians, as reported in your issue of Saturday last. It was with sincere regret that I noticed that the adoption of the Brabazon Scheme for providing interesting occupations for the aged and in- firm inmates of our workhouse had been rejected by a majority of one. rho scheme is one which had been most carefully considered. It came before the Board with a remarkable amount of evidence in its favour from numerous Unions where it has been accepted. It was moreover made perfectly clear that it would involve the Board in no financial responsibility whatever. It was, however, rejected, and in my judgment without adequate cause shown. I believe that any impartial reader of your report will agree with me, that all the argument was on one side,and that the side favourable to the adoption of the scheme. There was apparently no attempt to criticize the scheme iteelf, or to rebut the large amount of evidence brought forward in its favour. The opposition seems to have relied !von the two fol- lowing pleas—firstly, that Probably the scheme wonld net work, and, secendly, that it might conceivably cause some inconvenience to the permanent officials of the Workhouse. Now I am not aware that the circum- stances g the Warrington Union are so exceptional that a scheme which works with good effect elsewhere,would be found useless here. But even if this be so,the failure of the experiment could do no possible harm except in the inevitable disappointment of the ladies, who wish to devote themselves to the work. But, if these ladies are willing to incur the risk.need the majority of the Board be solicitous about their feelings The second plea mte appear to have more weight until we remember that the scheme need inveeve the officials in no extra work, and that, oven if it did, the officials exist for the good of the inmates and net the inmates for the good of the efficials. There is evidence that in other unions the officials have welcomed the introduc- tion of the scheme most gladly. I submit than that the majority of the Board have not in this case acted in ac- cordance with the best interests either of the public or of the inmates of the workhouse who are under their special care ; and we as their constituents have a right to expect more intelligible reasons for their decision than those they have given.

Most of those who have any real interest in the work- ing of our poor law system agree that it wants to be humanised in many of its departments. It must be re- membered that in every large workhouse there is a num- ber of aged and infirm inmates, many of them the vic- tims of terrible misfortune. There is something very pathetic in the thought of these people, living listless and aimless lives, growin.: weary of themselves through the very monotony of their existence, just waiting till the pauper's grave shall claim them for its own. What finer form of philanthropy can there be than helping to put some brightness and interest into these suffering aid worn-out lives? Is there not a great debt of social grati- tude due to those who will devote time and thought to such labour ? And vet when a comnatic of ladies off->rs to do this work for the town our Board of Guardians says "We will have none of it." As a ratepayer and one who feels deeply the pitifulness of these sad and weary lives whom they are anxious to help, I thank them for their noble attempto.nd trust they will persevere till the permission to do goad, for which they ask, is granted them.— I am, Sze., WM. HAMILTON DRUMMOND. 20, Bold-st., November 19, 1896.

DISTRESSING BURNING FATALITY.—OR Saturday, Mr. Churton held an inquiry at Frodsham Bridge Inn, into the circumstances attending the death of William Henry Ryder, aged three years and nine months, son of John Ryder, labourer. The evidence showed that Mrs. Ryder left deceased and two'other children inf the house at 10.38 on Tuesdiv forenoon./ whilst she went :to a neighbour- ing butch Ar's shop. On returning in five minutes she found her son's clothing on fire. She extinguishfd the flames. after which she and Mrs. Shore applied flour to the injured parts, the arms, neck and shoulders being fearfully burned. A few minutes later P.C. Price applied oil and dressed the wounds. Dr. Burton subse- quently arrived and prescribed what should be done. The little fellow, despite every attention, expired at 8 30 on Thursday morning. It was supposed that the child had climbed upon the fender and fallen into the fire.—A verdict of" Accidental death" was recorded, LECTURE ON THE PILGRIM FATRERS.—A lecture en- titled "The Story of the Pilgrim Fathers" was delivered on Thursday evening last week in the Union Church schoolroom by the Rev. A. H. Sayes. It was illustrated throughout with some fine lime-light views, generously loaned by " The Liberation Society." Mr. J. Moseley.. Williams presided over the gathering, and made some apt remarks anent the subject of religious equality. The lantern was under the able manipulation of Mr. H. Turton. It was unfortunate that the attendance was SO sparse,but all who were present seemed to appreciate this illustrated sketch of the pioneers of religious freedom.

div.head: CATHOLIC PRIEST AND THE SCHOOL OFFICER.
div.p: THE CATHOLIC PRIEST AND THE SCHOOL OFFICER.

This libel case came up for hearing in the Nisi Prius ' Court at Liverpool Assizes, on Tuesday morning befor- Mr. Justice Kennedy,Mr. Shee, Q.C., and Mr. T. F. Mar shall (instructed by Mr. R. Stuart, of Wigan and Newton-le-Willows), representing the plaintiff, John Ball, school attendance officer, of Ne ton-in-Makerfield, while Mr. Pickford, Q.C., and Dr. Sparrow were counsel for the defendant, Father Lennon. Mr. Pickford was pleased to say that an arrangement which had been made would obviate what would have been a long and in some respects a painful case. His client, Father Lennon, was the manager of some Catho- lic schools at Newton-in-Makerfield, and the plaintiff was the attendance officer of the district. Father Lennon, in the course of his duties as acting manager. as he intented for the interest of the school, wrote to the Education Department with regard chiefly to what he considered some defaults on the part of the Educa- tion Committee. In the course of that letter, however, he did use regarding the attendance officer expressions which went beyond what Father Lennon now felt that the circumstances of the case warranted. Under the circumstances, therefore, and notwithstanding the plea of justification upon the record, and though in writing what he did he was not actuated in any viay by personal feeling towards the plaintiff at all,but merely, by the motive of doing the best he could for the school, he felt that the expressions he used went beyond what the circumstances justified. He therefore felt that the straightforward thing was not to avail himself of the defence, and consented to a verdict of, or rather judg- ment for, 40s. and costs. Mr. Shee added that the plaintiff. in bringing the action, had net instructed him to ask for damages ; had he been obliged to open the case he should have been quite content to accept the offer made by Mr, Pickford,the only object in bringing the action being to enable the plaintiff to clear his character. The plaintiff's character had now been cleared in the opinion of all his many friends who were present to speak for him on that occasion,and if there had been any difference be- tween Father Lennon and him it was now ended.
His Lordship accordingly gave judgment for the plaintiff for 403. and costs.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY NT trARLESTOWN.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY NT trARLESTOWN.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

The all-absorbing topic in Earlestown and New- ton this week has been the libel action of Ball v. Lennon, which should have come on for hearing at the Liverpool Assizes on Tuesday. There was great expectation of some tasty disclosures and of some interesting reading in the local papers,but all hopes in this direction have been shattered by the friendly arrangement arrived at before the case was sub- mitted to a jury.

I have known Mr. Ball as School Attendance Officer for many years, and I can safely say that I have never observed any trace of incapacity, either morally or physically. In fact, "John Ball," as he is often spoken of with friendly familiarity, is well known as a most respectable, painstaking, public servant; although like most of. us he has his pecu- liarities, but these peculiarities do not by any means suggest incompetency. If there was any such suggestion I think the District Council could be trusted to deal fail' and impartially with its own servants.

I was pleased to notice that the District Council were successful in securing a couple of convictions against people for allowing nuisances to exist. If people will persist in promoting nuisances, and thus to a certain extent assisting in the propaga- tion of disease, they, of course, deserve to be punished. The Nuisance Inspector will, I am afraid, still find plenty of work to de, but if he has an. ex- ample made of a few more people who are of dirty habits, he will earn the thanks of those who believe that " Cleanliness is next to Godliness."

div.head: EARLESTOWN BAPTD.T CHURCH.
div.p: EARLESTOWN BAPTD.T CHURCH.

Special services in connection with the anniversary of the above place of worship were held in the church on Sunday. There were large congregations at each ser- vice, and excellent sermons were preached morning and evening by the Rev. Charles Williams, of Accrington, ex-president of the Baptist Union. On Monday evening a public tea meeting was held, at which about 125 were present. A public meeting was afterwards held, when addresses were delivered on "The church and tne world." Mr. E lward Mounsey, of Liverpool,presided and he was supported by Mr.J. C. Facie of Liverpool, Rev. J. S. Hughes, Hill Cliffs. Warrington ; and Rev. G. F. Perry, Walton ; and Rev. F. E. Miller, Earlestown. The first address was by Mr. J. C. Farrie, on 'The Church and the Labour Question." He said with re- gard to the relationship between capital and labour that the church had to do with these questions just as she had to do with any and every question which affected the wellbeing of mankind. Had the church to step ia and say that so many shillings per week must be paid, and that so many hours Der day must be worked, and masters must pay no less ? It would mak!, a very sad in istake if it stepped in and interfered in this way, as it had no scriptural warrant for it. There was another gospel brought up, a cold, hard, selfish, grasping law, which was that all the questions should be settled by the law of simply and demand. According to this gos- pel, human flesh and blood were no more than so much flesh and iron to be bought at its cheapest. If there be in our social system anything that keeps down the poor, anything that compelled men to work for unfair wages, which would not afford even a fair measure of the bare necessaries of life, he would say then it was the bounden duty of the Christian Church to work and pray, to teat and try and search until by God's grace these conditions were overcome. (Applause.) The next address was by the Rey. J. S. Hughes, on "The Church and Education." He riaid that early in the year we were all startled at the introduction of a Bill in Parliament which threatened a revolution in our educational system,a bill which seemed to many framed to destroy unsisctarian schools, and to be a blow in- directly aimed at the free churches of our land. Same of the people thought at the time that if this bill was only carried into law it would eventually succeed in sweeping the free churches clean out of the country. He I had no doubt that with many people, the wish was father to the thought ; but notwithstanding the great effort which was put forth on that occasi in they had survived as members of the free churches. The injustice of the bill forced them to gather their forces together. I and roused their latent powers, so that their united I forces succeeded in vanquishing the bill and it dis- appeared in a most extraordinary manner. But it ap- peared another bill was to be introduced. The Sectarian and the church p•ir. y were making another strenuous effort and were m sking certain demands which in some respects were more reasonable than they wire some months ago. They had learned by experience, but the fact that they were more reasonable made them more dangerous to them, for they were more likely to succeed because of their plausibleness. The money that was asked for was not required so much for increasing the efficiency of the schools as for pro- moting. the sectarian propaganda, and the Nonconform- ists objected to the money being granted for that pur- pose. What was their duty as members of a free church ? Their first duty was to be on the alert, to be ever watchful. The friends of aectarianiern were in power,and they might steal a march upon the free churchee. They must come to the conclesion that no grant must be made ot!t of the imperial funds to any elementary schools which was net granted to all of them. The efficiency of the church schools must not be gained at the sacrifice of the Board schools. He believed this agitation had arieen through the envy of their church friends at the success of the Board school system. If the Church schools received three-fourths of. their support, surely the people who paid towards the imperial funds should have some say in the management of these schools,and that these schools should be open to all the people of the nation. (Applause.) An address on "The Church and Recreation " was given by the Rev. C. F. Parry, of Walton. . During the evening selections of vocal and instrumen- tal music was given by the choir and Mr. J. Isherwood. On Tueseay evening a special service was held, when a powerful discourse was preached by the Rev. John Thomas, M.A., of Myrtle-street Chapel, Liverpool.

div.head: TRIAL OF THE ACCUSED AT THE ASSIZES. SENTENCE OF DEATH.
div.p: TRIAL OF THE ACCUSED AT THE ASSIZES. SENTENCE OF DEATH.
- Ppy OUR OWN' RZPORTER -4

James Bate, who resided at 11, Oliver-street, Warrington, was on Thursday and Friday tried in the Crown Court at the Liverpool Assizes, before Mr. Justice Bruce, on a charge of having at War- rington, between the 7th and Bth September, felon- iously, wilfully, and of malice aforethought, killed and murdered his wife, Catherine. The large number of Warrington people who journeyed to Liverpool to witness the trial was an evidence of the great interest taken in the case by people in the town. By half-past ten o'clock the seats allotted to the public were filled, but it was not until a quarter to eleven that a fanfare of trumpets heralded the approach of his lordship. He was accompanied to his seat by the High Sheriff of the County (Sir Peter Carlow Walker), the Under-Sheriff (Mr. Greenall, of Warrington), Archdeacon Diggle. and his Lordship's private Secretary. Prior to proceed- ing with the charge against Bite his Lordship delivered two deferred judgments. The first was that in the case of a gentlemanly-looking man, named Arthur Rowe, a commission agent, who had pleaded guilty to forging acceptances of bills of exchange. Whilst his Lordship was delivering judgment the prisoner trembled like an aspen leaf, and when four years penal servitude was pronounced he fell in a swoon and had to be carried to the cells 'below by the warders. When James Bate stepped into the box, he did not seem to be any the worse for his incarceration in Walton gaol since the Police Court proceedings. On the contrary he seemed to have grown a little stouter, and his face had under- gone some change in consequence of his having allowed his beard to grow. Mr. Collingwood Elope and Mr. Lancelot Sanderson (instructed by Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, Town Clerk of Warrington) prose- cuted on behalf of the Crown,and Mr. McKeand and Mr. McKeever (instructed by Mr. W. It J. Jenkins) defended. On being charged by the Clerk of Assize, Bate pleaded " not guilty" in a firm voice. The jury, as selected, was not challenged. His counsel ' then asked his Lordship to order all witnesses out of court. This request was acceded to, and Mr. Collingwood Hope opened the case for the prosecu- tion. He stated the facts of the case in a masterly manner, and at the conclusion pointed out the duty of the jury. The most important witness for the prosecution was the prisoner's little daughter ' "Maggie," twelve years of age. She was lifted oil the bench near his lordship, and close to the jury box, in order that the jury might be the better able to hear her statement. The sight of the little girl facing her father,and giving evidence on which per- haps his life or death depended was a pitiable one in theaextreme.As she gave her statement of what took place on the night of that memorable September 7th, the prisoner on several occasions was to be seen I wiping away tears which coursed down his cheeks. The position of the girl seemed to effect her,too.fcr she was not so clear in her statement, as on previ- ous occasions, and failed to answer some of the questions put to her by Mr. Mcßeand and his Lordship. The former drew attention to the fact that in her evidence the girl had made several statements which were not made before the magis- trates. Mr. Collingwood Elope brushed that objec- tion away by explaining that certain statements made before the Coroner were ruled inadraissable before the magistrates. The girl's evidence and cross-examination which was the staple element in the ease,occupied the greater portion of the morn- ing,and she seemed glad when it was over. We learn from Mr. Taylor,Police Court Missionary, that Iduring the progress of the trial,a respectable work- ingman in Liverpool offered to adopt the girl. The only new witnesses introduced by the presecution were Mr. and Mrs. Clancy,residing next door to the prisoner's huuse,who spoke of what they heard tak- ing place on the night in question. As the after- noon advanced it became apparent that it would bedimpossible to finish the case that day. Him Lord- ship shortly before four o'clock addressed the jury and stated that there was a very slender prospect of finishing the case that evening. He therefore thought it would be necessary to adjourn, a little after five o'clock,until the following morning. The Sheriff would make arrangements for the comfort of the jury, and if they desired to send messages home,the earlier they did so th 3 better. He would allow a short interval to allow the jury to send messages to their homes. This having been done, the hearing was proceeded with and continued un- til about 5.30 when an adjournment was made. Amongst the better known Warrington inhabitants present were Alderman Francomb,J.P., C.C., Mrs. H. Greenall, Mr. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk), Mr. L. anley Wilson (deputy town clerk), Councillor Wilkieson, Councillor Grace, and Mr. Luke Talbot (chief constable).
FRIDAY'S PROCEEDINGS. The proceedings were resumed yestterday before Mr Juatico Bruce.

Dr. Starkey Smith again entered he witnese b ox, and was cross-examined by Mr. McKeever. In reply to the counsel's questions, he said he heard a few particulars of the case before he made the post-mortem examination. Inspector Spinks told him that the woman and her hus- band ha o had a quarrel in their room. He made the post-mortem examination with an unbiassed mind. He had net been told since the post-mortem examination that the woman had several falls. The post-mortem examination occupied him three hours. There was no appearance in the body to lead him to believe that the deceased had suffered from Bright's disease. The microscope was not employed. All the ventricles of the heart were empty. The clot of blood was in the centre of the medulla oblongata. The liver was enlarged, which he thought was due to the drunken habits of the woman. He knew of cases of cerebral licernerrhage occurring after 33 years of age. There were constitutional and temporary causes of cerebral hcens- orrhage. Excessive drinking might lead to the conjes- tion or clogging of the bloodveseels,but he could not ay that it would :Muse cerebral hcemorrhage. Excitement alone might cause cerebral hcemorrhage if the arteries were dieeased. The cause of death in this case was an effusion of bl od on the brain A clot couid not be formed on the brain without a rupture of the walls of the blood- vessel. They examined carefully but could not find an rupture. He could not name the time it would take to form a clot of blood the size of half-a-walnut which he found.—Questioned by His Lordship, he said he was of the opinion that the clot was formed within an hour. It might take months or years to form a clot of that description.—ln answer to Mr. McKeever he said there would not have bean any difference in the appear- ance of the clot if it had been accumulating for some time, but in his opinion the woman could not have lived with the clot in the position he found it. It was the pressure of the clot on the medulla that caused death.— In answer to his Lerdship,he said he did not think there was anything to guide them by the appearance of the clot as to how long it had taken to accumulate.— Answering Mr. Mekeand he said there might have been intermittent hcemorrhage. If the blood vessel had been ruptured by a blow he would not expect to find that the softer mater had been lacerated. It was a fact that a person suffering from cerebral hoemorrha.ge reeled and staggered like a drunken man. It was difficult to distinguish whether a perms was suffering from cerebral hcemorrhage or from the results of drink. He also thought it was very difficult to say whether the clot was the cause of the woman falling or whether the clot was the resalt of a fall. There were abrasions, but the skin was net breken. A direct kick with the boots (produced) with the tips r retruding in front would be likely to cut the skin. Running kicks would be likely to cut the skin if they were administered straight.—Re- examined by Mr. Collinewood Hope witness said he was a bachelor of medicine in London, and a fellow of the Royal College of Surgeons of Englend. He had bean consulting surgeon for the Warrington Infirmary fir a number ef years, and had practised in Werrington for some thirty years. He found no trace of Briehtle disease There was nothing extraordinary in a rupture of the brain withwut a laceration. In his opinion a blow on the ferehead was the cause of the effusion of blood on the brain,and he did not think it could have been caused by a fall.—ln anewer to his Lor -Milo, he said the ap- pearance of the wound on the forehead had not the appearance of a fall downstairs. There was'nothing to , load him to the opinion in the condition of the woman that there wee anything else than a blow to account for her death.—Further examined by Mr. McKeever,witness said that cerehrel hcemorrhsge sometimes took place without any external marks of violence being visible.

The witness then left the tiox,after having beon cross- examined for about one hour and three-quarteri. Dr. Bowden said that fnr some years he was senior house surgeon at the Warrington Infirmary. Since then he had had private practice. He was a member of the Royal Collets of Surgeona. He made a post-mortem ex- amination of the body on September 9th, together with Dr. Starkey Smith. The not 14 were taken by Inspector Spinks at their dictation. Speaking generally he agreed on the whole with the observations of Dr Scarkev Smith. There c as a large eontusion on the forehead. After the Fcalp had been removed, he found an extra,vasation of blool. The tissues were pulpous. the cause of death was Ole pressure of a clot of blood on the brain,and that had been formed as the result of the contusion on the forehead. The nose was bruised and flattened. There was nothinc in the internal organs of the body to ac- count for death,—Cross-e,Amined by Mr. McKeever he

admitted that he gaid at the Police Court that the injury to the deceased's forehead might have been caused by a violent fall on setts. The witness was then cross-ex? amined at length on the same line as Dr. Starkey Smith, and in the main gave answers similar to those of Dr. Smith.

During, the examination of this witness, the Clerk of kssizes announced that no further case would be taken that day, and the jurymen its other cases were therefore at liberty for that day. 1 Mr. McKeever continued his cross-examination and the witness, in alluding to the question of cerebral hcemorritaire, said that unless one knew the facts of the case it was impossible to tell whether the seizure of cere- bral in:en:lord:lag° or a fall came first. There was no discolouration on the woman's back caused by till% stamping of the boots. He would expect to see discol- ouration if there was stamping on the body over the liver.--Re-examined by Mr. Colliagw od Hope, he said there was a contusion on the left hip at ite back, which might have been caused by a stamp of is boots pro- duced. Assuming that a kick was given in he stomach shertly before death, he would not be surprised to find disentouratien. It would not be possible for the prisoner to give a kick with the boots, without an abrasion of the skin. Oae fall would not be sufficient to cause the injuries he found. Supposing the injuries were the result of a series of falls about 10.30 p.m. he would not expect the deceased woman to be talking the same night at 11.30.
---,rite Court then adjoutned for luncheon, the case;for the Prosecution being finished.

THE DLFENCE. Mr. McKeever said without opening the defence at large his Lordship thought it proper that he (Mr. McKeever) should indicate the line of defence which the witnesses he intended to call would support. He was going to call four or five witnesses, and they would testity that on the night of the occurrence and before deceased went into her house she was seen in the neigh- bourhood of the house apparently and probably in a state of intoxication, and she had four separate and dis- tinct falls of a severe character. The witnesses would tell them that the deceased fell in Connor's yard whilst dancing with a man named Connor. Subsoquently she west to Mrs. Fearnley's, and fell there, as Mrs.Fearnley had already said. The deceased then went to Stewart's- yard, and there fell oil a heap of setts, and also on be- ingtaken to the corner of Brundrit's shop she there fell again. She was then assisted to her home. F.C. Corbett said he knew the deceased woman. He had known her for twelve or fourteen years. She was a very drunken woman. He remembered that on the 11th April last he saw her (the deceased) in the backyard of 11,01iver-street. She was fighting with her father who had a poker in his hand. He examined her head, and there were marks on the foreherad,nose,and chin,and one on the left side of the throat. He noticed the scar on her forehead when she was dead.—This witness was not cross-examined.

Jane Dawson examined by Mr. Rigby Swift, said she was the wife of E I ward Dawson, residing at 25, Oliver- street. On the 7ch September she saw Mrs. Bate going into Connor's. She first saw her about nine o'clock in the morning and also during the day. She was fetching beer. About 5.30 she heard a noise in Cotiner's yard like as if people were fighting. She west there and saw the deceased woman dancing with a man named Connor. She had had drink. Whilat danc- ing, the diFeased fell down on the floor. Connor pickecTher up. The yard was tiled. When she h +el been picked up she went to the end of the wall in the yard, and staggered.—By Mr. C. Elope : When were you first spoken to with regard to this matter P—After the inquest on the deceased woman.—Who was present ? Mr., Mrs., and Miss Connor and otners.—Were you a friend of the prisoner's mother P—Yes.—Was it at her request that you came here ?—No.—Did you know the police were making enquiries ?—Yes.—Did you think it worth while going b tell them what you saw ?—No. You said she had had drink and was tipsy. Have you seen her worse at any time ?—Yes—Did she make any complaint to you at the time ?—No.—Did you think sha staggered because she had had drink thought it was because she fell.
Dr. Bowden (recalled) was asked by his Lordship whether he saw an old scar on the deceased's head, and replied that he did not see it.

'Mrs. Dawson (recalled at the request of a juryman) was asked by him in what direction the deceased fell. She replied "On the back of her head." Annie Mather, wife of James Mather, labourer, 19, Ofiver•street, said she r.miembered the night of the 7th September last. She (witness), was against Mrs. Fearn- ley's door, and she saw the deceased helplessly drunk. The deceased shortly afterwards fell in the middle of the road and fell with her head against the side of the para- pet. Mrs. Fearnley picked her up and put her against the shutter of the house.—Cross-examined by Mr. C. Hope: She was not at the Coroner's Inquiry or Police Court P—Did you know Mrs. Faarnley gave evid- ence there ?—Yes--Did you hear what her evidence was ?—I read it in a paper.—Did you think it worth while to come forward to give your eviclencel?—l wasn't asked.—She was fairly drunk ?—Yes.—Could she walk upstairs ?—She would require a little help.—Mrs. Fearn- ley said that the &ceased fell on her back ; was that true P—No, she fell on her face.—Why did you not tell the police it was not true ?—I didn't care todo so,—Did you see a mark or bruise on the deceased's face ?—No. —Re-examined by Me. McKeever:The police never asked you to give evidence P—No. Mary Jane Steward, wife of Charles Steward,living at 15, Morris-yard, Silver-sqaare, said she remembered the 7th September. The deceased came to ask her te have a pint of beer. On leaving hr (witness's) house, the deceased fell down outside. Whoa she got up she said "Oh," and then proceeded out of the yard which was paved with long setts. She saw the child " Maggie" next morning, and asked her if it was true that her mammy was dead. She replied" Yes, she was going to the claset and fell downstairs."—Cross-examined by Mr. C. Hope: Did she say anything when she fell P—She said something had tripped her.—Have you seen her fall befere ?—Yds.—But she hasn't been hurt ?—Yes, but not seriously.

Ellen Dicicenson,wife of Nathaniel Dickenson, Forster- street,said that on the 7114 September she was in Win- wick-road between 9.30 and 10 o'clock at night, and she saw the deceased corning in an opposite direction. She was drunk and walked as one intoxicated. When she reached Rrnadrit's shop she fell on some stones. Wit- ness picked her up,o,nel she put her hand to her head and said "Oh Christ,my bleeding head." Se walked away with great difficulty, and was talking about titer head. Witness led her to Brundritt's shop, and afterwaris up Ohyer-st—Cross-,xamined by Mr. C. Hop., she said she was unaware of the inquest—Did you tell anyone about it P—l told a neighbour and my husband about it a week afterwards.—Why did you keep it to yourself for a week ?—I waq afraid; I did not know what my husband would say.—When she referred to her bleeding head did you think it referred to blood or was sho swearing P—l didn't notice her head ; I thought she was swearing.— How did she walk ?—She could hardly d) so. How did she fall ?—Sile fell on the back of her head, and it sounded on the floor. _ _ _

This was all the evidence for the defence. His Lordship said he wished to recall Dr. Bowden again. He Asked him whether, supposing the deceased had fallen on the back of her head as described by the last witness, that would be liable to cause cerebral hemorrhage. In reply, Dr. Bowden said he thought such a fall might cause cerebral hemorrhage, without leaving external marks, considering there was a fair amount of hair on the head when the fall took place. But the fall must have been fearful. His Lordship : If the women were beaten after the fall, would it be likely to accelerate death P—Certainly. Mr. McKeever then addressed the jury for the &fence. He s .id there was a well-known and broad distinction between trials on the criminal side and on the civil side in the war the evidence was weighed. lu a case that had been tried in the civil matt the rule was that the jury were directed to weigh the probabilities of the evidence on both sides for and against. But in the Crewn court where a man's liberty—much more when a man's life was at stake—the rule was net weighing and balancing of probability of one side or the other but it was that the case must be proved in such a way that no reasonable man could doubt or reject the con- clusion that the prisoneewas guilty. He ventured to ex- press the opinion that even if this were a civil trial,and if they were only called upon to weigh the evidence and - the probabilities hetween one side and the other, they would come to the conclusion that the weight of preba- bility was in favour of the defendant, and net for the prosecution. Let theni consider first of all,the case which the prosecution had to bring to find the prisoner Let them consider the evidence upon which they were trying tc prove the charge that the man was guilty of the wilful murder of his wife Considering the state of the ease before Inspector Soinks came upon the scene, and picking up the case oa Tuesday morning, the Bth of September, the little girl said that her mother had fallen downstairs. That was the state of the evidence then. Mrs. Wheelan was waiting until the little girl could be induced to change her story. There was no other eye- witness who could prove the case except the little girl, The little girl was seen, and certain things took place. and then the story crystallized itself into the state they had it now. Let them consider the evidence of the little girl. She was of tender years,and could be easily moulded by people who had an Influence over her. The jury saw how she gave her evidence. They would see that she was prepared to say e.verythiee that went against her father, and nothing for him. That was her frame of mind in that Court,but it was not her frame of mind on the morning after the murder. When cross-examined by his learned friend, Mr. McKeand, the girl was pre- pared to admit any absurd question put to her so long as it was against her father. What had changed her mind since the Bth September ? They did not know,but they could guess something. The child admitted that Mrs. Wheelan had seen her alone on the day after the alleged mnrclor. The learned counsel then proceeded to the threats hetd out to the little girl about her mother haunting her. Mrs. Wheelan appeared to have , laid herself out as the procure's of evidence for Inspector Spine'. Then after the girl had given her evidence in the l'elice Court, and had been sent to a home, why did an officer go to Liverpool to interview the child. There might be some good explanations but he thought it was a reasonable and fair suggestion to make when be said that the officer went in order to refresh her memory. Referring to the evidence of Mrs.

Wheelan he pointed out the contradiction which was mado between her evidence and the girl's with respect to the interview site had,aed the denial of Mrs. Wheelan that she used the words to the girl which the girl had given in evidence. How were the jury to make a selec- tion ? If the child were telling the truth, then Mrs. Wheelan was not, and he urged the jury to exclude everything said by the girl or Mrs. Wheelan. With re- gard to Mrs. Shaw's evidence they must remember that she was the daughter of Mrs.Wheelan.They must also re- member with regard to the evidence of Mr. and Mrs. Glances, that those witnesses were never brought before the Coroner or before the magistrates, although they lived next door to B ites, and in the house where Inspec- tor Spinks' plans were made showing the thinness of the walls and all the rest of it. It mig it be true that both heard a noise,but he submitted that it was not true that it occurred on the night of the 7th September, but at some other time. Then was the mother of the deceased a reliable witness ? It would be impossible for him to go through the mass of discrepancies and contradictions whieh there were between various witnesses in this case, but Mrs. Kelly contradicted Mrs. Wheelan, in several particulars, and how were they to get at the truth ? Mrs. Fearnley was in some respects a witness for the de- fence, though she was contradicted by Annie Mather in one substantial point. The only point they disagreed upon was whether deceased fell on her back or on her face. He contented that the statement made by the prisoner to Sergeant Cheney disposed of the whole of the evidence which had been brought by the prosecu- tion. Referring to the evidence of Dr. Starkey Smith, the learned counsel said that that gentleman had made it after having been told the story of the prosecution by Inspector Spinks, and there was nothing then said of falls, which there was evidence had taken place. He contended that the post-mortem examination was a meagre and unreliable see as there was no test for Bright's disease which would give a tendency to cerebral hcemerrhage. By the doctors' evidence it was impossible to say which came first, the licernorrhage or the fall. Both (lectors admitted that external violence might sat up haemorrhage without leaving any external mark whatever. Could they come to the conclusion that one of many falls had not set up internal bleeding? The prosecution had said that the beemorrhage was caused inside the house. That rested upon the evidence of Mar- garet Bate. Let them look at the absurdity of it. Here they had evidence of a woman being drunk and that she had falls and there were marks in such situations on the body which might have been caused by falls. Dr.Bowden had admitted that the bruises might have been caused by falls. In conclusion Counsel hbped that the jury would not be carried away by generalities but let the prosecution e newer him fairly and squarely and intelli- gently and if they could do so,thea let the jury do their duty.

Mr. Coßingwood Hope contend,d that he had shown evidence which pointed to the occurrence in the bedroom on the night of September 7,11 as the cause of death. His friend had asked them to put the girl's evidence on one side. Though her evidence was not exactly given in the same words as before the magistrates, there were only one or two deviations. She was but a young child, and yet Mr. McKeand with all his years of experience could not confuse her. It was a wonder she did not break down altogether. Was it right and reasonable to think that the witnesses for the prosegution had made a conspiracy to tell this story? Why should they do so ? Wag it a right, reasonable, and proper way to dispose of the evidence by saying that the witnesses had all leagued together in a conspiracy ? After alluding to the evidence as to what occurred in the back bedroom, he asked what was the object of the prisoner in taking the children to the other room ? Was it not in order that they might not see the work he had effected ? Was it not arie. +t that the children should be with their mother ? Again, when he said to tbe girl" Haven't I been a good dad .y to you ?" was not that an evidence of what was present in the prisoner's mind, and of what he had done ? His conduct the next morn- ing, he submitted, was not that of an innocent man. With regard to the defence, four or five witnesses had spoken to the deceased woman falling. But in each case the deceased was able to walk away, and on only one occasion did she complain. She went home, and was seen to light a candle, and consume some beer. Counsel maintained that the falls had nothing whatever to do with the deceased's .death. The doctors found the organs of the deceased woman healthy, and he contended that there was no reasonable doubt as to the prisoner's guilt. In conclusion he re- ferred to the responsibility of the jury, and asked them to do their duty,

div.head: SUMMING UP.
div.p: THE SUMMING UP.

His Lordship then proceeded to sum up. He said the substantial question for them to decide was whether the prisoner did cause the death of his wife by violence. It was not the business of the prosecution to say whether the prisoner actually intended to kill his wife to sub- stantiate the charge. If the prisoner intended to do serious injury and used his wife roughly, and did not care wh,ther he caused her death or not, he rendered himself liable to the capital charge. Before addressiag himself to what he might call evidence, he thought there was a important piece of circumstantial evidence ; and circumstances did not lie. On the plan there was marked the spot where there was a pool of nlood on the floor of the room, and also the position of the splashes of blood on the wall. They were in an upward direction and near to the place where the woman undoubtedly met her death. The question arose " What caused the spots of blood on the wall ?" That was an important matter. The defence, which had been ably conducted, had been unable to find any explanation as to the spots of blood. The medical evideace was to the effect that if the woman's head had been banged on the floor with violence blood would flew from her nose, and there might be some splashes on the wall. He had listened for some explanation from the defence with regard to those bloodstains, but had not heard any. He thought it would be found difficult to ex- plain that they were there as the result of the deceased's injuries in the street. Those splashes must have been caused inside the room. Proceeding to review the evidence at great length, he referred to the little eirl's position. He said she was in the terrible petition of having to Rive evidence against her father. He could scarcely conceive a girl in a more dreadful position. Speaking of her evidence and the statements she had made,he said it was very unlikely that she could have invented many of the expressions she made use of, as for instance the'remark she said her mother made with reference to giving her father 211. She was also too young to understand some of the remarks she made. He remarked that there was no doubt that the woman was a drunken woman, but that was no justification for treating her with such vio- lence. Concluding, he said the jury had a responsible duty to perform ; they had the prisoner's fate in their hands. If they were satisfied that the prisoner had caused the death of his wife it was their duty to convict, however painful it might be. On the other hand if they were satisfied that he had not done so it was equally their privilege not to convict.

div.head: VERDICT.
div.p: THE VERDICT.

The jury then retired to consider their verdict, and after about a quarter of an hour's deliberation, they returned, and in answer to the question of the Clerk of ASS.Ze the Foreman said " we find the prisoner

It is the unanimous desire of the jury that the prisoner have a very strong recommendation to mercy." (Some sensation). The Clerk of the Assize then asked the prisoner whether he had anything to say why sentence of death should not be passed upon him. The prisoner made no reply, and the Judge then put on the black cap. He afterwards said :"James Bate,after a most careful and lengthened inquiry the jury have come to the conclusion that you have been guilty of the crime of murder. I don't doubt that they have come to a right conclusion. I believe from the evidence it weuld have been 4ifficult to arrive at any other. They have accompanied their vernict with a recommendation to mercy. That pre- rogative of mercy does not rest with me. I can only say I will forward that recommendation to the prope.a quarter. It remains with me to pronounce sentence, it is not my sentence, but the sentence of the law, and to say that you are to be taken from hence to the place from whence you came, 4nd fr An thence to a place Af execution, when you shall be hanged by the neck until you be dead and that your body be buried within the precincts of the prison, in which you were last confined after your conviction, and may the Lord have mercy on your soul." The prisoner who was completely exhausted was Olen taken down below, resting on the arms of two warders. He muttered something on going down the steps, but it was inaudible.

THE GRAYDON GREAT WHEEL AT EARL'S COURT, Lendon, during six months and 29 days has earned the enor- mous sum of £36,314. "Must be coining money at every revolution."—Financial Times. THE GRAYDON GIGANTIC WHEEL AT BLACKPOOL. The Chairman at the statutory meeting stated:—" This undertaking has earned £l5 3s. 10d, per hour during the first few days." THE GRAYDON CASTLE GREAT WHEEL to be ereeted at New Brighton, will exceed in magnitude and novelty anything of the khad hitherto attempted. Spacious and magnificent saloons for refreshments, concerts, and en- tertainments at various stages will afford opportunities for leisurely enjoyment of the expansive view. The site offers a panorama unequalled throughout the wide world for living interest and importance. The vast docks of Liverpool, the ceaseless procession of magnificent ocean-going steamers and vessels on the Mersey. the beautiful undulating country as far as the Dee, the distant view of the Welsh hills, and the far-reaching sands on which thousands of visitors are dotted, will be spreai like a map below. OVER ELEVEN MILLION PASSENGERS were carried by the Wallasey Ferry steamers to and from their three piers during the past year (not counting season ticket holders), and on one dew alone nearly 130,010 persons passed through the turnstiles at New Brighton ferry. Thou- sands also arrive by road and railway. NEW BRIGHTON GRAY DON CASTLE. GREAT WHEEL It TOWERS COMPANY, LIMITED. This Company is formed for the purpose of acquiring a li- cence from Lieutenant James Weir Graydon for his inven- tions known as " Graydon's Castle, Wheel, and Towers," far which letters patent have been granted numbered 18,107, of 1893, and 16,927, of 1894, with all future improvements in -connection therewith ; and for erecting and working the same in the town of New Brighton, Cheshire; and for acquiring a site for the same, for the purposes of recreation and amuse- ment. The patents. and Lieutenant Graydon's rights as patentee, have been fully investigated and upheld by the courts of law. The court of appeal (Lord Justice Lindley, Lord Justice Lopes, and Lord Justice Rigby), declared that the defendant who ha I infringed the patents wasnot entitled to construct any such Gigantic Wheel, excepting under an agreement with Lieuteltent Graydon. The Company will acquire, on favourable terms, the whole of the valuable freehold property and any foreshore rights lately belonging to the New Brighton Palace Limited, and occupying a most conspicuous and eligible site of about three acres facing the sea. The exteesive and substantial buildings include a large and handsome central pavilion, tea gardens, theatre, aviaries, monkey house, bicycle instruction track, &c.. all of which, in addition to numerous shops and premises yielding handsome rentals, will be re-arranged to earn profits during! construction of the Great Wheel. The electric light installations, furniture and fittings throughout are most com- plete, and togetin r with the whole of the premises have been carefully maintained by the owners in excellent order. An independent valuation has been made on behalf of the Com- pany by Thomas Newby, Esq.. architect, surveyor, and valuer, of 31, Market-street, Manehester, who reports as follows : Tothe directors of New Brighton Graydon Castle Gre at Wheel and Towers Company, Limited. Gentlemen.—According to your instructions I have sur- veyed and valued the land and buildings belonging to the New Brighton Palace Limited, situate at New Brighton, in the county of Chester, and report as follows : The site contains 13,354 square yards. or thereabouts, free from chief rent, and has a frontage to the 6CA of about 201 listed yards. The buildings consist of a large handsome hall, capable of comfortably holding 5,009 persons, and specially adapted for promenade concerts and other entertainments. In close proximity, an . connected by a fine corridor, is a well-appointed theatre fitted up with every requisite. Winter gardens and tea rooms are also entered from the large hall by a severed way. There Is good lavatory accommodation and ample arrangements in various parts for refreshments. The other buildings are " The Grotto," which is artistically arranged and flooded for boating. A very large pavilion which could be adapted for any class of entertainment, and large swimming baths which could ba easily renovated. There are five large shops, with dwelling-houses attached, and ten lock-uo shops, which bring in a rental of £550 per annum ; and other five or six shot s could easily be arranged which would increase the amount by about £75. The situation of the property is unique, haying a full sea frontage opposite to the Rock Liehthouse and Battery, end within a few minutes of both the ferry steamers and the railway station. The land c'ose by is to be laid out as a Marine Park, which will greatly add to the value of this property. Taking into consideration the excellent position of the site and its surroundings and the stability of the buildings, I estimate the vaine of (the same at thirty thousand five hun- dred pounds (230,8 0). (Signed) THOMAS NEWhY. The following is the report of the eminent consulting engineer. J. 14. Tuft. Esq.. M. Inst., C. 14.. of 32, Victoria-st., Westminster, dated November 10, 1891 a To the Directors of the New Bri chton Graydon Castle Great Wheel and Towers Company Limited. Gentlemen —I have had under consideration fur some time the general designs for the above work, which were sub- mitted to me by Ir. J `MPS Weir Gra,- don, and I have con- fidence in stetine there is no engineering difficulty whatever in constructing the proposed structure in complete accord- ance with these drawings. The principal members of the Wheel and the Towers are to be constructed of mild steel, of a quality equal to that em- ployed for the larirest bridges in the country, and ample strength can easily he securrd to carry the loads to which the structure will be subjected, including the wind pressure of the most violent storms that can occur in this vicinity, Thenat 'reef the ground at the site of the propesed atm c- ture is also entirely satisfactory, and in my opinion there will be no trouble experienced in obtaining a perfectly stable foundation. Yours faithfully. J. E. TUIT. THE EARNING POWER OF THE GRAYDON WHEELS. The Earl's Court Great Wheel in six months and 29 days earned the eriormons amount of £311,314 odd.
